five hundred thousand brahmins, holding jeweled bells and chanting auspicious melodies, proceeded in succession;

twenty thousand great elephants, adorned in diverse ways, proceeded in succession; and eighty thousand precious chariots, with their banners, streamers, canopies, and exquisite ornaments, followed as a retinue.
Forty thousand infantrymen, all clad in armor and carrying ceremonial regalia, marched in formation;
furthermore, the most exalted devas of the form realm held hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of precious banners, pennants, and parasols, moving through the air in worship;
likewise, the various devas of the desire realm held hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of precious banners, pennants, and parasols, moving through the air in worship.

Furthermore, there were various devas of the desire realm who adorned the Bodhisattva’s chariot with all kinds of celestial precious ornaments; additionally, twenty thousand celestial maidens served as the Bodhisattva’s charioteers.
At that time, the gods, humans, and celestial maidens proceeded in orderly rows;
the gods felt no resentment and the humans felt no envy, all because of the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
At that time, five hundred Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu each constructed a palace and, with palms joined in reverence, bowed their heads and entreated King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!..."

May all things be accomplished for our benefit; may the God among Gods deign to visit my palace; may the Supreme Guide deign to visit my palace; may the One who Delights in Joy deign to visit my palace; may the One of Excellent Renown deign to visit my palace; may the One with Universal Vision deign to visit my palace; may the Peerless One deign to visit my palace; may the One Adorned with the Marks and Radiant with Merit deign to visit my palace.
Because he was thus praised for the causes and conditions that bring about success, the Bodhisattva was named Sarvārthasiddha.

Thereupon, King Śuddhodana, out of compassion for the feelings of the Śākyas, led the Bodhisattva into the palaces of the Śākyas; after four months had passed, having visited them all, he then brought the Bodhisattva back to his own palace.
Within his own palace there was a great hall named Ratnavyūha.

Once the Bodhisattva had entered that hall, King Śuddhodana summoned his kinsmen, elders of noble virtue, and all those related by marriage to the kingdom, and when they had all assembled, he addressed them, saying:
"My son is but an infant and lost his mother early; to whom now should the task of nursing him be entrusted?"
Who can protect me like a shadow so that I may survive?
Who can look upon me with a compassionate heart?
Who can nourish and raise me until I gradually grow to maturity?
"Who can take pity on and cherish him as if he were their own son?
At that time, five hundred wives of the Śākyas came forward and said to the king,
"We can nourish and raise the King's crown prince."
The elders of the Śākya clan all spoke thus:
"You youths are full of vigor and your minds are arrogant; you are not fit to nurture the Prince according to the proper seasons.
Mahāprajāpatī, who is his maternal aunt by kinship, possesses both compassion and kindness; she alone is capable of nurturing him."
All these Śākyas then reached a consensus and requested Mahāprajāpatī to serve as the foster mother.
At that time, King Śuddhodana personally took up the Bodhisattva in his arms, entrusted him to his maternal aunt, and said to her:
"Welcome, Lady!"
"You shall be his mother.

Having received the king's command, Mahāprajāpatī appointed thirty-two foster mothers to nurture him: eight to carry him, eight to suckle him, eight to bathe him, and eight to play with him, thus raising the Bodhisattva.
It is like the moon during the bright fortnight, from the first day until the fifteenth day, becoming pure and full; it is also like a nyagrodha tree planted in fertile, rich soil, gradually growing.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, King Śuddhodana again gathered with the Śākyas to deliberate:
'Should this crown prince become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin)?"
"Will he renounce the world to attain the Way of the Buddha?

At that time, there was a seer with the five supernatural powers named Asita, who lived with the youth Nāla of the maternal clan on Mount Himavat. He saw the immeasurable and extraordinary omens at the birth of the Bodhisattva and heard the various devas in the void proclaiming:
"A Buddha has appeared in the world."

Furthermore, he saw various kinds of fragrant flowers and various kinds of garments raining from the sky, while humans and devas came and went, leaping for joy. He then used his divine eye to observe everywhere and saw the prince of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu, whose merit and radiance illuminated the world and who had perfected the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Having seen this, he addressed the youth Nāla, saying: "You should know!

Within the city of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa, the prince of King Śuddhodana possesses the radiance of merit that shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions; he is a great treasure, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks."

If he remains a householder, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, possessing the seven treasures and a full thousand sons; he shall govern the entire earth as far as the ocean's edge, leading beings through the Dharma and subduing them naturally without recourse to weapons.

If he leaves the household life, he shall attain Buddhahood through his own awakening rather than by another, becoming a Teacher of Gods and Humans, whose fame shall be universally heard and who shall benefit all beings.
"I shall now go with you to pay my respects.

Then the seer Asita and the youth Nāla, like a king of geese soaring through the sky, withdrew their supernormal power and entered the royal city on foot. Arriving at King Śuddhodana’s palace, they stood at the gate and addressed the gatekeeper:
"You may go in and announce that Asita has come to visit the King."
Then the gatekeeper went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King! There is a seer at the gate named Asita; he wishes to have an audience with Your Majesty."
Having heard this, the king swept and cleansed the palace, arranged an exquisite seat, and led the seer inside.
Once the seer had arrived, he offered a blessing to the king, saying:
"May you be auspicious and noble; may your lifespan increase, and may you rule as a king according to the Dharma."
At that time, the king made offerings of various kinds of incense and flowers to the seer and invited him to take his seat.
Once the seer was seated, the king said:
"Great Seer!..."
"I have constantly thought of paying you homage, yet my wish has not been fulfilled; I do not know from where you have come now.
The seer said, "Great King!..."
"I have heard that you have a noble son, and I wish to see him; that is why I have come here.
The king said, "My son has just fallen asleep; please wait a moment."
The seer said:
"A true person of such caliber is awakened by their very nature; fundamentally, they have no sleep.
"Bhikṣus, you should know this!"
At that time, because the Bodhisattva was mindful of the rishi, he awoke from his sleep.

The king took him up in his arms and presented him to the rishi; the rishi knelt and received him, examining him thoroughly. He beheld the Bodhisattva’s body, complete with the primary and secondary marks, surpassing Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the four world-protecting kings, its radiance outshining a hundred thousand suns.
Having seen this, they immediately rose, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated themselves, and praised him in various ways, exclaiming that it was unprecedented:
"A Great Being has appeared in the world!"
Circumambulating him three times to the right, he cradled the Bodhisattva and thought to himself:

"Now a Buddha shall appear in the world; I regret that in my old age I have not encountered the Tathāgata, remaining forever in the long night of ignorance and constantly deluded regarding the True Dharma."
Thereupon, he wept with grief and distress, sobbing and choking with emotion.

When King Śuddhodana saw the seer Asita so overcome with sorrow that he could not restrain himself, the king, his maternal aunt, and all their attendants wept as well. They addressed the seer, saying:
"When our son was first born, we summoned physiognomists to divine whether his fate was auspicious; they were all filled with great joy, regarding it as most extraordinary."
"Now that the Great Sage weeps thus with compassion, none among us, his kinsmen, are without doubt; we pray that you will explain for us the matter of good or ill fortune.
Then the Rishi Asita wiped away his tears and said:
"I only wish that the Great King would not harbor anxiety."
I now lament with no other feeling than this: I am grieved that in my old age, the time of death is approaching, yet I have not heard the True Dharma nor beheld the appearance of a Buddha.

Great King, you should know that immeasurable sentient beings are being scorched and harmed by the fires of affliction; the Buddha is able to sprinkle upon them the rain of the nectar-like Dharma to extinguish them.
Immeasurable sentient beings wander through the wilderness of false views; the Buddha is able to show them the pure path to Nirvana.
Immeasurable sentient beings are bound within the prison of afflictions; the Buddha shall be able to grant them clemency so that they may attain liberation.
Immeasurable sentient beings are shut in by birth and death and cannot emerge on their own; the Buddha shall be able to open for them the gate of skillful means.
Immeasurable sentient beings are pierced and wounded by the arrows of affliction; the Buddha shall be able to extract them, causing them to escape this suffering.
"Great King!
Just as the udumbara flower appears only once in a great while, so too do the Tathāgatas appear in the world.
What I regret now is not having seen this occasion; it is because I consider myself deprived of such protection that I grieve."
"Great King!

If a person encounters the Buddha seated upon the Bodhi throne, subduing the hosts of Māra and turning the Wheel of Dharma, you should know that such a person will certainly attain the supreme fruit."
"Great King!
There were immeasurable sentient beings who, encountering the Buddha’s appearance in the world, upheld the True Teaching and attained arhatship.
I regret that at that time I was not included among those matters; for this reason, I grieve."
"Great King!
As recorded in the Vedas, a king’s crown prince will certainly not become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin). Why is this?"
"Because the thirty-two marks of a great man are extremely distinct.
The king asked,
"What are the names of these thirty-two marks?"
The seer said:
"As for the thirty-two marks:
the first is that there is a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon the crown of the head."
Second, his hair is coiled like a conch shell, curling to the right and deep blue-black in color.
Third, his forehead is broad, even, and well-proportioned.
Fourth, between his eyebrows is a tuft of white hair (ūrṇā-kośa) as bright as white jade or snow.
Fifth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
Sixth, his eyes are a deep azure-blue.
Seventh, he has forty teeth that are even, brilliant, and pure.
Eighth, his teeth are closely set without gaps.
Ninth, his teeth are white like the *muṇḍa* flower.
Tenth, he possesses the Brahma-voice.
11. Among tastes, he obtains the supreme taste.
12. His tongue is soft and thin.
13. His cheeks are like those of a lion.
14. His two shoulders are perfectly rounded.
15. His body measures seven cubits in height.
16. His chest is like that of a lion king.
Seventeenth, his four canine teeth are brilliant white.
Eighteenth, his skin and body are soft, smooth, and the color of purple-gold (*cāmpeya*).
Nineteenth, his body is perfectly upright.
20. His hands hang down below his knees.
21. His body is perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree.
22. A single hair grows from each and every pore.
Twenty-three: The body hairs curl to the right and point upward.
Twenty-four: The male organ is concealed within a sheath.
Twenty-five: The thighs are rounded and long.
Twenty-six: His calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer.
Twenty-seven: His heels are well-rounded and his toes are slender and long.
Twenty-eight: His insteps are high and prominent.
29. His hands and feet are soft, supple, and smooth.
30. His fingers and toes are all webbed. 31.
On the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet, there are wheel-marks with hubs and rims complete, possessing a thousand spokes and radiating brilliant light.
Thirty-second: The soles of his feet are flat, even, and rest entirely upon the ground.
Great King!
Your noble son possesses these thirty-two marks of a Great Man, distinct and clearly manifest. Such marks belong only to Buddhas; they do not belong to a Wheel-Turning King.
"O Great King, Noble Son!

Furthermore, there are eighty secondary marks; these do not accord with remaining a householder to become a Wheel-Turning King, but rather indicate that you will certainly leave the household life and attain the path of Buddhahood."
The King said: "Great Seer!
What are those known as the eighty secondary marks?"
The seer said:
"As for the eighty minor marks:
first, the nails of both hands and feet are all high and prominent."
Second, his fingernails are like red copper.
Third, his fingernails are glossy and lustrous.
Fourth, the lines on his palms are glossy and lustrous.
Fifth, the lines on his palms are deep.
Sixth, the lines on his palms are distinct and prominent.
Seventh, the lines on his palms are straight and fine.
Eighth, his hands and feet are not bent.
Ninth, his fingers are slender and long.
Tenth, his fingers are perfectly rounded.
Eleventh, the tips of his fingers gradually taper.
Twelfth, his fingers do not bend inward.
Thirteenth, his sinews and veins are not prominent.
14. The ankles do not protrude.
15. The soles of the feet are level.
16. The heels are full and well-rounded.
Seventeenth, the color of his lips is beautiful and red like the *bimba* fruit.
Eighteenth, his voice is not coarse or harsh.
Nineteenth, his tongue is soft and its color is like that of red copper.
20. His voice is like the sound of thunder—clear, resonant, and elegant.
21. His sense faculties are fully developed.
22. His arms are slender and long.
23. His body is pure, refined, and beautiful.
24. His body is soft and supple.
25. His body is level and upright.
Twenty-sixth, his body is free from deficiency.
Twenty-seventh, his body is gradually slender and straight.
Twenty-eighth, his body is steady and unwavering.
29. His body parts are well-proportioned.
30. His kneecaps are perfectly rounded.
31. His body is light and exquisite.
Thirty-two: His body emits radiance. Thirty-three:
His body is free from crookedness or curvature.
Thirty-four: His navel is deep.
35. The navel is not off-center.
36. The navel is symmetrical in its position.
37. The navel is pure and clear.
38. His body is upright and majestic. 39.
His body is utterly pure, emitting light everywhere that dispels all darkness.
40. His gait is like that of an elephant king.
41. His gait is like that of a lion king.
42. He walks like a bull king. 43. He walks like a swan king.
44. His gait is clockwise.
45. His abdomen is full. 46. His abdomen is exquisite.
47. The abdomen is not crooked. 48.
The features of the abdomen are not prominent.
49. The body is free of moles.
Fifty: his canine teeth are round and straight. Fifty-one:
his teeth are white, even, and closely set.
Fifty-two: his four canine teeth are equal in size.
53. His nose is high, well-formed, and straight.
54. His two eyes are bright and pure.
55. His eyes are free from impurities.
56. His eyes are beautiful.
57. His eyes are long and wide.
58. His eyes are upright and well-proportioned.
Fifty-nine: His eyes are like blue lotuses.
Sixty: His eyebrows are fine and long.
Sixty-one: All who see him give rise to joy.
62. The color of his eyebrows is deep blue-black.
63. The tips of his eyebrows gradually taper to a fine point.
64. The two eyebrows meet slightly at their inner ends.
65. His cheeks are full and rounded.
66. His cheeks are without deficiency.
67. His cheeks are free from blemish.
Sixty-eight: His body is free from deficiency and beyond reproach.
Sixty-nine: His sense faculties are serene and tranquil.
Seventy: The tuft of hair between his eyebrows is brilliant white and pure.
Seventy-one: His forehead is broad and even.
Seventy-two: The crown of his head is perfectly rounded.
Seventy-three: His hair is beautiful and black.
Seventy-fourth, his hair is fine and soft.
Seventy-fifth, his hair is not disheveled.
Seventy-sixth, his hair is fragrant and pure.
Seventy-seventh: His hair is lustrous and moist.
Seventy-eighth: His hair bears five *svastika* marks.
Seventy-ninth: His hair is colored and curls in spirals.
Eightieth: His hair possesses the mark of the *nanda* and *vakra-keśa* (curling) like the *makara* fish.
Great King!

These are the eighty secondary marks of the Noble Son. If a person is endowed with these eighty secondary marks, they should not remain at home; they will certainly leave the household life and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When King Śuddhodana had heard these words from the seer Asita, his body and mind became serene; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet, and spoke this verse:
“You are one whom Śakra and all the devas Reverently bow their heads in homage;
You are one whom all the ṛṣis and celestial beings Have come to honor and revere.”
"You are a shrine and temple for all the world; therefore, I prostrate before you, Sovereign King. "O Bhikṣus!
King Śuddhodana provided Aśita the Rishi and the youth Nāla with various kinds of food and drink, as well as exquisite garments, and after circumambulating them to the right, he prostrated himself."
Then the seer Asita placed his hand upon the left shoulder of the youth Nāla and departed through the air.
At that time, the seer said to the youth:
"Before long, a Buddha will appear in the world; you should go to him and request to leave the household life, for this will bring you great benefit throughout the long night."
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: Entering the Temples of the Gods At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“After the Bodhisattva was born, twenty thousand young maidens from the families of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, elders, and the wealthy were all designated as the Bodhisattva’s court ladies. The king and his ministers likewise each had twenty thousand young maidens designated as the Bodhisattva’s court ladies; all these women were born on the same day as the Bodhisattva.”
At that time, the elders of the Śākya clan went to King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"Great King!
You should now take the Prince to visit the celestial temple to pray for ultimate auspiciousness."

The King then granted his permission and immediately dispatched the relevant officials to cleanse all the city walls, marketplaces, streets, and alleys. All those with impaired faculties—such as the blind, the deaf, and the mute—as well as all inauspicious things like rubble, filth, and excrement, were completely removed and cleared away. The drum of merit was struck, the gong of auspicious signs was tapped, and all the gates through which they would pass were adorned with elaborate decorations.

Furthermore, various kings, elders, householders, and brahmins gathered together at the appointed time; they were accompanied by countless court ladies and a retinue of chariots and cavalry. All the auspicious jars were filled to the brim with fragrant oils and scented water. Sons of brahmins lined the roads, chanting auspicious verses, and all the celestial shrines and temples were magnificently adorned. In this manner, every such matter was fully prepared.
At that time, King Śuddhodana entered the inner palace and said to Mahāprajāpatī,
"I wish to take the Prince to the celestial temple.
He also commanded the palace attendants that they must all prepare themselves with full adornment.
Mahāprajāpatī adorned the Bodhisattva with various precious garments; at that time, the Bodhisattva smiled with a joyful countenance and spoke these words:
"Where are you now taking me?"
The maternal aunt replied,
"I am taking the Prince out to pay his respects at the celestial temple.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
"From the moment of my birth, the three-thousandfold world system shook;
the sun and moon, the World-Protectors, Brahmā, Śakra, and all the devas, nāgas, and others,
descended upon Jambudvīpa and came together to prostrate at my feet."
What deity has appeared before me?
Lead me to his abode.
I am the God among Gods, the most supreme among all deities.
In heaven there is none equal to him; who else could possibly surpass him?
It is for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions that he has come to be born here;
seeing my majestic spiritual power, all are filled with joy.
"Therefore, you should know that I alone am the God among Gods.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Thus, as the assembled hosts of the military praised him auspiciously, the city gates and towers were adorned, and all the streets, lanes, marketplaces, and gates were completely purified."

At that time, King Śuddhodana personally escorted the Bodhisattva in a carriage as they departed, accompanied by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, wealthy elders, householders, and great ministers, as well as various kings and the Śākya clan. Attendants followed in front and behind, filling the thoroughfares with burning incense and scattered flowers. There were immeasurable numbers of elephants, horses, carriages, and military hosts, all holding precious banners, streamers, and canopies, performing various kinds of drumming, music, singing, dancing, and theatrical displays. Hundreds of thousands of devas drove the Bodhisattva’s carriage, while immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of devaputras and celestial maidens, from the midst of the sky, scattered various heavenly flowers and played drums, music, and stringed songs.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, possessing such majestic power, proceeded to the temple of the gods.

Having arrived at the temple, the king himself took up the Bodhisattva and entered within; as his feet crossed the threshold, all the divine images rose from their seats to welcome the Bodhisattva, paying him homage with deep reverence.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans within the assembly all laughed with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, crying out:
"Excellent! Excellent!
This is most rare!"
The kingdom of Kapilavastu shook in six ways, and the forms of various devas each manifested their own bodies,
reciting these verses: "A mustard seed compared to Mount Sumeru, A cow’s footprint compared to the vast ocean,
The sun and moon set against a firefly— How could they ever be considered equals?"
I am now like a mustard seed, And further, like the footprint of an ox, Also equal to a firefly; Therefore, I ought to revere them.
The Bodhisattvas are like the sun and moon, And likewise like the vast ocean.
Though he be equal to Mount Sumeru, it is not fitting that you fail to revere me.
Through merit, wisdom, and majestic power, those who pay homage obtain great benefit;
if one abandons arrogance, they shall be born in heaven and realize nirvana.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Bodhisattva manifested his entry into the celestial temple, thirty-two thousand devaputras and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"O Bhikṣus!
For this reason, I at that time consented to enter the celestial temple.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Precious Ornaments. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

At that time, there was a great minister named Udāyin, who was well-versed in astrology and calendrical science. Together with five hundred attendants, when the moon had departed from the constellation Ashvinī and was in conjunction with the constellation Bharaṇī, he came to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"Please have precious ornaments fashioned for the Crown Prince."
The King replied, "Let them be fashioned quickly.

The five hundred Śākya ministers likewise each offered to fashion ornaments for the Bodhisattva, namely: finger-rings and head-ornaments, jeweled necklaces and earrings, jeweled belts and necklaces, jeweled sandals and bells, jeweled chimes and golden nets. Once these various ornaments had been completed, the Puṣya constellation was in conjunction with the moon.
At that time, the Śākya kinsmen took these precious ornaments and went to the king’s presence, each saying:
"Great King!
We have fashioned these ornaments; we pray you present them to the Prince."
The King said, "Wait;
first you all provide various offerings, and I shall now also fashion ornaments for the Prince.
The Śākya kinsmen addressed the King again, saying:
"What we offer is no different from what you have always received;
it is merely our wish that the Prince would allow us each to serve him for seven days.
When morning came, Mahāprajāpatī went to the Stainless Radiance Garden and, having adorned the Bodhisattva with various precious ornaments, she took him in her arms and carried him into the garden.

At that time, eighty-four thousand court ladies came forward to welcome the Bodhisattva; ten thousand young maidens gazed upon him; ten thousand young women of the Śākya clan looked up to him with reverence; and five thousand Brahmins offered praise to him. Such was their heart of longing and admiration that none grew weary of it.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Bhadra, who adorned the Bodhisattva with various crafted ornaments and garments.
At that moment, the radiance of the Bodhisattva’s body eclipsed the luster of all those jewels so completely that they no longer appeared at all, like a mass of ink set against Jāmbūnada gold.
At that time, there was a deity in the garden named Vimala (Stainless). He immediately manifested his form before King Śuddhodana and the Śākya clansmen, and spoke these verses in praise:
"Even if the three thousandfold world system were filled to the brim with pure gold, A single *liǎozhū* (one-tenth of an ounce) of Jambū-river gold would render it colorless by comparison."
Even if Jambūnada gold were to fill the three thousandfold world system,
the light from a single pore of the Bodhisattva would outshine it until it lost its color.
His radiance is most perfectly complete, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits.
Such a pure body— how could it rely on external adornments?
The radiance of the sun, moon, stars, and pearls, and the light of Brahmā, Śakra, and all the devas,
when set against the body of a Bodhisattva, cannot manifest at all.
Arising from the ripening of prior pure karma, his manifold marks adorn him naturally;
he does not require inferior persons to offer him ornaments.
You should set aside what you have offered—these various precious jewels used for adornment.
"You consider yourself beautiful;
however, the Bodhisattva has no desires and requires nothing that is not necessary for a Bodhisattva. You should take this and give it to Chandaka.
Having spoken this verse, the celestial deity suddenly vanished.
The King and all the Śākyas were filled with a sense of profound wonder;
leaping for joy, they exclaimed:
"The Śākya clan shall surely flourish!"

10. Chapter on Displaying the Writing Arts. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "When the Bodhisattva was seven years of age, having prepared hundreds of thousands of auspicious and majestic rites, he was to be conducted to the school.

Ten thousand young boys and ten thousand young girls surrounded and attended him. Ten thousand chariots carried delicacies and various precious objects, which were distributed as alms at every crossroads and marketplace throughout the city of Kapilavastu. Simultaneously, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played together, and a rain of celestial flowers fell from the sky. Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of court ladies, their bodies adorned with necklaces of various jewels."
Some were on the balconies and railings of towers, while others were in the windows and doors of palaces, gazing toward the Bodhisattva and scattering various exquisite flowers from afar.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with ornaments, each holding a precious vase filled with fragrant water, sprinkled it along the path before him.

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others each appeared with half their bodies in the sky, holding flower garlands, necklaces, and precious jewels, which hung suspended above him.
Surrounded by all the Śākyas, they followed King Śuddhodana as he led the Bodhisattva to the schoolhouse.

At that time, as the Bodhisattva was about to ascend into the schoolhouse, the preceptor Viśvāmitra beheld the Bodhisattva approaching with unsurpassed majesty and virtue; realizing himself unfit to be the Bodhisattva’s teacher, he was seized with great shame and fear, and fell to the ground in a faint.
At that time, a son of the Tuṣita heaven named Wondrous Body (Sudarśana) assisted him in rising and settled him upon a seat; then, ascending into the air, he spoke these verses:

"All the various arts and crafts in the world, Which you have practiced throughout immeasurable eons, In order to bring these youths to maturity, You follow worldly custom and ascend to the school hall."
Furthermore, wishing to subdue all sentient beings, To lead them into the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna,
Skillfully understanding causes and conditions and knowing the Four Truths, They are able to extinguish all realms of existence and attain cool serenity.
The God among Gods is most honored; none can surpass him who bestows the nectar of immortality.
Though the mental activities of all sentient beings differ, he is able to know them all within a single thought-moment.
"If one can even awaken to the dharma of quiescent extinction, how much more so should one study the written words?
When the devaputra had spoken this verse, he immediately made offerings of exquisite celestial incense and flowers to the Bodhisattva and suddenly vanished.
At that time, King Śuddhodana commanded the young attendants and the nurses to look after the Bodhisattva, while the King returned to his own palace.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva held in his hand a tablet of heavenly *candana* wood, inscribed with celestial script and adorned with celestial perfumes and luminous *maṇi* gems; he then asked his teacher: "Is there..."
“The Brahmī script, the Kharoṣṭhī script, the Puṣkarasāri script, the Aṅgāra script,
the Mahātti script, the Caṅgu script, the Yavanānī script, the Parśuka script, the Aparāntaka script,
the Drāviḍa script, the Keralaka script, the Dākṣiṇātya script...”
The Na script, the Ugraka script, the Saṃghika script, the Abhamu script, the Anulu script,
the Dāradha script, the Khasa script, the Cīna script, the Huṇa script,
the Madracara script, the Mitraka script, the Puṣya script, the Deva script, and the Na... [script].
The scripts of the gods, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, the mahoragas, the asuras, the garuḍas,
the kiṃnaras, the mṛgās, the mayūs, the vāmanadevas, the antarikṣadevas, and the godānīs.
The script of Uttarakuru, the script of Pūrvavideha, the script of Varṣā, the script of Nivṛtti,
the script of Praṇīta, the script of Sāgara, the script of Vajra, the script of Lekhapratiṣṭhita,
the script of Vibhakti, the script of Anuprabuddha, and the script of Śāśvata.
The scripts of Kṣetraṇa, Mukhapā, Nikhapā, Pāṭalīkhā, Dīrghottaraṇī,
Yāvada, Padasandhi, Mātṛkālīnī, Sarvadharmagaṇakha, and Vasi.
The Vidānuloma script, the Niṣadha script, the Hulucimāna script, the Dhāraṇīpeca script,
the Gaganapilikhita script, the Sarvavakṣatiniścaya script, the Sāgara-saṃgraha script, and the Sarvabhūta-huḥ.
Loutuo asked, "Of the sixty-four scripts mentioned above, which one would you like to teach me?
At that time, Viśvamitra heard what he had never heard before; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he cast aside his pride and spoke in verse:
“How rare is this person of pure and supreme wisdom!
Having already mastered all phenomena himself, he enters the schoolhouse and asks questions from the lowest rank; the name of the writing he speaks of has never been heard before.”
The mark of the invisible crown is most supremely lofty; his countenance is majestic and none can gaze upon it.
His wisdom and spiritual power are foremost; may he instruct and admonish me with skillful means.
Reflecting on my own meager and shallow nature, how could I possibly learn? I have merely heard the name of this scripture, yet its true meaning remains unknown.
This is the Supreme Heaven, the God among Gods; within the world, there is none second to it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At that time, there were ten thousand youths who were together with the Bodhisattva before their teacher. When they studied the alphabet together, as they chanted the letter ‘A,’ the sound of ‘all conditioned phenomena are impermanent’ issued forth;
when they chanted the long vowel ‘Ā,’ the sound of ‘benefiting oneself and benefiting others’ issued forth.”
When pronouncing the syllable *i*, there issues forth the vast sound of all fundamental [mantras];
when pronouncing the syllable *i*, there issues forth the manifold sounds of all diseases in the world;
when pronouncing the high-pitched syllable *u*, there issues forth the sounds of all worldly afflictions and disturbances.
When pronouncing the syllable *u*, there issues forth the sound of the narrow and inferior wisdom of all sentient beings in the world;
when pronouncing the syllable *e*, there issues forth the sound of the various faults and afflictions that are sought after;
when pronouncing the syllable *ai*, there issues forth the sound of supreme dignified conduct.
When pronouncing the syllable *u*, there issues forth the sound: "Death and exposure have flowed across to the other shore.
When pronouncing the syllable *o*, there issues forth the sound: "All are born by transformation.
When pronouncing the syllable *oṃ*, there issues forth the sound: "All things are devoid of self and what belongs to a self."
When pronouncing the syllable *A*, there issues forth the sound that all phenomena are utterly extinguished and vanish;
when pronouncing the syllable *Ka* with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of the entry into and exit from karmic results;
when pronouncing the syllable *Kha*, there issues forth the sound that all phenomena are like empty space.
When pronouncing the syllable *ga* (with the rising tone), there issues forth the sound of entering the profound Dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
when pronouncing the syllable *ga*, there issues forth the sound of eliminating all the dense cataracts of the darkness of ignorance;
when pronouncing the syllable *o*, there issues forth the sound of extinguishing the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) for sentient beings.
When pronouncing the syllable *ca*, there issues forth the sound of contemplating the Four Noble Truths;
when pronouncing the syllable *cha* (with the tone of a carriage), there issues forth the sound of the eternal severance of craving;
when pronouncing the syllable *ja*, there issues forth the sound of crossing to the further shore of all birth and death.
When pronouncing the syllable JA, there issues forth the sound of subduing all hosts of māras;
when pronouncing the syllable NYAṄ, there issues forth the sound of awakening all sentient beings;
when pronouncing the syllable ṬHA with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of forever severing all paths.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, there issues forth the sound "ṭha";
when pronouncing the high-pitched syllable *ṭha*, there issues forth the sound that cuts off all demonic afflictions and disturbances;
when pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, there issues forth the sound that all objective spheres (*viṣaya*) are impure.
When pronouncing the word *na* with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of eternally uprooting subtle afflictions;
when pronouncing the word *ta* with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of the non-differentiation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena;
when pronouncing the word *tha* with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of power and fearlessness.
When pronouncing the syllable *da* (with the rising tone), there issues forth the sound of generosity, ethical discipline, and straightforwardness;
when pronouncing the syllable *ta*, there issues forth the sound of seeking the seven treasures of the noble ones;
when pronouncing the syllable *na* (with the rising tone), there issues forth the sound of universally knowing name-and-form.
When pronouncing the aspirated voiced consonant *ba*, there issues forth the sound of realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
when pronouncing the letter *pha*, there issues forth the sound of attaining the fruit and entering into direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*);
when pronouncing the aspirated voiced consonant *bha*, there issues forth the sound of liberation from all fetters.
When pronouncing the syllable *ba*, there issues forth the sound of severing all existence;
when pronouncing the syllable *ma* with a rising tone, there issues forth the sound of extinguishing all pride;
when pronouncing the syllable *ya*, there issues forth the sound of penetrating all phenomena.
When pronouncing the syllable *ra*, there issues forth the sound of revulsion toward birth and death and delight in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
When pronouncing the syllable *ra* with a high tone, there issues forth the sound of severing all branches of birth and death.
When pronouncing the syllable *va* with a high tone, there issues forth the sound of the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*).
When pronouncing the syllable *śa*, there issues forth the sound of all *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
when pronouncing the aspirated syllable *ṣa*, there issues forth the sound of subduing the six sense bases and attaining the six supernormal powers;
when pronouncing the syllable *sa*, there issues forth the sound of manifesting the realization of all-knowledge.
When pronouncing the syllable *ha*, there issues forth the sound that forever destroys all karma and afflictions;
when pronouncing the syllable *cha*, there issues forth the sound that no words or letters can express regarding all phenomena.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When the Bodhisattva was in the schoolhouse with the other boys, they chanted the alphabet together, producing sounds that manifested immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates. This caused thirty-two thousand boys and thirty-two thousand girls to all resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, he manifested his entry into the schoolhouse.”
Chapter Eleven: Contemplating Agricultural Labor The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“As the Bodhisattva gradually grew up, on one occasion he went out of the city with other Śākya youths to tour the countryside. Upon reaching a garden, he saw various farmers laboring diligently at their tasks.”
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a heart of compassion and lamented that the world endures such suffering!
He then thought: "Where is there a place of seclusion?"
"I shall contemplate the cessation of suffering within that place. Then he saw a Jambu tree in the grove, its branches and leaves lush, verdant, and lovely.

At that time, the Bodhisattva sat cross-legged beneath that tree, free from all sensual desires and evil states; with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, he dwelt in the joy and happiness of the first dhyāna. With internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, through the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, born of concentration, he dwelt in the joy and happiness of the second dhyāna. Free from the feeling of joy, abiding in equanimity as taught by the Noble Ones, mindful and clearly conscious, he experienced the happiness of which the Noble Ones say, "One who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily," and thus he dwelt in the third dhyāna. Having abandoned both pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, he entered the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses pure mindfulness.
At that time, there was an external seer possessing the five supernatural powers who was traveling through the air from south to north;
upon reaching the Jambu tree, he was unable to fly over it and said to his companions, "Why am I now unable to fly over this Jambu tree?"
His heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end as he spoke these verses:
"We were once able to pass over Mount Sumeru and the Vajra Mountains—
such firm and solid mountains— coming and going without any hindrance."
Just as a great elephant, charging through a small forest thicket,
encounters no obstacles therein, so too is this matter. Furthermore,
he has once flown past the palaces of the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
None of these have ever been difficult for me; there is nothing whatsoever that can obstruct me.
By whose power now is my supernormal power so constrained, that within this Jambū forest I linger, unable to pass?
At that time, there was a deity in the forest who spoke in verse, answering:
“The crown prince of King Śuddhodana Is as perfect as the pure moon;
His physical marks are like the sun first rising, And his countenance is like a blooming lotus.”
Beneath the shade of this Jambu tree, he sits upright, contemplating the profound samādhi;
having cultivated virtuous deeds throughout accumulated kalpas, he is thus able to dispel heat and attain coolness.
"By the majestic spiritual power of this Great Being, you shall not be able to pass beyond this.

At that time, having heard these verses, the seers beheld from afar the Bodhisattva’s radiant majesty and his peerless marks and signs of excellence; each gave rise to a sense of rare and extraordinary wonder and all spoke thus:
"Who is this person, whose majestic appearance is such as this?"
Is this Śakra, or one of the Four Heavenly Kings, or the Māra King, or a Dragon King, or Maheśvara, or Viṣṇu, or a Cakravartin Universal Monarch?
Then the various seers praised him with a verse:
“Your physical form surpasses the four world-protectors, Śakra, Brahmā, the sun, the moon, and Maheśvara;
In merit, marks, and signs, none can equal you— Pure and free from defilement, you must be a Buddha.”
At that time, the forest deity replied to the seer in verse:
“Śakra-devānām-indra and the World-Protectors, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
If these were compared to the majestic radiance of a Bodhisattva, They would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.”

At that time, having heard these verses, the various seers descended from the air and approached the Bodhisattva. Seeing that the Bodhisattva had entered a profound meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) with body and mind unmoving, they praised him in verse:
“The fires of affliction in the world— The Honored One is a pool of cool clarity.
With the unsurpassed Dharma, May he cause them to eliminate their feverish distress.”
Furthermore, another seer spoke a verse in praise, saying:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance; The Honored One is the lamp of wisdom.
With the supreme and pure Dharma, May you dispel the darkness for them.”
"Furthermore, there was another seer who spoke a verse in praise, saying:
'The world is an ocean of sorrow and affliction; The Honored One is its great ship and raft.
With the most supreme Dharma, He shall ferry them across to the further shore.'"
Furthermore, another seer spoke a verse in praise, saying:
"The world suffers from the pains of old age and sickness; The Honored One is the Great King of Physicians.
With the subtle and wondrous Dharma, He shall rescue them and bring about their healing."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the rishis had finished praising the Bodhisattva, they prostrated, circumambulated him, and departed through the air.
At that time, King Śuddhodana did not see the Bodhisattva for a short while; he became despondent and unhappy, speaking these words:”
"Where is the Crown Prince now?
he asked, and immediately dispatched his ministers to search for him everywhere.

One minister arrived at the Jambu tree and saw the Bodhisattva sitting upright there in deep contemplation; while the shadows of all other trees shifted with the passing sun, only the shadow of the Jambu tree remained still and unmoving.
At that time, the minister, witnessing such a sight, felt a sense of wonder and returned to report to the king, saying:
“The Prince sits in solemn meditation beneath a Jambu tree; Though time passes, the shadow of the tree does not shift.
Adorned with various marks and signs of excellence, His majestic virtue and radiant light surpass those of Śakra and Brahmā.”

At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana went beneath the Jambu tree and beheld the Bodhisattva’s body, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and radiant with majestic splendor. He praised him in verse:

“Like a torch burning on a mountain peak at night, Or like the bright moon suspended in the void, The Prince dwells in peace, entered into deep dhyāna; Beholding him now, I am both joyful and afraid.”
12. Chapter on Displaying Arts. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva had grown to adulthood, on one occasion King Śuddhodana was engaged in conversation with the elders and senior members of the Śākya clan."
Then the Śākyas addressed the Great King, saying:
"The Prince has gradually grown to maturity. Countless seers and experts in physiognomy all declare:

'If the Prince leaves home to lead the religious life, he will certainly attain Buddhahood; if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four quarters of the world, governing beings through the ten wholesome paths and reigning as a Dharma King, endowed with the seven treasures.'"
What are the seven?

First is the wheel-treasure, second is the elephant-treasure, third is the horse-treasure, fourth is the jewel-treasure, fifth is the woman-treasure, sixth is the minister-treasure of the military, and seventh is the minister-treasure of the treasury.
"He possesses a full thousand sons, who are handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing enemies.
Great King!
If you cause the crown prince not to leave the household life, there will certainly be a successor to the Wheel-Turning Sage King, and all the minor kings shall submit to him."
"We should arrange a marriage proposal to cause him to develop attachment, so that he will naturally not go forth as a renunciant.
Then King Śuddhodana said to the Śākyas:
"Whose daughter possesses such virtue that she is fit to be his consort?"
At that time, there were five hundred ministers, each of whom said to the king:
"My daughter possesses the virtues worthy of being the consort of the Crown Prince.
King Śuddhodana replied:
"The Crown Prince’s consort is certainly difficult to choose; we do not know which woman could satisfy his wishes.
We should ask the Crown Prince what kind of woman may serve as his consort."
Then those Śākyas went to where the Bodhisattva was and each asked him:
"What kind of girl has the Prince chosen to be his consort?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to the Śākyas:
"Seven days hence, I shall explain this matter.
The Bodhisattva reflected and spoke in verse:
"The realm of existence has boundless faults, And serves as the cause of all suffering and affliction."
It is like a forest of poisonous trees, and also like a mass of fierce fire.
Now, though dwelling within the deep palace and enjoying the company of court ladies, this place is extremely difficult to inhabit;
it is as if one were treading upon the edge of a sharp blade.
"It is not as good as dwelling in meditative concentration, alone within the mountain forests.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the Bodhisattva gave rise to great compassion and contemplated skillful means to deliver sentient beings. He addressed the ministers and spoke in verse:
"The lotus grows from within the mud, yet it is not defiled by the mud."
The King’s virtue moves the multitudes, and he shall become the one honored by all.
Among the immeasurable sentient beings of the world, they shall realize the nectar of immortality through me;
therefore, I manifest the possession of wife and children, yet I am not defiled by the five desires.
I now follow in the footsteps of the Buddhas of the past, Without falling away from my various meditative concentrations;
In choosing a spouse for marriage, one should select a worthy match, And not take an ordinary woman as a consort.

A person of pure countenance, endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, who speaks truthfully according to his heart and is free from negligence—I now write down what he cherishes; you should seek him well according to this description.
If one possesses youth and excellent deportment, yet does not rely on that beautiful appearance to give rise to arrogance;
being without pride, stinginess, or envy, and without flattery, deception, or any afflictions.
Always upright and sincere, they give rise to a compassionate heart; They pity all sentient beings as if they were their own beloved children.
Delighting in the practice of giving and free from all faults, They make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Even in dreams, no unwholesome thoughts arise; she has never conceived and remains perpetually chaste.
Always taking her own mind as her teacher, she is not arrogant, maintaining a humble disposition like that of a lowly person.
Not craving flavors or sensual pleasures, possessing a sense of shame and modesty while remaining free from malice,
never taking refuge in non-Buddhist paths, one always accords with the true and correct principle.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are ever pure; Lethargy and drowsiness are entirely abandoned.
There is no unwholesome thought in what they do; They constantly practice virtuous deeds, never forsaking them.
She serves her parents-in-law as she would her own parents; she cherishes those around her as if they were herself.
She sleeps only after her husband has fallen asleep and rises before him; she is well able to understand all principles and meanings.
“Only such a woman as this shall I take; how could I take one who is common and inferior as my queen!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the minister delivered this letter to King Śuddhodana. Having seen the letter, the king addressed his ministers, saying:”

"You should take this letter to the city of Kapilavastu and observe among the various clans—whether they be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or even among the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes—to find a maiden who possesses all these virtues; you shall then marry her as the Crown Prince's consort."
He then spoke in verse:
“Whether Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra,
if there is a daughter endowed with these virtues, you should come quickly and inform me.”
"What the Prince’s heart delights in is to take the Dharma as his primary concern;
you should now examine him with discernment, regardless of his lineage.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
At that time, having received the king’s command, the ministers sought throughout the city of Kapilavastu for a maiden of such virtuous character.

There was a minister named Daṇḍapāṇi who had a daughter named Yaśodharā; she was of exquisite and perfect beauty, foremost in her loveliness—neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor slender, neither too pale nor too dark, possessing the full grace of a woman like a precious jewel.
Thereupon, the minister went to the house of Daṇḍapāṇi and saw Yaśodharā.
At that time, Yaśodharā bowed to the minister and asked him,
"For what reason have you come here?"
The minister presented the Prince’s letter to Yaśodharā and spoke these verses:
“The Crown Prince of the Great King of the Śākyas, His countenance is upright and most lovely;
He possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, And the eighty minor characteristics are all perfected.”
"In the Prince's letter, he describes the virtues of a wife; a woman such as this may become my consort.
At that time, Yaśodharā saw the Bodhisattva’s letter, took it and read it, and with a serene smile replied to the minister:
"The virtues described in the letter are now all complete in me; only the Prince should be my husband."
"You should quickly inform the wise of this intention, so that the unworthy do not dwell together with us.
At that time, having witnessed these events, the minister returned and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!..."

In the city of Kapilavastu, I searched everywhere and found a virtuous woman worthy of being the Prince’s consort; she was upright and exquisite, with the foremost of physical marks—neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor slender, neither too pale nor too dark, possessing the full grace of a woman like a precious lady.
The king asked,
"Whose daughter is she whom you have mentioned?
She replied:
"The daughter of the minister Daṇḍapāṇi is named Yaśodharā.
The king then reflected to himself:
"The Prince’s marks and signs surpass those of the world; [how could she be his match?]"
Only one who is fully endowed with both virtue and beauty can serve as the Crown Prince’s consort.
Why must those you have mentioned possess every excellence?

I shall instead create precious vessels of sorrowlessness and distribute them to whoever comes according to the Prince’s whim; I will secretly station spies to observe his preferences, and whomever he favors, him I shall betroth as his consort.

He then dispatched goldsmiths to craft many vessels for Aśoka, further embellishing them with the seven precious gems. He beat the drums to proclaim a decree throughout the city of Kapilavastu, announcing that all women who knew themselves to possess virtue and beauty worthy of being the Prince’s consort should assemble at the royal palace on the seventh day.
When the seven days had passed, all the women gathered together.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was seated upon a noble couch in the great hall, surrounded by his court ladies.
Then King Śuddhodana secretly dispatched an inner attendant:
"Observe the direction in which the Bodhisattva’s mind is inclined and report it to me immediately.

At that time, all the beautiful women of the city of Kapilavastu adorned their bodies with necklaces and ornaments; they approached the Bodhisattva, yet upon briefly beholding his majestic radiance, they were unable to look up at him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva bestowed the vessels of *aśoka* jewels upon them one after another; having all received these generous gifts, they departed with downcast faces.

Then Yaśodharā, surrounded by her attendants, arrived last. Her appearance was upright and her features peerless; she gazed intently at the Bodhisattva without blinking for a moment, smiling serenely as she spoke these words:
"Why alone do you not deign to bestow upon me the *aśoka* jewel? Is it perhaps because my person is unworthy of being taken?"
The Bodhisattva replied, "I have no real grievance against you; it was simply that you arrived later and the precious vessels were all gone.
He then took off his finger-ring and gave it to him; the ring was worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Having received the ring, Yaśodharā spoke again, saying:
"Why is the gift so meager?
Is my person truly of such inferior worth?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva completely removed all the precious necklaces and ornaments he was wearing and presented them to her.
Yaśodharā said,
"Why should I now take away the jewels that adorn the Prince's person?"
"I shall personally present these various precious ornaments to the Prince.
Having spoken these words, he refused to accept them and returned to his own place.
Then the King’s messenger reported all that had occurred to the King, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know that the Prince’s heart is set upon Yaśodharā, the daughter of the minister Mahānāman.
Upon hearing these words, the King immediately dispatched the National Preceptor to the house of Mahānāman with these instructions:
"I have heard that you have a daughter worthy of being the consort for the Crown Prince; therefore, I have been sent to seek her. You should understand this intention.
At that time, having received the King's command, the State Preceptor went to the house of Daṇḍapāṇi and explained the matter in detail.
At that time, Daṇḍapāṇi replied to the state preceptor, saying:
"According to the family tradition passed down through successive generations in my house, if there is one whose skill and ability surpasses others, I shall give my daughter to him as a wife."

The Crown Prince was raised within the deep seclusion of the palace; he has never studied the martial and civil arts, calligraphy, mathematics, painting, military strategy, quick-wittedness, physical prowess, or any of the various worldly skills. Why should my daughter be given in marriage to one who possesses no such arts?
"You should convene all the Śākyas to test their skills and talents; whoever is most preeminent shall obtain this maiden.
When the National Preceptor heard these words, he returned and informed the King.
Upon hearing these words, the King was filled with grief and distress, and he thought to himself:
"I previously commanded the Śākya kinsmen to attend upon the Prince, yet they all reported to me, saying:
'The Prince is not courageous.'"
"The words of Daṇḍapāṇi may have arisen from this very reason.
At that time, the Bodhisattva went to his father the king and said:
"Great King, why are you so sorrowful?"
The king remained silent, even when questioned three times.
The king then dispatched others to explain his intention.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva smiled with serene joy and came forward to address the king, saying:
"Is there indeed anyone in the world with such extraordinary skill and marvelous artistry as ours?
The king was delighted and asked him further:
"Are you now able to compete in arts and skills with others?"
When he had asked this three times, the Bodhisattva replied:
"Great King!
You should simply summon someone skilled in extraordinary arts at once; I can manifest various feats of skill before you."
At that time, King Śuddhodana established a testing ground outside the city of Kapilavastu and issued a proclamation throughout the world:
"Seven days from now, all those who are skilled in the arts shall assemble at this site to witness the Prince demonstrate his various talents."
On the seventh day, five hundred Śākya youths, led by the Bodhisattva, set out from the city together to go to the site of the trial of skill.

At that time, the minister Daṇḍapāṇi adorned his daughter, placed her upon a jeweled chariot, and surrounded her with attendants to come and observe the arts. He erected a pillar as a proclamation, decreeing that whoever displayed skills surpassing all others should be given the maiden as his wife.

At that time, King Śuddhodana dispatched his general with the most excellent white elephant to welcome the Bodhisattva. Devadatta arrived at the city gate first and, seeing this supreme elephant adorned with the highest splendor, asked:
"Whose elephant is this?"
He replied, "The Great King has sent this elephant to welcome the Crown Prince.

Upon hearing these words, Devadatta gave rise to a heart of jealousy; relying on his own strength and filled with arrogance, he stepped forward, seized the elephant’s trunk, and struck it with his hand, whereupon the elephant died.
As Nanda continued on his way toward exiting the city gate, he saw that white elephant lying dead across the road.
He asked, "Who killed it?
and they replied:
"Devadatta! Nanda then dragged him backward by the hand and placed him by the side of the road.
The Bodhisattva soon arrived and asked:
"Who killed the elephant?
The charioteer replied, "Devadatta seized its trunk with his left hand and struck it with his right; at that moment, the elephant died instantly upon the blow."
The Bodhisattva sighed and said,
"Devadatta has acted most unwholesomely!
He then asked his charioteer:
"Who was able to move it?
He replied,
"Nanda dragged it by hand and overturned it onto the side of the road."
The Bodhisattva exclaimed, "Excellent, Nanda!

At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upon his precious chariot and, with the toe of his left foot, lifted the white elephant and gently cast it into the air. It leaped over the sevenfold city walls and traveled one *krośa*; where the elephant fell, a great pit was formed, which people thereafter called the "Elephant Pit."
At that time, the devas in the void were all greatly rejoiced and, marveling at this unprecedented event, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva, from within his chariot, lowered his left foot And with his toe cast the elephant beyond the city walls.
With certainty, he shall be able to use the power of his wisdom To transport all sentient beings across the city of death."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with the elders and senior members of the Śākya clan, the state preceptor, the ministers, and an immeasurable assembly, gathered at the site of the arts competition; five hundred Śākya youths all arrived at this arena."
At that time, the Śākyas invited Viśvamitra to serve as their instructor for the arts, and they said to Viśvamitra:
"You should observe among our youths who is most skilled in writing and who has studied most extensively."
Vaiśramitra, having already known that the Prince had mastered all scripts such that none could surpass him, smiled toward the youths and spoke in verse:
"Whatever characters exist in heaven or among men,
the Prince has investigated them all, reaching their very depths."
Among you and me, who could possibly equal him?
He taught me the scriptures, yet I do not know their names;
having just now compared them, I find he is the most supreme among gods and men.
At that time, the five hundred Śākyas came forward and said to the King:
"We previously knew that the Prince was proficient in the arts of writing and learning such that none could equal him, yet we had not yet realized that he surpassed others in the art of calculation."
At that time, there was a great minister named Aśvajit who was extremely proficient in arithmetic. King Śuddhodana said to Aśvajit:
"You should examine these youths and see who is the most excellent in calculation."

At that time, the Bodhisattva himself began the counting, instructing the young boys to place their tally sticks in succession; however, they were unable to keep pace with the Bodhisattva’s count, and all five hundred boys, one by one, fell into confusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the youths, "You all call out the numbers and I shall calculate them.

The youths called out the numbers one after another, but the Bodhisattva moved his counting sticks and called them out with such speed that they could not keep up; he was entirely without error. Even when five hundred youths called out the numbers all at once, he remained perfectly clear and unconfused.
At that time, Aṇṣuṇa felt a sense of wonder and praised him with a verse:
“Excellent! Your mental wisdom is marvelous and swift; none among the five hundred Śākyas can equal it.
Formerly, they all claimed, ‘I am skilled at calculation,’ but now we know the Prince is immeasurable.”
Then the Śākyas and all the humans and devas cried out with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent!
The Prince is also foremost among those skilled in calculation."
They all rose from their seats, joined their palms in homage at their heads, and addressed the Great King, saying:
"Excellent, Great King! You have swiftly attained a most excellent benefit!"
"Now, the Crown Prince’s eloquence and wisdom are both preeminent.
Then King Śuddhodana said to the Bodhisattva,
"Could you perhaps compare your calculations with those of Arjuna?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Great King!
This matter is acceptable."
Then that mathematician asked the Bodhisattva:
"Is there a name for a number beyond one hundred koṭis that you understand?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I know it very well! Aṇṣuṇa said,
"If the Prince knows, please explain it to me."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"One hundred koṭis is called an ayuta; one hundred ayutas is called a niyuta; one hundred niyutas is called a bimbara;
one hundred bimbaras is called a kharva; one hundred kharvas is called a nikharva."
One *akṣobhya* is called one; one hundred *akṣobhyas* is called a *vibhava*; one hundred *vibhavas* is called a *uṃsaka*;
one hundred *uṃsakas* is called a *vahula*; one hundred *vahulas* is called a *nāgabala*;
one hundred *nāgabalas* is called a *tiṭṭhabala*; one hundred *tiṭṭhabalas* is called a *bī*.
One *pāpata-prajñapti* is called a *he-tou-xi-luo*; one hundred *he-tou-xi-luo* is called a *jia-luo-po*;
one hundred *jia-luo-po* is called a *he-du-yin-tuo-li*; one hundred *he-du-yin-tuo-li* is called a *seng-he-da-lan-po*;
one hundred *seng-he-da-lan-po*... [is called a *seng-he-da-lan*].
One *bha* is called a *gaṇanāgati*; one hundred *gaṇanāgatis* is called a *nirartha*;
one hundred *nirarthas* is called a *mudrāpala*; one hundred *mudrāpalas* is called a *sarpapala*;
one hundred *sarpapalas* is called a *viṃśatibodhi*. One hundred *viṃśatibodhis*...
One *avaivartika* is called a *sarvasaṃjñeya*; one hundred *sarvasaṃjñeyas* is called a *vibhūtaṅgama*;
one hundred *vibhūtaṅgamas* is called a *tara-lakṣa*.
If there is one who understands this number, they will be able to calculate and know the quantity of atoms in Mount Sumeru.
Beyond this is a number called *duṣāgāramaṇi*; if there is one who understands this number, they will be able to calculate and know the quantity of *lakṣas* of Ganges sands.
Beyond these numbers, there is a number called *duṣāgamaṇiśiri*; if one understands this number, one is able to calculate and know the *koṭis* of sands in the Ganges River.
Beyond this number, there is a number called *bahana-vajrottiṅga*;

beyond that, a number called *iṭa*; beyond that, a number called *kuluṣi*; beyond that, a number called *koṭabhiṇa*; and beyond that, a number called *sāvanikha*. One who understands these numbers is able to know the *koṭis*, *lakṣas*, and *niyutas* of the sands of the Ganges.
Beyond this, there is another number called *agaḷasara*; one who understands this number can know a hundred *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-śatasahasra*.

Beyond this, there are further numbers that follow into the *paramāṇu-rajas-pāramāṇu-rāja*; once these numbers are reached, no sentient beings whatsoever can know them, except for the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas in their final birth, who alone are able to understand them.
Aṇḍaśuna said: "Prince,
how can one understand the number of atoms?"

The Bodhisattva replied: "Generally, seven *paramāṇu* (extreme atoms) form one *aṇu* (atom); seven *aṇu* form one *truti*; seven *truti* form one particle visible to the eye within a window; seven particles visible to the eye form one particle on a rabbit’s hair; seven particles on a rabbit’s hair form one particle on a sheep’s hair; seven particles on a sheep’s hair form one particle on a cow’s hair; seven particles on a cow’s hair form one nit (*yūka*); seven nits form one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); seven mustard seeds form one barley grain (*yava*); seven barley grains form one finger-joint (*aṅguli-parvan*); twelve finger-joints form one span (*vitasti*); two spans form one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits form one bow-length (*dhanus*); one thousand bow-lengths form one *krośa*; and four *krośa* form one *yojana*."
"Now, who among this assembly is able to know the number of atoms within a single yojana?
Aśvajit replied, "Even upon hearing what the Prince has said, I am already bewildered and distressed; how much more so for others of shallow understanding and little learning?"
"I only pray that the Prince will explain for me: how many atoms are there within one *yojana*?
The Bodhisattva replied:

"The number of atoms in a *yojana* is equal to one *nayuta* of *akṣobhya*, plus thirty *koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra*, plus sixty thousand *koṭi*, plus thirty-two *koṭi*, plus five *lakṣa*, plus twelve thousand *lakṣa*."
Calculating in this manner, one obtains the number of dust particles in one *yojana*.

Likewise, Jambudvīpa in the south is seven thousand *yojanas*, Aparagoyānī in the west is eight thousand *yojanas*, Pūrvavideha in the east is nine thousand *yojanas*, and Uttarakuru in the north is ten thousand *yojanas*;
these four continents together constitute a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Ten billion sets of four continents constitute one trichiliocosm; within it are ten billion great oceans,
ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion Iron Ring Mountains, ten billion heavens of the Four Great Kings,
ten billion Trāyastriṃśa heavens, ten billion Yāma heavens, and ten billion Tuṣita heavens.
Ten billion gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, ten billion gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
ten billion gods of the Brahmakāyika Heaven, ten billion gods of the Brahmapurohita Heaven, ten billion gods of the Brahmakāyika-sabhāgata Heaven,
ten billion Mahābrahmā Heaven, ten billion Parīttābha Heaven, ten billion Apramāṇābha Heaven, ten billion Ābhāsvara Heaven, ten billion Parīttaśubha Heaven...
The Śuddhāvāsa devas, ten billion immeasurable Śuddhāvāsa devas, ten billion Śubhakṛtsna devas, ten billion Anabhraka devas,
ten billion Puṇyaprasava devas, ten billion Bṛhatphala devas,
ten billion Avṛha devas, ten billion Atapa devas, ten billion Sudṛśa devas, and ten billion...
There are one billion *Sudṛśa* gods and ten billion *Akaniṣṭha* gods;
this is what is called a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

Its dimensions—whether extending for a hundred *yojanas*, a thousand *yojanas*, a hundred thousand *yojanas*, a *koṭi* of *yojanas*, a hundred *koṭis* of *yojanas*, or a *niyuta* of *yojanas*—can be known through such successive measurements of *yojanas*.
The measure of a single atom is beyond the reach of any numerical calculation; because the atoms within this trichiliocosm are thus incalculable, they are termed "asaṃkhyeya" (incalculable).

When the Bodhisattva spoke these numbers, Ānanda and all the Śākyas were filled with great joy; they conceived a sense of rare wonder and leaped for immeasurable delight. They all removed their exquisite garments and various precious necklaces and offered them to the Bodhisattva.
He praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Then Aṇṣuṇa spoke these verses:
“Koṭi, śata, and ayuta; likewise there are nayuta, further still, bimbara and vibhūta;
the names of numbers reach their limit at akṣobhya.”
Furthermore, he surpasses those who are immeasurable in number; the Prince is able to know all these things.
O Śākyas, you should now all listen: there is no one in the world equal to the Prince.
Even if one were to take all the grasses and trees of the three thousandfold world system and break them into counting-slips for a wise person, they would not suffice for comparison;
how much less so for the five hundred Śākya youths?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all cried out:
'Excellent! Excellent!'"
The devas in the void praised him with these verses:
"The minds of various sentient beings Of the past, present, and future—
Their superior, middling, and inferior categories— He knows them all in a single thought-moment."
"How much more so this calculation, that he could not understand it clearly?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Bodhisattva subdued all the Śākya youths; in contests of skill, leaping, and running, he was supreme in every respect."
At that time, the devas in the sky spoke again in verse:
“Through many kalpas of practicing giving and precepts, And through the power of patience, diligence, and compassion, The Bodhisattva has attained such a light body and mind;
Listen now as he moves with swift agility.”
You see this Great Being constantly dwelling here, yet you do not know that in a single thought-moment he travels to the ten directions;
he wanders through Buddha-lands everywhere, receiving their teachings in person, yet you have never known him to come or go.
Thus, for the Son of Śākya to attain such supreme excellence is not at all a cause for wonder.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, five hundred youths were engaged in a wrestling match, divided into thirty-two teams.
Nanda stepped forward and displayed his great prowess, but as soon as the Bodhisattva raised his hand and lightly touched his body, he was struck down by the power of that touch and fell instantly."

Devadatta constantly harbored arrogance and treated the Bodhisattva with contempt, claiming that his own power and majesty were equal to those of the Bodhisattva; he stepped boldly out from the crowd and moved through the testing grounds, rushing forward with the intent to defeat the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, neither hurried nor slow, remained calm and composed without any anger or resentment as he waited for him. He gently grasped [Nanda] with his right hand and lifted him up effortlessly, crushing his pride. He threw him three times into the air; out of compassion, he ensured that Nanda suffered no injury.
Then he addressed the Śākyas: "All of you should come and wrestle with me."
Simultaneously giving rise to anger and resentment, they rushed forward with fierce intent; however, as the Bodhisattva pointed at them, they all fell prostrate.
At that time, the humans and devas cried out in unison:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
The devas in the void rained down various celestial flowers and praised him in verse:
"Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions Were to possess great strength like that of Nārāyaṇa,
A person of supreme wisdom, in a single thought, Would cause them all to fall prostrate at the mere pointing of a finger."
Even if Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains were ground to dust by the Great Being’s hand,
how much more so could he surpass the frail and unstable people of this world when compared to the Prince?
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree with great compassion, He shall subdue the demonic hosts of the desire realm;
Furthermore, he shall moisten all living beings with the nectar of immortality— It is certain that no one can overcome this Bodhisattva.
At that time, the minister Daṇḍapāṇi said to the Śākya youths:
"I have already observed your various skills; now let us test your archery to see who is the most excellent."
Thereupon, they agreed to shoot at an iron drum. Ānanda said,
"The iron drum may be placed two krośas away."
Devadatta said, "A iron drum may be placed at a distance of four krośas.
Sundarananda said:
"One may place the iron drum at six *krośas*.
The minister Daṇḍapāṇi said:
"One may place the iron drum at eight *krośas*."
The Bodhisattva said:
"You may take an iron drum and place it ten *krośas* away, and likewise place seven iron pigs and seven iron *tāla* trees ten *krośas* outside [the city]."
At that time, Ānanda shot an arrow that reached two *krośas* and passed through two iron drums;
Devadatta shot an arrow that reached four *krośas* and passed through four iron drums;
and Sundarananda shot an arrow that reached six *krośas* and passed through six iron drums.
The minister Dhanus could shoot a distance of eight *krośas*, passing through eight iron drums;
this was his limit, and he could not go beyond it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva drew his bow to shoot, but the bow and its string snapped simultaneously. The Bodhisattva looked around and sought another excellent bow.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was filled with great joy and replied to the Bodhisattva:
"The former kings possessed a bow kept in the celestial temple, which has always been honored with offerings of incense and flowers."
"That bow is so taut and strong that no one can string it.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Try sending it here."

The king then dispatched a messenger to fetch the bow and arrows of the former kings and presented them to the Śākya youths; however, none of these Śākyas were able to string them, whereupon he presented the bow to the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva sat in a state of composure; with his left hand he grasped the bow and his right index finger placed upon the string. Suddenly he drew it as if without exerting any effort, and the sound of the bowstring resounded throughout the city of Kapilavastu.
The inhabitants within the city were all struck with terror and asked one another, "What is this sound?
At that time, the humans and devas simultaneously cried out:
"Excellent, excellent!
The devas of the void spoke this verse in praise:
"When the Bodhisattva drew the bow, He remained serene and unshaken."
"My aspirations shall be fulfilled; I shall subdue Māra and attain perfect enlightenment. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body and mind were peaceful and secure, and his movements were composed and dignified. Thereafter, he drew the bowstring and shot at the iron drums, piercing them all through; the iron boars and iron trees were likewise penetrated without exception. The arrow sank into the earth, forming a well, which thereafter was called by the people 'The Arrow Well'."
At that time, all the humans and devas cried out with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent!
Though the Prince has never practiced or studied since his birth, he is already able to possess such artistic skills."
The devas in the void spoke in verse:
“Observing the Bodhisattva’s archery now, it is not yet enough to be considered rare;
he shall sit upon the seat of the former Buddhas and realize great bodhi.”
“Taking meditative concentration as the bow, and emptiness and non-self as the arrow,
one cuts through the net of all views and shoots down the enemy of afflictions.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In this way, he was skillfully able to perform all manner of feats: leaping with agility, racing and outrunning others, wrestling and boxing, calligraphy, seals, arithmetic, archery, charioteering, walking on water, the dexterity of riding mounts, and the prowess of using hooks and ropes."

He was thoroughly proficient in all manner of miscellaneous arts, including vital points (marmans), gambling, physiognomy, painting, carving and engraving, music and song, dance, comedy and jesting, massage, the transformation of various precious gems, sorcery, dream interpretation, and the examination of domestic animals.
