He was thoroughly proficient in the treatises on poultry, the treatises on elephants, the treatises on horses, the treatises on archery, the Vedas, the treatises on logic, the treatises on discipline, the Śigra treatises, the Viśiga treatises, the treatises on grammar, the treatises on kingship, the treatises on non-human beings, the treatises on birds and beasts, the treatises on phonology, and the treatises on epistemology; he mastered all human arts and crafts, as well as the supernatural skills of the devas that transcend those of humans.
Thereupon, the minister Dandapāṇi addressed King Śuddhodana and the entire assembly of the Śākyas, saying:
"I now offer my daughter to be the consort of the Crown Prince."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, in accordance with worldly custom, manifested his residence within the palace; he lived there enjoying himself with eighty-four thousand court ladies, of whom Yaśodharā was the chief consort."
Upon first arriving at the palace, she did not observe the superficial etiquette of women; suddenly she bared her head and never covered her face.
King Śuddhodana and Udāyin secretly marveled at this matter, and the ladies-in-waiting of the inner court all proclaimed:
"The Queen has now arrived for the first time and ought to display modesty; why does she manifest such unconventionality without any sense of shame?"
"Such is the extent of their frivolity, shallowness, and even their contempt.
Having heard these words, Yaśodharā spoke this verse for the sake of the palace women:
"If there is no flaw, what need is there to conceal it?
In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, all are entirely pure.
Like a mani jewel placed upon a lofty banner,
its radiance shines forth, manifesting itself to all.
Whether silent or speaking, they are always free from private concealment;
adorning themselves with all manner of meritorious virtues,
though they wear garments of grass or old, tattered clothes.
It does not burden the body, but only increases its beauty.
If a person harbors evil within while outwardly adorning their appearance,
they are like a jar of poison coated with honey.
Such persons as these are truly terrifying;
they are like venomous snakes that must not be approached.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who abandons evil associates, [they shall attain peace].
Closely associating with virtuous friends, one eliminates the sins of sentient beings.
Establishing the Triple Gem, one's merit shall not be in vain;
the actions of body, speech, and mind will all become entirely pure.
"O great seers, you who are able to know the minds of others shall naturally possess clear discernment; there is no need for concealment.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that Yaśodharā possessed such wisdom and eloquence, was filled with great joy. He immediately bestowed upon Yaśodharā exquisite garments and precious pearl necklaces of immeasurable value, and praised her in verse:
“The Prince is endowed with all virtues, And you are most worthy of him;
Now these two pure beings Are like clarified butter and its essence.”
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Four.
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Thirteen: Awakening through Music At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When the Bodhisattva was dwelling in his deep palace and was about to renounce the world, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings constantly made offerings to the Bodhisattva with various kinds of requisites, joyfully praising him."
Furthermore, at another time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others each reflected:

"The Bodhisattva has for a long night brought sentient beings to maturity and gathered them in through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Now that the faculties (*indriya*) of these beings have matured, why does the Bodhisattva remain for so long within the deep palace, instead of leaving home, attaining enlightenment, and delivering them?"

"If we do not arrive in time, I fear that [the Bodhisattva] will move on, making it difficult to preserve his virtuous mind; once he later attains perfect enlightenment, there will be no way for us to be saved.
Having formed this thought, he went before the Bodhisattva, prostrated himself in hope, and spoke these words:

"How may I behold the Bodhisattva renounce the world to study the Path, sit upon the seat of enlightenment to subdue the hosts of Māras, and attain equal and perfect awakening? How may he be fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; how may he turn the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel of twelve aspects in three revolutions, manifest great supernormal powers, and satisfy all the various aspirations of sentient beings?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva has not attained awakening through another;

he has always been his own teacher. He thoroughly understands all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas and the practices to be performed; he knows the appropriate and inappropriate times; he sports with supernormal powers without ever falling away, responding to the faculties of sentient beings."

Just as the ocean tide never errs in its timing, through his supernormal knowledge he knows for all sentient beings the time to gather and benefit them, the time to subdue them, the time to deliver them, and the time to set them aside; he knows the time to preach the Dharma, the time to remain silent, the time to cultivate wisdom, the time to recite and chant, the time to engage in reflection, and the time to dwell in solitude. He knows the time to go to assemblies of kṣatriyas, assemblies of brāhmaṇas, and assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When all bodhisattvas in their final birth are about to renounce the household life, it is the natural law that the Buddhas, Tathāgatas of the infinite asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions, through the power of their supernormal knowledges, cause the musical instruments and stringed songs within the palace to produce subtle and wondrous sounds to exhort and invite the bodhisattva, speaking these verses:
'The sounds of the palace ladies' stringed songs Seek to delude the Bodhisattva with desire;'"
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, This sound has been transformed into the words of the Dharma.
In the past, the Honored One beheld sentient beings suffering, And made a vow to be their refuge and protector.
Excellent! If you recall your former practices, Now is precisely the time for you to renounce the world.
Venerable One, recall how in the past, for the sake of sentient beings, you gave away your own flesh, hands, and feet without stinginess;
you practiced the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Because you sought the supreme merit of Bodhi, there is no one in all the worlds who can equal you.
These sentient beings are possessed of anger and delusion, yet the Honored One subdues them all through loving-kindness and compassion.
Toward those who are ignorant, deluded, and hold false views, the Honored One is able to give rise extensively to great compassion.
Having accumulated boundless merit and wisdom, his meditative concentrations and supernormal powers are utterly pure.
The radiance of his body reaches the ten directions, Like the moon shining everywhere when free from clouds;
The sounds of countless musical instruments are subtle and wondrous, Exhorting the Bodhisattva to quickly leave the household life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt within a most supreme and exquisite palace, wherein all necessities were fully provided. The halls, pavilions, and towers were adorned with various jewels; banners, streamers, and precious canopies were arrayed everywhere; they were further embellished with jeweled bells and nets, and hung with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of silken ribbons and various precious necklaces."

All the bridges and pathways were constructed from planks of various precious gems; everywhere there were jeweled incense burners burning all kinds of famous incenses, and pearl-canopied curtains were spread and hung above them.

There were various ponds with clear and cool waters, where seasonal and non-seasonal flowers bloomed everywhere; within those ponds, ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, kingfishers, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvaka birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds.

The ground is composed entirely of lapis lazuli; its radiance is lovely like a clear mirror, so exquisitely adorned that nothing can serve as a metaphor for it. Among humans and devas, there are none who behold it without joy.
Again, at one time, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, the sounds of musical instruments played by the various court ladies spoke these verses:
“O Honored One, remember the great vows you made in the past, Out of compassion for all sentient beings who have no refuge.
If you realize the great Bodhi of the Deathless Nectar, Rescue and deliver them, causing them to be free from suffering and affliction.”
Just as the Buddhas of the past practiced their conduct, dwelling alone in empty mountains and forest wilds,
they realized the Tathāgata’s omniscience and bestowed wealth and treasures upon those who were destitute.
In the past, you have already practiced great giving, Capable of relinquishing all wealth and treasures;
For the sake of all sentient beings, you have rained down the rain of Dharma— Now is precisely the time for you to go forth into homelessness.
Your reverence is flawless in pure precepts, having practiced them constantly throughout many kalpas from of old;
you liberate sentient beings from all afflictions—now is precisely the time for you to renounce the world.
You have cultivated hundreds of thousands of various forms of patience, enduring all the harsh words of the world;
having always subdued yourself through patience, now is the very time—go forth into homelessness quickly.
Your venerable practice of diligence is most steadfast; having cultivated it for a long time, you have subdued the hosts of Māra and extinguished all three evil realms.
Now is precisely the time for you to go forth into homelessness.
The Honored One has removed all defilements through supreme meditative concentration;
He showers the rain of nectar to satisfy all living beings, filling the world with those who suffer from thirst and want. Now is precisely the time; it is fitting that you leave the home life.
With boundless great wisdom, you have severed the delusions of wrong views and ignorance;
O Honored One, please reflect upon your former great vows—the present is precisely the time for you to swiftly renounce the world.
In the past, you have already practiced immeasurable billions of sublime deeds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Through all these sublime deeds, you have distributed [their benefits] among all sentient beings throughout the world.
The palace ladies’ stringed songs were most subtle and exquisite, seeking to move the Bodhisattva with sensual desire;
yet through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, they were all transformed into the sounds of the Dharma.
Venerable One, recall how in the past you were a king;
when someone came before you to beg, you gave him your royal throne and your kingdom, joyfully relinquishing them without regret.
In the past, the World-Honored One was once a brahmin named Śuka, who was exceedingly diligent;
with compassion and filial piety he made offerings to his parents, bringing countless brahmins and other sentient beings to maturity on the path of goodness,
and after casting off this body, he was reborn in the heavens.
Venerable One, you recall how in the past, when you were a rishi, King Kali, in his rage, severed your limbs;
yet you gave rise to a heart of great compassion without resentment, and from the places where you were wounded, milk flowed forth.
Formerly, when I was the son of Śamatha, my parents lived in the mountains practicing austerities together.
A king, by mistake, struck me with a poisoned arrow; embracing loving-kindness and free from resentment, I died with joy.
Venerable One, recall how in the past you were a golden deer;
seeing a man crossing a river who was being swept away, you gave rise to a heart of compassion to rescue him, yet later when he turned upon you to harm you, you felt no anger or resentment.
Venerable One, recall how in the past you were a seer;
when a precious jewel fell by mistake into the great ocean, you roused a mind of diligence to drain that sea, until the dragon king, struck with terror, returned the jewel.
In the past, when you were a great seer, you protected with a compassionate heart a dove that had sought refuge in you.
When someone came to you demanding this dove, you cut flesh from your own body and weighed it until its weight was equal to the bird’s;
thus did you provide protection until the end of your life.
Furthermore, in the past, when the Honored One was the seer Śamatha, someone came and asked how many leaves were on a tree;
knowing their exact number, he answered them, yet that person did not believe him until a deity came to testify.
In the past, you were once a parrot; Śakra transformed himself into a man to question you:
"Since the tree upon which you rely has withered and broken, why do you guard it and not leave?"
The answer was: "By relying on this, they grow and flourish. Śakra then conceived a sense of wonder and immediately caused the withered tree to bloom and flourish once more.
"Venerable One, you are one who upholds merit; you establish all sentient beings in the world and place them within the Buddha’s boundless ocean of virtues."
Thus, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, they praised the Bodhisattva’s manifold virtues;
transforming the lute melodies of the court ladies into song, they entreated the Bodhisattva to quickly renounce the household life.
In the distant past, you made vast and noble vows, To uproot the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.
Please recall the deeds you performed in former times; Now is precisely the time for you to renounce the world.
Venerable One, recall how in boundless kalpas past, you joyfully bestowed gold, silver, and various rare treasures,
as well as your head, eyes, royal throne, and wife and children, upon those who came to beg.
In the past, as King Śivadhvaja-damṣṭra, Candra-pradīpa-maṇicūḍa, Mahākāruṇika, Dṛḍhavīrya, Sunetra,
and other such kings, all possessed great power and were able to practice generosity.
The Honored One was able to maintain the precepts throughout many kalpas; those precepts were as pure as a bright pearl.
He upheld and guarded them with firm resolve, without the slightest transgression, just as a wild ox cherishes its own tail.
Venerable One, recall how you were once a great elephant king;
when a hunter struck your body with an arrow, you gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and offered no retaliation, relinquishing those six tusks to maintain your precepts.
Venerable One, recall how you cultivated various forms of patience throughout many eons; because of that cultivation of patience, you endured manifold sufferings.
Please recall how, in a former life as a bear, you saw a man frozen with hunger and nurtured him with warmth.
When he returned home and encountered hunters, they brought him back to be slaughtered together, yet your heart felt no resentment.
By the power of firm and steadfast diligence, you have cultivated all practices for the sake of Bodhi;
you shall subdue the King of Māra and his hosts—now is the very time for you to go forth.
Venerable One, recall how in the past you were a swift and noble steed, leaping through the air to benefit all worlds;
in the land of the yakṣas, you rescued sentient beings and established them in a place of fearlessness.
Thus practicing diligence for boundless eons, using the power of supernormal knowledges and wisdom to eliminate afflictions,
with a mind perfectly tamed and settled in tranquil meditative concentration, he benefits all sentient beings thereby.
In the past, when you were a king, you caused all sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome deeds;
because these beings practiced such goodness, at the end of their lives they were all reborn in the Brahma world.
The Venerable One’s wisdom can discern the wholesome and the unwholesome, And fully understands the various faculties and natures of sentient beings;
His wisdom can penetrate all principles and paths— Now is precisely the time; depart quickly into the homeless life.
Venerable One, you take pity on sentient beings who have fallen into wrong views within the ocean of suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
you purify the perilous and evil paths of saṃsāra and manifest the true path to nirvāṇa.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise praise the various merits of the Bodhisattva;
they transform all their court ladies into the melodies of stringed songs, exhorting the Bodhisattva to quickly leave the household life.
In former times, the Honored One was a king named Śubhavasu,
Śrīnemi, Kṣemaka, and Kṛkī; Jñānaśrī, Prabhāsa, Dṛḍhadhanus,
Śīlacandra, Prabhākara, Guṇaprabha, Kṛtajña, Tyāgavān, and Mahātejas.
The royal seers Candrarūpa and Caṇḍavīrya, Vardhamāna who sought the sublime Dharma for the sake of awakening,
Sunetra of the Moonlight’s supreme conduct, Dharanirenu who courageously gave away his sovereignty over all quarters,
Ratnamālā who offered his pure body as a gift— These and countless other kings likewise did so.
He is able to relinquish all that is difficult to relinquish, raining down the Dharma-rain for all Tathāgatas.
In the past, he encountered Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving them all without fail.
To seek Bodhi and deliver sentient beings, now is precisely the time; go forth into the homeless life with haste.
At first he served Akṣayadarśin, meeting the Buddha Dṛḍhaketu;
with a single thought of purity, he beheld Vairocana.
Again he encountered Candana Buddha and made an offering of a grass torch.
Furthermore, when the Buddha entered the city, he scattered powdered gold upon the ground;
meeting the Buddha Dharmeśvara, he praised his teaching, saying, "Excellent!
Encountering the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, he uttered but once, "Namo Buddhāya."
I beheld the Buddha Great Mass of Light and made offerings with golden flowers;
I encountered the Tathāgata Banner of Light and presented him with handfuls of beans;
furthermore, I saw the Buddha Wisdom Banner and the Tathāgata Free from Sorrow.
Holding gruel as an offering, he made a great vow before that Buddha.
Again, meeting the Buddha Ratnakeśin, he made offerings with bright lamps;
seeing the Tathāgata Puṣpārca, he made offerings with excellent medicines.
Furthermore, he encountered the Buddha Abhayadatta and offered him a precious necklace;
to the Buddha Vajragarbha, he offered a *padma* jewel;
seeing the Buddha Śālarāja, he made offerings of pure milk.
To the Tathāgata Śrīkīrti, he offered a lion throne;
he also beheld the Buddha Satyadarśin and the Tathāgata Uccamati,
whom he once prostrated to and circumambulated.
I made offerings with robes upon seeing the Buddha Ugradatta;
I gave sandalwood incense upon seeing the Buddha Tiṣya;
And I made offerings with a wondrous bowl upon seeing the Buddha Mahāvyūha.
He offered utpala flowers and encountered King Light Buddha, making offerings with exquisite jewels;
he further beheld Śākyamuni Buddha and presented him with golden lotuses; he also encountered King of Constellations Buddha.
I praised the virtues of the Tathāgata; I also saw the Buddha Sūryamukha and offered him the *alaṃkāra-śrotra* flower;
I further encountered the Buddha Sumati and scattered *tathāgata-mūrdhan* flowers; I also saw the Buddha Nāgavikrāmin.
He bestowed mani-jewels as offerings; he further encountered the Buddha Āyuṣprabheda and presented him with various precious canopies;
he also saw the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja and offered him an exquisite and wondrous seat; he met the Buddha Siṃhadhvaja.
I offered him a net of various jewels; Again I saw the Buddha Holder of Virtue, whom I honored with music;
Again I encountered the Buddha Kāśyapa, to whom I offered various powdered incenses; Again I saw the Buddha Radiant Light.
He made offerings with exquisite flowers; he further encountered the Buddha Abhibhū and presented him with a magnificent, superior terrace.
He again saw the Buddha Lokasundara and offered him a beautiful garland of flowers; he further encountered the Buddha Tathāgata.
Having once renounced the throne of a celestial king, he beheld the Buddha Difficult to Subdue and offered him various exquisite incenses;
again, encountering the Buddha Great Radiance, he sacrificed his own body as an offering;
and again, he beheld the Buddha Honored Flower.
He offered precious ornaments and encountered the Buddha Dharmadhvaja,
scattering various exquisite flowers; he also saw the Buddha Kṛtaprabha and presented him with an utpala flower, making offerings with all his heart.
Thus, as well as other immeasurable Buddhas, each and every one was honored and served with all manner of offerings,
never in vain; may the Honored One remember the Buddhas of the past and recall the offerings made to all the Tathāgatas.
I pray that the Honored One will remember and quickly go forth into homelessness;

for the Honored One remembers how, upon meeting the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past, you attained the pure patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), as well as the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) without any loss.
From that time on, you have been able to travel to all buddha-fields, serving all Tathāgatas in a single thought-moment.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the five desires and royal sovereignty are all unstable.
For the sake of all sentient beings oppressed by suffering, I pray that you will quickly leave the home life to rescue and deliver them.
The court ladies played stringed instruments and sang with pure melodies, seeking to delude the Bodhisattva with sensual desire;
yet through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, all the sounds produced were transformed into proclamations of the Dharma.
The afflictions of the three realms are like a fierce fire;
deluded and unable to leave them, one is constantly burned by them.
They are like floating clouds, vanishing in an instant.
Having gathered, they disperse again, like a gathering at a play.
Moment by moment they do not abide, like lightning in the sky;
their shifting and ceasing are as swift as a torrential waterfall.
Driven by craving and ignorance, one revolves through the five destinies in an unceasing cycle, like a potter’s wheel.
Attached to the five desires, one is like a bird caught in a net.
Sensual desire is like a hostile thief; it is truly terrifying.
To dwell amidst the five desires is like treading upon a blade;
to be attached to the five desires is like embracing a poisonous tree.
The wise abandon desire as if it were a pit of filth;
the five desires are darkening and can cause one to lose mindfulness.
They are always to be feared, for they are the cause of all suffering.
It causes the branches of birth and death to grow;
because of it, one drifts and sinks within the river of birth and death.
The Noble Ones abandon it, just as one discards mucus or spittle.
Like seeing a rabid dog, one flees in haste;
like a blade smeared with honey, like the head of a venomous serpent,
like the edge of a spear or halberd, or like a jar filled with filth.
Unable to relinquish them, it is like a starving dog gnawing on a dry bone;
they arise from false perception, like the moon reflected in water.
Like an echo in a valley, like a mirage, like an illusion,
like a bubble on water— born from conceptual discrimination,
they possess no substantial reality.
Deluded and attached, they claim that things are eternal and cannot bring themselves to renounce them.
When old age, sickness, and death arrive, they destroy their youth and vigor; all [beings] loathe this.
Those who possess wealth and treasures, yet do not know how to practice renunciation,
will suffer distress when it is scattered and lost by the five families.
It is just like a tree whose flowers and fruits are lush and abundant.
The multitude loved it, yet its branches and leaves withered and fell;
they abandoned it and paid it no heed. The aged, the weak, the poor, and the sick are likewise thus.
The world detests it, like a bolt of lightning-fire that consumes a great tree, or like a dilapidated house that will soon collapse.
There is a Dharma capable of bringing liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death;
I pray that the Honored One will renounce the world and preach such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death entangle and bind sentient beings.
Like the *māluka* creeper winding around a *nyagrodha* tree,
they rob one of their vital strength and damage all the sense faculties.
Just as heavy frost withers all the groves,
so youthful vigor and exquisite beauty are thereby corrupted and destroyed.
It is like a mountain fire that approaches from all four sides.
Wild beasts are within it, Panicking and suffering in distress.
Those dwelling in birth and death Are likewise so;
I pray you will quickly leave the home-life To rescue and deliver them.
The World-Honored One observes the suffering of illness, which afflicts and torments sentient beings,
like a grove of flowers withered by frost.
The World-Honored One observes the suffering of death, wherein love and affection are forever severed.
Separated from one's kin, never to behold them again;
like a flowing stream that never turns back, or like falling petals,
it can harm even the powerful and deprive them of their autonomy.
Travelling alone without companion, one departs according to one's karma;
all life is swallowed by death.
Like the garuḍa, which is able to devour all dragons, [death devours all beings].
Also like a king of elephants, being devoured by lions;
like a makara fish, able to swallow everything;
and like a fierce fire, burning down a forest.
"May the Honored One recall how, in the past, you made a great vow;
now is precisely the time, and it is fitting that you quickly renounce the world.
These palace ladies and musicians wish to delude the Bodhisattva."
Through the spiritual power of all Buddhas, these are transformed into the sound of Dharma.
All conditioned phenomena must eventually perish;
like lightning in the sky, they do not remain for even a moment.
They are like fragile earthenware, like borrowed objects,
like decaying grass or walls, and like sandy banks.
Depending upon causes and conditions, they possess no solidity or substance.
Like a lamp in the wind, like a mass of foam on the water,
like a bubble upon the surface of the water,
and like a plantain tree that has no solid core within— it is like an illusion, like a magical transformation.
It is like an empty fist; things arise through successive mutual dependence, yet fools do not understand and thus give rise to false attachments.
It is like human labor, as well as hemp and flax.
Through the combination of wooden segments, a rope is formed;
separated from this combination, it no longer constitutes a rope.
So too, when the twelve links of dependent origination are analyzed one by one, [they lose their causal efficacy].
In the past, present, and future, they have no intrinsic nature;
they cannot be found when sought, and it is likewise so.
Just as a seed is able to produce a sprout, [so too is the nature of phenomena].
The tooth and the seed are neither identical nor separate.
From ignorance, volitional formations arise;
ignorance and formations are likewise so.
Neither identical nor separate, its essential nature is empty and quiescent;
within the midst of causes and conditions, it cannot be found.
It is like a seal pressed into clay: the seal does not exist within the clay.
There is no seal within the mud; it must depend upon the mud for the seal.
The pattern and image can be seen; depending upon the sense faculty and the object, visual consciousness arises through the conjunction of these three factors.
It is said that there is "seeing," yet the object does not reside in consciousness, nor does consciousness reside in the object.
Within the faculty, the object, and consciousness, seeing fundamentally does not exist;
it is merely a false conceptualization through discrimination.
The arising of objects and characteristics is observed by the wise to be entirely devoid of marks, like illusions, dreams, and the like.
It is like drilling for fire: when the wood, the drill, and human effort—these three factors—come together, fire is produced;
yet within these three elements, there was originally no fire.
A temporary conjunction is called a "sentient being," yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is entirely unobtainable.
It is like the throat, together with the lips and tongue.
When struck and moved, it produces sound; yet within each individual part, the sound cannot be found.
It is only through the conjunction of various conditions that this sound exists.
Moment after moment they continue in succession, yet no real dharma exists;
they are like an echo in a valley, where the sound cannot be apprehended.
It is like a lute: the strings, the instrument, and the hands—
The sound arises from a combination of conditions; fundamentally, it has no coming or going.
Within these various conditions, one cannot find the sound;
nor can it be found by seeking it apart from conditions.
The internal and external aggregates are all entirely empty and quiescent;
they are without self and without person, and there is no life-principle.
In the past, you encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Having already realized the most supreme, true, and wondrous Dharma,
I pray that the Honored One will now, for the sake of all sentient beings,
rain down the nectar of the Dharma so that they may be fully satisfied.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Bodhisattva heard these verses, he focused exclusively on awakening with right mindfulness and without indolence.
For what reason?

Throughout the long night, the bodhisattva respects, reveres, and makes offerings to the True Dharma and its teachers; he gives rise to profound pure faith and seeks the True Dharma, delighting in the True Dharma and abiding in the True Dharma. Without ever feeling weary or satisfied with what he hears, he brings enlightenment to sentient beings.

They conceive deep respect for the masters who bestow the Dharma; they expound it for others without any expectation of reward, nor do they seek wealth or treasures by means of the Dharma; and when preaching the Dharma to the assembly, they are never stingy or parsimonious.

With courageous diligence and single-minded earnest seeking, they take the Dharma as their reliance, guarding the treasury of the Dharma; abiding in patience, they practice Prajñā and master skillful means.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"For many kalpas, the Bodhisattva has remained far removed from the faults of the five worldly desires. Yet, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, he manifests as dwelling within the realm of greed and desire. Through the power of his accumulated and increased store of all roots of goodness and superior merit, he manifests the enjoyment of vast and subtle realms of the five desires, yet his mind remains sovereign over them."

At that time, the Bodhisattva recollected the vows he had previously made; by virtue of those ancient vows, his contemplation of the Buddha-dharma became fully manifest before him. He gave rise to great compassion and observed the world: how prosperity and flourishing inevitably return to decay; and how birth and death abound with various afflictions, dangers, and terrors. Desiring to swiftly sever these and enter Great Nirvana, he reflected further.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “The Bodhisattva has long since understood the faults and afflictions of birth and death;

he neither grasps nor clings to them. He joyfully seeks the true merits of a Tathāgata and dwells in the quietude of an araṇya. His mind constantly delights in benefiting himself and others, and he practices with courageous diligence toward the unsurpassed path for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, benefit, tranquility, and nirvāṇa. He constantly gives rise to great kindness and great compassion, being able to gather in all sentient beings through the four means of integration without weariness, regarding all sentient beings as if they were his only child.”

His mind was unattached to any sensory objects; he established great assemblies for giving to increase his merit, remaining far removed from stinginess and greed, and practiced generosity without expecting recompense. Throughout the long night, he was courageous and diligent, skillfully subduing the afflictions of greed, anger, pride, stinginess, and envy, never for a moment forgetting the mind of omniscience.

Donning the great armor of generosity and clad in the mail of diligence, they deliver sentient beings with a heart of great compassion; their power of wisdom is firm and strong, never regressing, and with an impartial mind toward all beings, they cause everyone’s aspirations to be fulfilled according to their inclinations.
Knowing the timely and the untimely, and awakening to what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, they dedicate [their merit] toward Bodhi.

Within the act of giving, they maintain purity in the three spheres; with vajra-wisdom, they sever the four māras. Having accomplished the practice of precepts, they are well able to guard the actions of body, speech, and mind; even regarding minor transgressions, they harbor great dread, keeping their minds constantly pure. Amidst all defilements—malicious words, insults, derision, slander, beatings, humiliations, and imprisonment—they are never once disturbed.
Fully endowed with patience, their minds are pliant and well-tamed; the deeds they undertake are always steadfast, and their virtuous intentions never regress.
Possessing mindfulness and wisdom, they constantly cultivate right concentration; attaining the light of insight, they are able to shatter all darkness.

The mind constantly contemplates and perceives the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and impurity; it has already skillfully cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

Furthermore, they constantly abide in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, deeply penetrating dependent origination and awakening to reality; they always know for themselves without relying on the understanding of others, and roam within the three gates of liberation. They understand all phenomena to be like illusions, dreams, shadows, the moon reflected in water, images in a mirror, mirages in the heat, and echoes in the wind.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since many kalpas past, the Bodhisattva has constantly dwelled in such wisdom, such merit, such diligence, and such benefit throughout the four modes of deportment."
The Buddhas of the ten directions further caused the musical instruments of the palace maidens to produce subtle and wondrous sounds to exhort and inspire the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, wishing to transform the palace maidens, they enabled them to immediately realize four dharma-gates.
What are the four?
First, they gather [beings] through skillful means: generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
Second, they ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels continues without interruption, preserving the nature of omniscience and never retreating from their power of aspiration.
Third, their power of wisdom is firm and stable, and they do not abandon sentient beings through great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Fourth, they possess the power of the provisions for superior wisdom, which discerns all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Because the Dharma-gate of Great Adornment has been manifested before them, and for the sake of bringing about the accomplishment of the various court ladies within the palace,
he immediately at that time performed a great supernormal power (*mahā-ṛddhi*),

causing all the court ladies to understand and realize the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates expressed in the words emerging from the musical sounds— namely, the vast mind and the mind of compassion for sentient beings.
Seeking the bodhicitta, they give rise to the profound resolve and engender pure faith in the Buddha-dharma;
remaining free from arrogance, they revere the true Dharma, distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome, and maintain mindfulness of all Buddhas.
They practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the six supernormal powers.

Regarding the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*),
the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*),
each of these is analyzed in terms of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
"Impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, non-attachment, cessation, the knowledge of the exhaustion of birth, and even nirvana"—
by means of his bodhisattva supernormal powers, he caused such sounds to emerge from the music.
When the various court ladies heard this sound, they were filled with wonder; they leaped for joy and experienced a state never before known.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"While the Bodhisattva resided in the royal palace, he was able to cause eighty-four thousand court ladies to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, having heard this Dharma, attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and spoke subtle verses, exhorting the Bodhisattva to leave the household life with all haste.
Chapter 14: The Dream Vision At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"After the devas had exhorted the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva then appeared in a dream to King Śuddhodana. Within the dream, the king beheld the Bodhisattva, having shaved off his hair and beard, departing through the palace gate, surrounded by immeasurable devas as he went."
Then, having awakened from his dream, the king asked the women of the inner quarters:
"Is the prince currently in the palace,
or has he gone out for a tour of observation?"
The palace attendants replied, "The Prince has been in the palace and has not gone out to sightsee.
The King’s mind still harbored the suspicion that the Bodhisattva had already departed; filled with despondency and distress as if an arrow had pierced his heart, he reflected thus:
"Since the signs of the events in my dream are thus, I know for certain that the Prince will surely renounce the household life.
She further thought:
"From this day forward, do not allow the Prince to go out on excursions again; instead, have the court ladies entice him with the five desires to engender in him a sense of attachment."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, for the sake of the Bodhisattva, constructed three seasonal palaces:
the first was warm to withstand the deep winter; the second was cool to meet the scorching summer heat; and the third was temperate, being neither cold nor hot.
Furthermore, he constructed a heavy gate that was difficult to open or close; it required five hundred men to open or shut it, and the sound of its opening or closing could be heard forty *li* away.

He questioned all those who were well-versed in astronomy, thoroughly skilled in the methods of physiognomy, and possessed of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), commanding them to provide a prediction in advance. All such persons declared:
"The Prince shall escape through the Auspicious Gate by leaping over the city wall."
When the king heard this, his grief and distress increased all the more. Monks!
Later, on one occasion, the Bodhisattva desired to go out for an excursion and thus commanded his charioteer:
"You may prepare the carriage; I shall go out for a short while.
The charioteer reported to the king:
"Today the Prince wishes to go out for an excursion."

Upon hearing this, the King immediately dispatched messengers to sweep and adorn the gardens. He further commanded the relevant officials to level and clear the roads, sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground and scattering various famous flowers. Between the jeweled trees, silk banners and canopies were suspended, adorned in succession with pearl necklaces. Golden and silver jewel bells hung everywhere; stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced exquisite and subtle sounds. From the city to the garden, everything was decorated all around, so magnificent, brilliant, and pure that it resembled a celestial palace.

Furthermore, he caused that all loathsome things—such as the aged, the diseased, and corpses—as well as those with impaired faculties, such as the deaf, the blind, and the mute, and all other inauspicious matters, were driven away from the roadside.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva, accompanied by his officials and attendants leading and following him, departed through the eastern gate of the city.

At that moment, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as an old man: his hair was white, his body frail, and his complexion withered; leaning on a staff, he walked bent over, gasping for breath with his head bowed. His skin and bones were joined together while his flesh and sinews had wasted away; his teeth were missing, and mucus and saliva flowed together; now standing and now walking, he would suddenly collapse or fall prostrate."
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva asked the charioteer:
"Who is this person? His appearance is such as this."
Then, by means of his supernatural powers, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven caused the charioteer to report to the Bodhisattva:
"This is an old man.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'old age'? He replied:

"Generally speaking, what is called old age refers to having passed through youth and gradually reached a state of decay. The faculties wither and mature; physical strength becomes feeble; food and drink are no longer digested; the body becomes emaciated; one no longer possesses majesty and is held in contempt by others; every movement and posture is accompanied by intense suffering, and the remainder of life is but brief. For these reasons, it is called old age."
He asked again:
"Is this man alone like this, or is it so for all?
The charioteer replied:
"All the worlds are exactly like this.
The Bodhisattva asked again,
"Will my own body also become like this?"
The charioteer replied,
"All who are born, whether noble or base, possess this suffering. At that time,
the Bodhisattva was filled with sorrow and distress, and said to the charioteer:
"What leisure do I have now to go to the gardens for wanton play?
I must devise a means to escape from this suffering.
Having said this, he immediately turned his carriage around and returned to the palace.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"Did the Prince enjoy himself today while sporting in the gardens?
The charioteer replied:
"Great King, you should know!

As the Prince went out of the city and reached the middle of the road, he suddenly encountered an old man upon the path whose strength was failing and whose body was utterly exhausted. Upon seeing him, the Prince immediately returned to the palace."
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"These are the signs of my son’s renunciation; what the seer Asita said is likely true."
Thereupon, they further increased the five sensual pleasures to entertain him. Monks!
On another occasion, when the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens saw that the Bodhisattva had returned to dwell among the five sensual pleasures, they reflected thus:
"I should now further manifest signs and appearances for the Bodhisattva so that he may attain awakening and quickly leave the household life.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again summoned his charioteer and addressed him, saying:
"I wish now to go to the gardens to sightsee; you must quickly report this to the Great King and prepare a retinue of carriages, for I shall go out for a short while."
Having heard this, the King summoned his ministers and addressed them, saying:
"Previously, when the Crown Prince went out through the eastern gate of the city, he encountered an old man on the road and returned midway, filled with sorrow and displeasure."

Now, as he again seeks to go forth to the pleasure groves, it is fitting that the entire route from the city to the gardens be made pure and clean. Let silken banners and canopies be suspended, incense be burned, and flowers be scattered; do not allow filth, impurities, or any inauspicious sights such as the aged, the sick, the dead, or those afflicted by disease to remain upon the roads.
The officials, having received the decree, prepared the procession with even greater magnificence than before.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, accompanied by his retinue and preceded and followed by attendants, departed through the southern gate of the city.

Then, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a sick man—severely ill, withered and jaundiced, gasping for breath, his flesh and bones withered away, his appearance frail and emaciated, lying amidst filth and excrement in great suffering, attended by two people standing by the roadside.
He again asked the charioteer,
"Who is this? and the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva:
"This person is ill.
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'ill'?"

He replied: "What is called 'sickness' arises entirely from immoderate diet and unrestrained desire; the four elements become disordered and hundreds of ailments arise. One finds no peace in sitting or lying down, and every movement is fraught with peril. The breath grows faint and the life remains but for a moment; for these reasons, it is called sickness."
He asked again:
"Is this man alone like this, or is it so for all?
The charioteer replied:
"All the worlds are exactly like this.
He further asked:
"Will my own body also become like this?"
The charioteer replied,
"All who are born, whether noble or lowly, possess this suffering. At that time,
the Bodhisattva was sorrowful and unhappy, and he said to the charioteer:
"What leisure do I have now to go to the gardens for wanton play?
I must contemplate a skillful means to escape this suffering.
Having said this, he immediately turned his carriage around and returned to the palace.
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"Has the Prince gone out from the city today for sightseeing and pleasure?
The charioteer replied:

"Your Majesty, you should know that when the Prince went out of the city and reached the middle of his journey, he suddenly saw by the side of the road a sick man whose strength was utterly exhausted and who was undergoing great suffering. Upon seeing him, the Prince immediately returned to the palace."
Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"These are the signs of my son’s renunciation; the words of the seer Asita are not false."
Thereupon, they further increased the five sensory pleasures to entertain him. Monks!
On another occasion, when the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven saw that the Prince had returned to indulging in the five sensory pleasures, they reflected thus:
"I should now further manifest signs and appearances for the Bodhisattva so that he may attain awakening and quickly renounce the household life.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again summoned his charioteer and addressed him, saying:
"I wish now to go to the gardens for sightseeing; you should prepare the carriage, and I shall go forth for a short while."
The charioteer again reported this to the Great King; having heard it, the King said to the charioteer:
"When the Prince went out through the eastern and southern gates previously, he returned in sorrow after seeing an old man and a sick man. Now, you should have him go out through the western gate."

My heart apprehends that he will not be joyful upon his return; it is fitting that you dispatch both those within and without to adorn the roads, with incense, flowers, banners, and canopies surpassing those of former times, and ensure that inauspicious matters such as old age, sickness, and death do not appear by the roadside.
The officials, receiving the decree, adorned [the funeral bier] with twice the splendor as before.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, accompanied by his various ministers and attendants leading and following him, departed through the western gate of the city. Then, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested as a dead man lying upon a litter, strewn with incense and flowers, while the members of the household followed behind, wailing and weeping as they escorted him.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva felt profound compassion in his heart and asked the charioteer:
"Who is this person, adorned above with incense and flowers?
And why is there such a great retinue weeping for him in sorrow?"
Then, by means of their supernormal powers, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven caused the charioteer to reply to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"This is a dead man.
He asked again:
"What is meant by death?
He replied:

"What is called death is when the consciousness departs from the body and the life-faculty has already ceased; one is forever separated from parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen through the severance of affectionate ties, never to behold them again."
After life has ended, the spirit travels alone back to its different destination; affection and aversion no longer recognize one another.
Such a death is truly to be pitied.
He asked again:
"Is it only when this person dies that all [these things] must naturally occur?
He replied to the Bodhisattva:
"Whatever is born must inevitably return to death.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva became deeply unsettled and spoke these words:
"If there is such suffering of death in the world, how can one act with negligence amidst it?"
"What leisure do I have now to visit the gardens? I must contemplate a skillful means to seek liberation from this suffering.
He then turned his carriage around and returned to the palace.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"Did the Crown Prince go out today to the gardens for pleasure?
The charioteer replied,
"Great King, you should know this!"

As the Prince went out of the city, he suddenly saw by the roadside a dead man lying upon a bier, being carried by four men, while his kinsmen wailed in grief. Upon seeing this, the Prince was struck with sorrow and displeasure; he then turned back from the middle of the road and returned to the palace.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"These are the signs of my son’s renunciation; the seer Asita was not mistaken.
Thereupon, he increased the five sensory pleasures even further to provide him with entertainment.
"O Bhikṣus!
On another occasion, when the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens saw that the Prince had returned to his palace and was dwelling amidst the five sensual pleasures, they reflected:
'We should now manifest further signs for the Bodhisattva so that he will quickly renounce the world.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva again summoned his charioteer and addressed him, saying:
"Today I wish to go to the gardens for sightseeing; you may prepare the carriage, for I shall go out for a short while."
The charioteer again reported this to the King, his father. Having heard this, the King said to the charioteer:

"Previously, when the Prince went out through the three gates, he encountered old age, sickness, and death, and was filled with sorrow and displeasure. Now, you must have him exit through the northern gate; adorn the road with incense, flowers, banners, and canopies so that it surpasses what it was before, and ensure that no further inauspicious occurrences such as old age, sickness, or death are present by the roadside."
The officials, having received the decree, prepared [the carriage] more magnificently than before.
At that time, the Prince, accompanied by his various ministers and attendants leading and following him, departed through the northern gate of the city.

Then, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven transformed himself into a bhikṣu, wearing dyed robes and with his hair and beard shaven; holding a *khakkhara* staff in his hand, he walked while looking at the ground, his appearance dignified and his deportment composed.
The Crown Prince saw him from afar and asked,
"Who is this man? Then,
by means of his supernormal powers, a deity of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven caused the charioteer to reply to the Bodhisattva:
"Such a person is called one who has left the household life.
Thereupon, the Prince descended from his carriage, paid his respects, and asked him:
"What benefit does one who has left the household life derive?"
The bhikṣu replied:

"I have seen that for householders, birth, old age, sickness, and death are all impermanent; they are all phenomena of decay and instability. Therefore, I have abandoned my kinsmen to dwell in seclusion, diligently seeking skillful means to escape these sufferings."

The noble path of outflows-free cultivation that I have practiced, walking in the True Dharma to subdue the sense faculties, giving rise to great compassion to bestow fearlessness, acting with equanimity toward all beings to protect and care for them, remaining unstained by the world to attain eternal liberation—this is therefore called the Dharma of leaving home.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva felt profound joy and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Among gods and humans, this alone is supreme; I shall certainly practice and study this path."
Having seen this, he mounted his chariot and returned.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"Did the Prince find any pleasure during his excursion?"
He replied: "Great King,
you should know that when the Prince went out just now, everything along the way was magnificent and auspicious, with nothing inauspicious."

Suddenly there appeared a man wearing dyed robes, with his hair and beard shaven, carrying an alms bowl and a monk’s staff as he walked; his deportment was dignified and his manner was composed and deliberate.

The Prince immediately descended from his carriage and paid his respects; once their conversation was concluded, he prepared his chariot and returned home, never knowing what had actually been discussed.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he thought to himself:
"The words of the seer Asita are not false."
"Then, they further increased the subtle and exquisite five objects of desire to entertain him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, wishing to cause the Bodhisattva to leave the household life with speed, again caused the King, his father, to have seven dreams:"
First, he dreamed that the banner of Śakra was being carried out through the eastern gate of Kapilavastu by a great multitude of people.
Second, he dreamed that the Prince, riding upon a great fragrant elephant and attended by a retinue of guards, departed through the southern gate of Kapilavastu.
Third, he dreamed that the Prince was riding in a chariot drawn by four horses and departed through the western gate of Kapilavastu.
Fourth, he dreamed that a precious wheel emerged from the northern gate of Kapilavastu.
Fifth, he dreamed that the Prince was at a crossroads, raising a drumstick to strike a drum.

Sixth, he dreamed that within the city of Kapilavastu there was a tall tower, from which the Prince cast down various kinds of precious jewels on all four sides, and countless sentient beings vied with one another to carry them away.
Seventh, he dreamed that not far from the city, six men suddenly raised their voices in lamentation and weeping.
After King Śuddhodana had this dream, his heart was filled with great fear; he woke up abruptly and summoned his ministers, telling them:
"During the night I had such a dream; you should call a dream-interpreter for me to explain its meaning."
Then a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a brahmin, donned a deer-skin garment, stood outside the palace gate, and proclaimed these words:
"I am well able to interpret the Great King's dream."
Upon hearing this report, the ministers summoned him into the palace.
King Śuddhodana then related his dream in detail, saying to the brahmin:
"What kind of omen is such a dream as this?"
The brahmin said:
"Great King, you should know!

As for the dream of the imperial banner being carried out through the eastern gate by a multitude of people, this is the omen that the Prince shall go forth into homelessness, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas."
"Great King, you should know this!

As for the dream in which the Prince mounted a great fragrant elephant and, accompanied by attendants and guards, departed through the southern gate of the city—this is the manifestation of the Prince having already left the household life, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and acquired the ten powers (*daśabala*)."
"Great King, you should know!

As for the dream in which the Prince mounted a chariot drawn by four horses and departed through the western gate of the city, this is the omen that once he has left the household life, the Prince will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*)."

"Great King, you should know that the dream of the precious wheel exiting through the northern gate of the city is an omen that once the Prince has left the household life, he will realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the wheel of Dharma."
“Great King, you should know this!

As for the dream in which the Prince stood at a crossroads beating a drum with a mallet, this is an omen that after the Prince has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the gods will transmit the news of it even unto the Brahma world.”
"Great King, you should know!

As for the dream in which the Prince cast down treasures from atop a high tower and countless sentient beings vied to carry them away—this signifies that once the Prince has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he shall rain down the treasures of the Dharma among the eight classes of gods and humans. These are the images of various dharmas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
“Great King, you should know!

As for the dream in which, not far from the city, six men suddenly raised their voices in lamentation and weeping: this is an omen that once the Prince has left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the six heretical teachers will experience mental anguish and distress.”
At that time, after the emanated man had explained the dream to King Śuddhodana, he said:
"Great King! You should rejoice;
do not give way to sorrow or distress."
"Why is this? This auspicious dream shall yield a great fruit.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

When King Śuddhodana heard the brahmin’s explanation of the dream’s significance, he feared that the Prince would leave home to study the Way; thereupon, he further increased the provisions for the five desires.
At that time, Yaśodharā also dreamed twenty kinds of terrifying things; she suddenly awoke, her heart trembling with alarm and fear, losing her composure.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"What is it that you fear? Yaśodharā wept and said:
"O Prince! I have just dreamed that the entire great earth shook in every direction;
furthermore, I saw a large, fresh white parasol that had always provided me shade suddenly snatched away by Chandaka and carried off."
Furthermore, he saw the banner of Śakra toppled and lying on the ground;
he saw the necklaces upon his body being swept away by the water;
and he saw the sun, moon, and stars all falling from the sky.
Again, he saw his own hair being cut off and carried away by one wielding a precious sword;
again, he saw his own body, which was subtle, exquisite, and upright, suddenly become hideous;
again, he saw his own hands and feet all broken.
Furthermore, he saw that his body was naked and red without cause;
he saw that the bed upon which he sat had sunk into the earth;
and he saw that the four legs of the bed on which he constantly sat and lay with the Prince had all broken off.
Furthermore, he saw a mountain of jewels on all four sides steep and lofty, being consumed by fire and crumbling to the ground;
he further saw a jewel tree within the Great King’s palace blown down by the wind;
and he further saw the bright sun obscured, leaving heaven and earth in darkness.
Again, he saw the bright moon in the sky, surrounded by a multitude of stars, suddenly vanish within this palace;
again, he saw a great luminous torch emerge from the city of Kapilavastu;
and again, he saw the guardian deity of this city, handsome and pleasing to behold, standing at the gate and wailing with bitter lamentation.
Again, he saw this city transform into a desolate wilderness;
again, he saw that the trees, springs, and ponds within the city had all completely dried up;
and again, he saw powerful warriors grasping weapons and galloping in all four directions.
"O Prince!
My mind is deeply unsettled by such a dream; will my body not soon meet with death?
Will I not be separated from those I love?"
"What omen is this? Is it auspicious or inauspicious?
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva reflected within his mind:
"The time for my renunciation has arrived; this is a portentous sign that has caused this consort to see such a dream."
He comforted Yaśodharā, saying:
"Queen, you should not harbor such fear now. Why is this?"

Dreams are inverted and lack any real substance; even if one were to see in a dream the collapse of the imperial palace or the falling of the sun and moon, what injury or damage could this cause to the queen’s body?

"Chanda, take the parasol and depart; since it was said that [the throne] was snatched away in a dream, all such things are but empty falsehoods. I shall simply rest in peace and need not feel any anxiety.
That night, the Bodhisattva himself had five dreams:
first, he dreamed that his body lay upon the great earth, with his head resting on Mount Sumeru, his hands upholding the great ocean, and his feet treading upon the Bohai Sea.
Second, he dreamed that there was a grass named "Establishment" (*pratisthā*) which grew from his navel, its tip reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Third, he dreamed that four birds came from the four directions, their feathers variegated and mottled; as they alighted upon the Bodhisattva’s feet, they were transformed into white.
Fourth, he dreamed that white beasts with black heads all came to kneel and lick the Prince’s body.
Fifth, he dreamed that there was a mountain of excrement, vast and towering in form, over which the Bodhisattva walked about on all sides without being defiled by it.
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Fifteen: On Leaving the Home Life At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the stillness of the night, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:”
"If I were to leave home in private without first informing my father, the King, there would be two kinds of faults:
first, it would violate the teachings of the Dharma; second, it would not accord with worldly propriety."

Having reflected thus, he departed from his dwelling and proceeded to the palace of his father, the King. He emitted a great radiance, such that all the terraces, halls, pavilions, and gardens were doubly adorned and illuminated by its brilliant light.
Having encountered the light, the King immediately awakened and said to his attendant:
"What kind of light is this?
The night has not yet ended; could it be the light of the sun?"
The attendant replied,
"It is not the light of the sun.
He then addressed the king again with a verse:
"The terraces, pavilions, and multi-storied towers, the walls, and the gardens—none of these cast any shadows;
therefore, this is not the light of the rising sun."
The mandarin ducks and kingfishers, the peacocks and kalaviṅkas—
before these flocks of birds had yet begun to soar or sing,
this light appeared; it is most rare and unprecedented, never seen before.
It causes the mind to rejoice, removing heat and attaining coolness.
This must be a person of supreme virtue, whose radiance shines here.
Then the king rose from his reclining position and surveyed the ten directions in detail.
Then he beheld the body of the Bodhisattva, whose majestic virtue was unsurpassed.
With a heart of profound and utmost reverence, he intended to offer his respects;
yet by the Bodhisattva’s supernormal power, the King was firmly prevented from rising.
Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed his father, the King, saying:
"Great King, do not be distressed; do not create obstacles for me.
Now I wish to leave the home life; please, out of compassion, grant me your permission."
When the King heard these words, he contemplated what stratagem to employ;
weeping, he turned toward the Bodhisattva and spoke thus:
"My great rank and the wealth of the nation—I am able to relinquish it all."
"Setting aside the matter of leaving home, I have nothing else for which I would not sacrifice.
With a wondrous voice, the Bodhisattva again addressed his father, the King:
"I have privately four aspirations that have not yet been fulfilled according to my original heart's desire."
"Great King, if you grant me this, I shall sever all hope for renunciation.
My first wish is that I never grow old; my second wish is that I remain forever youthful;
my third wish is that I always be free from illness; and my fourth wish is that I never die."
Having heard these words, the king addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"This matter is exceedingly difficult; it is not within my power to accomplish it.
Though the various sages may live for an eon, they ultimately end in destruction."
"Who is it that seeks to leave behind birth, old age, and death, And alone pursues a body of eternal permanence?
The Bodhisattva replied to the king:
"If these four vows are difficult to obtain, I now seek but one vow: Never again to undergo a future existence."
When the King heard the Bodhisattva’s words, his affectionate heart grew slightly thin. He spoke thus:
“I too now rejoice; may I benefit all sentient beings and cause your vow to be fulfilled.”
"Though he spoke these words, his heart still harbored burning affliction.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva withdrew with joy; though he came and went again, no one was aware of it."
When morning dawned, the King summoned his kinsmen and the Śākya clansmen and spoke to them thus:
"Yesterday at midnight, the Prince came to request ordination; if I grant him this, the kingdom will have no successor."
"What skillful means can you now employ to cause him to turn his mind away from this?
Then the Śākyas said to the Great King:
"We shall together protect the Prince; by what power could he possibly leave the home life by force?"

At that time, the King, his father, commanded his kinsmen to station five hundred Śākya youths outside the eastern gate of the city of Kapilavastu. These youths were heroic, majestic, and valiant, invincible in battle. Each youth was escorted by five hundred chariots for combat, and beside each chariot stood five hundred strong men holding halberds in front;
there were likewise five hundred at each of the southern, western, and northern gates, as previously described.

Upon the city walls, men bearing swords and staves were stationed in a continuous perimeter; furthermore, the long-standing Śākya ministers sat in rows at the four crossroads, all fully prepared for duty. The King himself selected five hundred stalwart warriors, clad in armor and wielding spears, who mounted elephants and horses to patrol the four sides of the city day and night without a moment’s rest.
At that time, the Great Queen Mahāprajāpatī gathered the palace ladies within the royal precincts and spoke these verses:
"Tonight, none of you shall yield to sleep;
you must erect a sublime, lofty banner, illuminated by mani-jewels."
Pearl necklaces on all four sides also emit a great radiance,
illuminating the midst of the palace so that all may behold it as clearly as the sun.
Celestial music is performed there, and from the strings emerge subtle and wondrous sounds.
Flower-crests hang like half-moons, adorned with jeweled garlands and lion motifs;
armlets, bracelets, and rings—various ornaments to grace the body.
The doors and windows are fitted with double bolts, secured firmly with keys and locks.
Whenever he enters or exits, you shall attend him in person;
at every movement and pause, you must remain fully aware. You who serve him should carry weapons:
battle-axes and nooses, spears, halberds, and lances.
Do not give rise to thoughts of pride or indolence; guard the palace gates and courtyards on all sides.
You who protect the Prince must do so as one protects one's own eyes, lest he abandon the world like the departure of a king of elephants.
"The precious throne lacks an heir, and the land is devoid of majesty.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, there were twenty-eight yakṣa generals, with Pāñcika-rāja as their leader, who resided together in the palace of Vaiśravaṇa and deliberated among themselves, saying:"
"The Bodhisattva now wishes to leave the household life; what offerings shall we provide for you?
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the host of yakṣas, saying, "The Bodhisattva is about to leave the household life; you should support and receive his horse's hooves."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"Tonight the Bodhisattva intends to go forth from home; you should provide protection, assistance, and support."
At that time, there was a son of heaven among that assembly named Śāntamati, who spoke these words:
"I shall cause all the soldiers, court ladies, and guards protecting the Bodhisattva in the city of Kapilavastu to fall into a deep sleep, so that they are entirely unaware."
"Furthermore, the Devaputra Vyūharati spoke thus:
'I shall now cause all the elephants, horses, and various other creatures within and without that city to become silent and free from sound.'"
Furthermore, the divine son Vyūhamati spoke these words:

"I shall, from that place, manifest a jeweled path in the void of space, paved with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and rubies; I shall scatter various famous flowers spread thickly upon it, and hang silken banners and canopies arranged along both sides of the road."
"Furthermore, there were various great elephant kings, with King Airāvaṇa as their leader, who spoke thus:
'Upon the tip of my trunk, I shall manifest a multi-storied pavilion, within which are celestial maidens who provide accompaniment by drumming, dancing, and singing.'"
"Furthermore, there were various great dragon kings, with King Varuṇa as their leader, who spoke thus:
'We shall emit clouds of sandalwood incense and aloeswood incense, raining down sandalwood powder and aloeswood powder, so that wondrous fragrances will pervade and fill the void.'"
Furthermore, there was a Devaputra named Dharmacārin, who spoke these words:
"I shall now dispatch all the beautiful women within my palace, so that their appearances may be transformed and ruined, making them unfit for proximity."
"Furthermore, there was the Devaputra Vikramin, who spoke these words:
'I shall awaken the Bodhisattva during the middle watch of the night.
Śakra-devānām-indra spoke thus:"
"I shall now also reveal the path for that bodhisattva.
Thus, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others, all provided protection and assistance to the bodhisattva according to their respective capacities.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upright in the Music Hall and reflected:
'All Buddhas of the past have made four kinds of subtle and wondrous great vows.'"
What are the four?

"First, may I, in the future, personally realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attain sovereignty over all dharmas to become a Dharma King; through the wisdom of diligence, may I rescue and deliver all sentient beings who are bound by the prison of craving and afflicted by suffering, causing them all to be liberated."

"Second, there are sentient beings who possess this thicket of the dark forest of birth and death, afflicted by the cataracts of ignorance and delusion; for them, one takes emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as a lamp and medicine to shatter all obscurations of darkness and remove their heavy hindrances, thereby accomplishing such gates of skillful wisdom."

"Third, there are sentient beings who erect the banner of arrogance and give rise to the notions of 'I' and 'mine'; with their thoughts, perceptions, and views inverted, they cling to false and illusory constructs. For them, I preach the Dharma so that they may attain understanding and realization."

"Fourth, seeing that sentient beings dwell in a state of non-quiescence, transmigrating through the three periods of time like a whirling firebrand or like a ball of thread entangling itself, he preaches the Dharma for them so that their bonds may be severed."
Thus, these four kinds of vast vows and right mindfulness appeared before him.

At that time, by means of their supernormal powers, the Dharma-practitioner Devaputra and the assembly of Śuddhāvāsa devas caused the bodies and appearances of all the court ladies to become utterly disfigured, and the palace where they resided to appear like a cemetery.
Having manifested this, he addressed the Bodhisattva from the midst of the sky, saying:
“Your countenance is pure like a lotus flower; In merit and wisdom, none can compare.
One should observe women and keep far away from them; Why then do you give rise to a mind of attachment toward them?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied with a verse:
"I now contemplate this realm of lustful desire; All things are subject to transformation and decay, like a putrid corpse.
I vow to forever emerge from the entanglements of craving, And never again give rise to attachment within it."
"At that time, the Bodhisattva saw that all the beautiful women within the palace had their physical forms transformed and decayed;
some had their garments fallen away, exposing their bodies in ugliness; some had their hair disheveled and their flower crowns shattered;
some had their countenances withered and their necklaces broken and scattered; and some had their lips and mouths crooked and askew."
Some had eyes with squinting corners; some were gasping for breath as if on the verge of death; some had tears and spittle flowing together; some coughed incessantly;
some waved their hands and kicked their feet; some had faces that were bluish-white and hideous, terrifying to behold;
some had their skin cracked open and fouled with pus and blood; some wailed piteously; others were possessed by great... [fear].
Some were laughing; others were gnashing their teeth; some were talking incoherently; some stood leaning against walls;
some sat precariously perched upon couches; some lay with drums as pillows; some slept while embracing lutes;
some, while asleep, held flutes in their mouths and made sounds by biting them; some took various musical instruments and threw them about in disorder; or they stared blankly.
They slept with their faces turned toward the ground, some with mouths agape, others with eyes closed;
some were voiding excrement and urine amidst a stifling stench, some had their heads covered, while others lay with their heads bared,
tossed about in utter disorder, sprawling hither and thither.
"The former physical beauty and fine features have all been transformed and ruined by the various supernatural powers of the devas.
Having observed such various signs as these, he reflected with tranquil mindfulness:
"The female body is impure and wretched; it is only the foolish commoner who gives rise to false craving for it."
Arousing a heart of great compassion, he spoke these words: "Alas!
The world!"
Alas! The world is most terrifying;
ordinary people, being ignorant, do not seek liberation.
This place is deceptive and devoid of anything desirable, like a painted vase filled with foul filth and poison;
it is difficult to cross and one cannot escape from it by oneself, like an old elephant mired in deep mud;
it is a place of intense suffering, like a slaughterhouse where all life is severed.
This place is impure, like a herd of swine in a latrine;
this place is flavorless, yet one falsely conceives it to have flavor, like a starving dog gnawing at a hollow bone;
this place is self-consuming, like a moth rushing into a bright candle.
This place is exhausted and parched, like aquatic creatures cast upon dry land;
this place is desperate and straitened, like a weary deer destroyed by fire;
this place is terrifying, like a condemned prisoner led to the marketplace.
In this place there is sinking, like a shipwrecked vessel upon the sea;
in this place there is peril and dread, like a blind man falling into a deep valley;
in this place there is no profit, like a gambler whose wealth has been entirely lost.
This place is devoid of moisture, like parched grass and wood during a great drought;
this place is capable of causing injury, like a sharp blade smeared with honey, which the ignorant and witless lick in their quest for flavor;
this place is subject to depletion, like the dark fortnight of the moon gradually coming to an end.
"In this place, all wholesome dharmas are extinguished without remainder, just as the fire at the end of an eon consumes everything.
Having spoken thus, he carefully deliberated through various similes; subsequently, he likewise observed his own body in succession from head to foot in the same manner.
Then he spoke in verse:
"My craving moistens the field of karma; Following conditions, I undergo birth and death.
Accumulating all manner of impurities, They combine and form this body."
Spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, and heart; Small and large intestines, the receptacles of the raw and the cooked;
Skin, flesh, and marrow; Hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
Its movements are like those of a mechanical device; It is a den for all manner of worms.
Excrement and filth are ever full; pus and blood flow constantly.
It is invaded by the anxieties of birth and death, and oppressed by old age, sickness, hunger, and thirst.
