The wise contemplate this suffering as being entirely like a hostile enemy.
"One should discard this illusory body; why then give rise to grasping and attachment?
Having thus contemplated his own body, the Bodhisattva focused his mindfulness before him and remained silent for a long time in stillness.
In the midst of the void, there were hosts of devas who addressed the Devaputra Dharmacārin, saying:
"The Bodhisattva is about to renounce the household life; now he lingers as if giving rise to doubt and regret."

Why is this? I see that when the Bodhisattva gazes upon the court ladies, he sometimes smiles joyfully and at other times frowns with displeasure; could it be that the Bodhisattva has given rise to attachment?
"However, his mind is like the great ocean; we, being ordinary and shallow, cannot fathom it.

The Deva Dharmacārin said, "For immeasurable kalpas, the Bodhisattva has relinquished all—head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—and made vows seeking unsurpassed bodhi with a mind that never regresses. How much less, now that this is his final body, would he give rise to attachment for base desires?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat, drew aside the curtain of the net made of the seven precious gems, and emerged slowly and with composure. Standing with palms joined, he maintained right mindfulness toward all the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Having formed this thought, he immediately beheld Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the Four Great Heavenly Kings and the Sun and Moon Deva Sons, each leading their respective retinues. From the east came the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, head of the Gandharvas, leading an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of Gandharvas who played various musical instruments, danced, and sang to the accompaniment of stringed music. They arrived at the city of Kapilavastu, circled it three times, and remained suspended in the air, joining their palms and bowing their heads in homage toward the Bodhisattva.

“The Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, leading his retinue of kumbhāṇḍa lords, came from the south accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kumbhāṇḍas. Each held a precious vessel filled with scented water; they arrived at the city of Kapilavastu, circumambulated it three times, and remained suspended in the air, joining their palms and bowing their heads in homage toward the Bodhisattva.”

“From the west, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, leading the lords of the nāgas and spirits, arrived from the western direction. Accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great nāga hosts, each holding various miscellaneous treasures, pearls, necklaces, and diverse flowers and incense, they further scattered clouds of incense, clouds of flowers, and clouds of jewels.

They also stirred subtle, light, and fragrant breezes. Upon reaching the city of Kapilavastu, they circled it three times and remained suspended in the air, joining their palms, bowing their heads, and paying homage to the Bodhisattva.”

“From the north, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, leading his retinue of yakṣa lords, arrived from the northern direction. Accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great yakṣas, they held precious jewels in their hands whose radiance surpassed that of hundreds of thousands of worldly lamps and torches. Clad in armor and grasping bows, swords, spears, halberds, pikes, wheels, lances, tridents, and crossbows, they reached the city of Kapilavastu, circled it three times, and remained suspended in the air, joining their palms and bowing their heads in homage toward the Bodhisattva.”

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue of all the devas numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads, carrying celestial flower garlands, powdered incense, unguents, robes, precious parasols, countless banners and streamers, and necklaces, arrived at the city of Kapilavastu. He circumambulated it three times and remained suspended in the air, joining his palms, bowing his head, and paying homage to the Bodhisattva.

"The Sun and Moon Devas arrived from the left and right, also bringing various articles of offering; they remained suspended in the air, joining their palms and bowing their heads in salutation toward the Bodhisattva."

At that time, the Bodhisattva surveyed the ten directions, gazing up at the void and the various constellations, and beheld the four world-protecting Great Heavenly Kings, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others. He further saw Śakra Devendra, the Lord of Devas, each leading hundreds of thousands of his own retinues as attendants before and behind, filling the entirety of space; the Puṣya star was then in conjunction with the moon.
At that time, the devas raised their voices and said:

"The Bodhisattva now desires to seek the supreme Dharma; this is precisely the right time. He should quickly renounce the household life, for he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
'Tonight, in this stillness, the time for renunciation has arrived.'"
He then approached Chandaka and said to him: "Chandaka!
You should bring me Kanthaka."
At that time, having heard these words, Chandaka thought to himself in secret:
"It is only midnight; what need is there for Kaṇṭhaka?
He then addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"Both inside and outside, all is profoundly peaceful; there are no matters of urgent distress, nor of good or evil. I do not understand why the Crown Prince needs Kaṇṭhaka. At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed Chandaka and spoke in verse: "My person is already complete In every auspicious matter;
I have attained the supreme path, And am about to realize the fruit of enlightenment. Therefore, I must now depart; Do not obstruct my way.
If you wish to bring me back, You must first attain the Way yourself. Only then shall you be able to lead me back."
"When you wish to leave to renounce the world, do not now disobey me.
Thereupon, having heard these verses of the Bodhisattva, Chandaka’s entire body trembled and shook, unable to support itself.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again to Chandaka:
"I now desire to subdue the thieves of the afflictions and fetters for the sake of all sentient beings; therefore, I must have that Kanthaka."
"Do not oppose my will; quickly saddle him and bring him here.
At that time, Chandaka deliberately spoke in a loud voice, hoping that everyone within the palace would hear and know it, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"The Prince has always been free from error, and in all his actions he invariably chooses the proper time. Why do you now seek Kaṇṭhaka?"
The devas dwelling in space, through their supernormal powers, caused all of them not to perceive anything at all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva secretly addressed Chandaka in verse:
"Chandaka, you should know: I now observe this place."
All things are utterly terrifying, like a cemetery;
they are as if dwelling with rākṣasas, or like the burrows of maggots in a carbuncle,
or similar to the fluids within a womb, where one lies sprawled and disordered.
I perceive the suffering of the five desires; my mind is profoundly unsettled.
I have no wish to dwell in this palace, but rather to wander and observe within the gardens.
Having beheld the sufferings of old age and sickness, as well as the sight of a corpse, [my heart is turned away].
"I am determined to leave the household life; you must quickly fetch Kaṇṭhaka.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"When the Prince was yet an infant, the physiognomists performed a divination and reported to the King:"
"The Prince possesses the marks and signs of a Great Man; he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).

I have also heard that wise men of the world practice various austerities—some do not clip their nails, some hang themselves upside down, some clothe themselves in tree bark, some pluck out their own hair, some observe the prohibitions of cattle or deer, and some scorch their bodies with the five heats. They cultivate such causes of suffering while praying for the fruit of happiness. How much more so for the Prince, who is destined to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents and endowed with the seven treasures!
All the world says that the Prince will surely obtain this position of a Wheel-Turning King.
What the seer prophesied cannot be false; how could he thus abandon such a precious throne?
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Chandaka:

"In the past, the seers prophesied only that I would become a Wheel-Turning King, yet there were also prophecies that I would attain the Way of the Buddha; between these two prophecies, which one is definitive?"
"Be careful not to speak falsely.
Chandaka replied,
"In the past, the seer Asita joined his palms and said:"
"Great King, you should know that the King’s crown prince will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he will never remain at home as a wheel-turning monarch."
Why is this? Because the marks of a Buddha are clearly manifest, whereas the marks of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) are not so clear.
However, the Śākyas kept this secret and did not transmit it, fearing that the Prince would leave home to study the Way; they did not think the Prince would still remember this matter.
The Bodhisattva spoke, saying: "Chanda!

From the time I descended from Tuṣita to be born, through my stay in the womb until my emergence, I have not forgotten any of those events; how much less could I forget the prophecy bestowed upon me by the seer?"
"Chanda! The devas further exhorted me, saying:
'The Bodhisattva will swiftly go forth into homelessness; he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall turn the Wheel of Dharma.'"
"Therefore, you should know that I shall certainly attain Buddhahood. Chanda!

I would rather have my limbs severed, eat food mixed with poison, enter a great mass of fire, or throw myself from a high cliff than remain at home to enjoy the five sensual pleasures. Such worldly objects of the five desires are entirely impermanent and most truly terrifying."
He then spoke in verse:
"In the past I experienced the five desires, But now I truly dread their cause of suffering.
The stream of craving accumulated since beginningless time Is like the ocean, difficult to fill."
Chasing after flames only increases thirst; dwelling in a dream, one does not yet realize it is a dream.
An unbaked clay vessel is not firm; though filled with fine food, it is mixed with various poisons.
Floating clouds will surely dissipate; dewdrops do not remain for long.
Illusions delude the mind; bubbles arise and vanish in an instant;
the plantain tree lacks solidity; an empty fist deceives small children;
a serpent’s head is not to be approached; and a poisonous vine is ultimately difficult to touch.
"The wise should keep far away from it, just as one avoids a deep pit.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Bodhisattva had spoken this verse, he further addressed Chandaka:"

"I have also previously been among the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Six Desire Heavens; I have also been born in that Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception."

I recall that throughout immeasurable past lives, deluded and confused by coarse and base desires, I have undergone all manner of sufferings—beating, abuse, and bondage—and have had my body and life harmed, leading to death and entry into the evil realms.

Now, having conceived a profound sense of weary detachment toward this world, I have no craving or defilement even for the most excellent and sublime realms of the devas; how much less would I indulge in or feel attachment for the five desires of this human realm?
Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses sovereign power, he ultimately cannot escape the afflictions of birth and death.

I observe that the wilderness of the world’s afflictions is most terrifying; there is no refuge and nothing to rely upon. Furthermore, beings are constantly submerged in the river of birth and death, where the treacherous rapids of sorrow and lamentation flow, the surging waves of anger and resentment surge, the whirlpools of craving and desire swirl, and the rākṣasas of various views constantly lie in wait for people. Within this, I cultivate the six perfections as my boat and raft, with wisdom as the oars and rudders, and faith as its sturdy hull. Having myself crossed over, I shall further gather in all sentient beings and cause them to reach the other shore.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Is the Prince’s mind now resolved?
The Bodhisattva replied to Chandaka, speaking in verse:
“‘Candaka, you should know: I have now reached a firm resolve;
for the sake of benefiting myself and others, I have aroused the mind of diligence.’”
Immovable like Mount Sumeru, I shall never be able to turn back;
even if thunderbolt-hail, swords, spears, and halberds,
or lightning-fire and glowing iron balls were to fall upon the crown of my head.
"Never, within the realm of the mundane, Will he give rise to a heart of attachment.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, leaping for joy in the midst of the void, rained down various celestial flowers and spoke in verse:
"Most supreme and pure as space, Unable to be defiled by smoke, clouds, dust, or mist."
"Without attachment to any realm of experience, they shall fulfill sublime benefits and attain Bodhi.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Śāntamati and the Devaputra Vyūharatī caused all the people of the city of Kapilavastu to fall into a deep sleep.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Chandaka: "Chandaka!
Do not cause me to give rise to grief or resentment now; you should quickly saddle Kanthaka and bring him here."
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"It is now only midnight; it is not yet the hour for departure. The entire palace and city are under guard; who ought to open the gates and locks here?"
Then, Śakra-devānām-indra, by means of his supernormal powers, caused all the gates to open spontaneously.
Having seen that the palace city gates were open, Chandaka was filled with agitation and longing; his grief intensified as he wept once more, saying:

"I am without a companion! All the fourfold army within and without this city, the Śākya ministers, the king, and the princes, as well as Yaśodharā and the ladies of the inner court, are all fast asleep and unaware."
"Where do you wish to go now?
To whom shall I speak further?
The Prince’s mind is thus resolved; though I now entreat him most earnestly that he not depart, I consider myself powerless and am unable to restrain him."
Then the assembly of devas in the void spoke to Chandaka, saying: "Chandaka!
Quickly prepare and bring Kaṇṭhaka; do not cause the Bodhisattva’s heart to be filled with grief and distress."

Why is this? Have you not seen the assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattvas, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, each with their own retinues, reverently making offerings, their brilliant radiance shining forth and illuminating all of space?
Having heard these words, Chandaka said to Kaṇṭhaka: "Kaṇṭhaka!
The Prince shall now mount you and depart."

He immediately took the finest golden bridle, jeweled saddle, and various ornaments to adorn the King of Horses; weeping with tears streaming down his face, he presented them and praised the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I pray that whatever the Prince desires may all be fulfilled, that all obstacles may be entirely eliminated, and that the world shall attain peace and happiness."

"When the Bodhisattva had mounted this horse-king, at the moment he first lifted his hoof, the great earth in the ten directions shook in six ways. He ascended into the void and proceeded, while the Four Great Kings supported the horse's hooves and Brahmā and Śakra revealed the jeweled path."

At that time, the Bodhisattva emitted a great radiance that illuminated all boundless worlds; those who were to be delivered were all delivered and liberated, and sentient beings suffering from affliction were all freed from their suffering.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva turned his gaze back and looked down upon the city of Kapilavastu, saying these words:

'If from this day forward I do not reach the ultimate limit of birth and death, I shall never again behold the city of Kapilavastu, much less walk, stand, sit, or lie within it. Thereafter, the multitude erected a stūpa at this spot."
“O bhikṣus! At that time, once the Bodhisattva had departed from the palace, the court ladies within the palace all woke up and searched for him everywhere, but they could not find the Bodhisattva.”
Yaśodharā broke out into loud wailing and rolled upon the ground; she tore out her own hair and snapped her necklaces, crying out in grief:
"How painful this is!"
How bitter it is! What can I rely upon now?
Since the Prince has abandoned me and departed, what is the use of my remaining alive?

Weeping and lamenting in inconsolable grief, the palace women gathered together, wailing and mourning as if fish had lost their water or a tree had been severed at its roots; the sound of their sobbing could be heard beyond the palace walls.
At that time, the palace ladies reported to the King, their father: "Tonight, upon waking from sleep, we did not see the Prince.
The official in charge of the stables also said:
"Now, Kanthaka has been lost."
Upon hearing this, the king raised his voice in a great cry and spoke these words:
"Alas, alas! Where has my beloved son gone now?"

Having spoken these words, he fainted and fell to the ground. An attendant official immediately sprinkled cold water on his face, and after a long while he regained consciousness. He then summoned all the officials in charge of security and commanded them, saying: "You generals have already failed to exercise due diligence and caused me to lose my son.
You must now divide yourselves into internal and external parties and search for him with all speed. If you find him, entice him with kind words and bring him back to the palace."

At that time, having received the king’s command, the ministers informed one another and set out on their mission to search for the Bodhisattva; yet, by the supernatural power of the devas, they were unable to see him at all.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva departed from the city of Kapilavastu and reached the kingdom of Mithilā; by the time night had turned to dawn, he had traveled a road of six yojanas. The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others who had escorted him thus far suddenly vanished once their task was completed."
When the Bodhisattva had reached the forest of asceticism where the sages of antiquity once practiced, he immediately dismounted from his horse and consoled Chandaka,
saying: "Excellent,
Chandaka!"
Among the people of the world, some follow with their minds but not their bodies; others follow with their bodies but not their minds. Now, both your mind and body follow mine entirely.

People of the world vie to serve those who are wealthy and noble, yet they abandon and distance themselves from those who are poor and lowly. Now that I have renounced my kingdom and come here, you alone are able to follow me.
"Excellent, Chandaka!
This is truly rare. Now that I have reached this secluded and open place, you may take Kanthaka and return together."
He then untied his own hair-knot, took the maṇi jewel, and entrusted it to Chandaka, saying: "Chandaka!
Take this jewel and return to the palace; present it to the Great King and speak these words:"

"The Prince now has no further longing for worldly dharmas; he does not seek to be born in heaven to enjoy the five desires, nor is he unfilial, nor does he harbor any heart of anger, resentment, or hatred. Furthermore, he seeks neither wealth, rank, nor emoluments; rather, seeing all sentient beings迷失 (lost) on the right path and submerged in birth and death, he has left the home life solely for the sake of rescuing and delivering them. We pray only that Your Majesty will not give rise to anxiety."
"Great King!

If you say that I am still young and should not yet renounce the world, you should use my words as a skillful means to petition him: 'Are birth, old age, sickness, and death subject to fixed times? Though a person may be in the prime of youth, who can escape them alone?'"

In ancient times, there were various Wheel-Turning Sage Kings who abandoned their kingdoms to seek the Way and retired to mountain forests; none of them returned midway to indulge in the five desires.
My own private resolve is likewise: unless I have attained unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall never return.
"Both my inner and outer kinsmen hold me in affection and regard; you must skillfully explain my intentions to them so that they may understand.
Furthermore, take off the necklace I am wearing and give it to Chanda, saying:"
"I have gone forth from home now in order to sever the root of all suffering and to fulfill this vow;
do not harbor any anxiety. He then removed his other ornaments for the body and said to Yaśodharā:

"In this world, those born must inevitably part from what they love; I have now gone forth to study the Path in order to sever these various sufferings. Do not give rise to groundless grief through attachment."
He then spoke to the various court ladies within the palace and addressed the young youths of the Śākya clan, saying:
"I now wish to break through the net of ignorance so as to attain the light of wisdom; once my task is completed, I shall return to see you all."
At that time, having heard the Bodhisattva’s bitter and urgent words, Chandaka wept with grief and distress, throwing himself upon the ground and speaking thus:

"Since I lack the power to make the Prince return to the royal palace, if I were to return from here alone, the King, my aunt, and all the Śākyas would surely become enraged and lash me, rebuking me by saying:
'Where have you abandoned the Prince?'"
"I shall certainly have no words with which to offer a reply.
The Bodhisattva replied, "Chanda!"
Do not harbor such anxieties. Why is this?
If one in this world takes the words of those they love and recounts them in detail to that person, they will surely receive their affection or even be granted rewards; therefore, do not worry.
"Chanda! Return quickly to the palace so that the Great King does not give rise to grief and distress.
Thereupon, Chanda rose from the ground and wailed aloud; Kanthaka lowered his head, bent forward with both forelegs, licked the Bodhisattva’s feet, and let out mournful cries as tears flowed down.
At that time, the Bodhisattva stroked the crown of Kanthaka’s head with his hand and said to him:
“Kanthaka! You have completed your task; do not weep any longer, for I shall reward you greatly.”
"O monks! The Bodhisattva reflected thus:
'If one does not shave off the hair and beard, it is not the way of a renunciant.'"

Thereupon, he took the maṇi sword from Chandaka and shaved his own hair. Having finished shaving his hair, he cast it into the air. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beholding this rare event, was filled with great joy; he immediately caught it in the air with a celestial robe and returned to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to honor, serve, and make offerings to it.
"At that time, having shaved off his beard and hair, the Bodhisattva observed that he was still wearing precious robes upon his body and thought to himself:
'The garments of one who has left the household life should not be like this.'"
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a hunter, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe and holding a bow and arrows, standing silently before the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva said to the hunter:
"What you wear is the very garment of all Buddhas of the past; why, by wearing this, do you commit a transgression?"
The hunter said:
"I wear the kāṣāya robe to lure the herd of deer; when the deer see this garment, they come near me, and it is because of this that I am finally able to kill them."
The Bodhisattva said:
"You wear the kāṣāya solely for the purpose of killing, whereas I, if I were to obtain it now, would seek only liberation.
Could you give me this kāṣāya?"
"If you give it to me, I shall give you a *kauśeya* garment; why do you begrudge that coarse and tattered robe?
The hunter replied, "Excellent!"
"O Benevolent One!
These wretched garments are truly not to be regretted.
He then took the kashaya robe and presented it to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva felt great joy in his heart and immediately gave him the kauseya garment.
Then, by means of supernatural power, the Śuddhāvāsa deva suddenly resumed his original form and flew up into the air, returning to the Brahma Heaven in the space of a single thought-moment.
Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva felt a redoubled sense of profound reverence for the kāṣāya.
Thereafter, the people erected a stūpa at this spot.
At that time, the Bodhisattva shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya, and with his appearance thus transformed, spoke these words:
"Only now can I truly be called one who has left the household life.
Thereupon, he sent Chanda back with Kanthaka; with tears filling his eyes, he bid farewell to Chanda.
Having bid farewell to Chandaka, he proceeded with calm composure and measured steps through the forest of asceticism where the seer Bāhuka dwelt.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When Chandaka saw that the Bodhisattva’s resolve was irreversible, he led Kaṇṭhaka back in sorrow; thereafter, people erected a stūpa at this spot."

Thereupon, having bid farewell, Chandaka gazed afar at the Bodhisattva; his head was bare of its celestial crown, his body devoid of necklaces, and all manner of precious garments were entirely absent. Raising his hands to strike his breast, he wept with bitter sorrow, his hopes extinguished as he stood choked with emotion and paced about.
Kanthaka let out a mournful cry, tossing his head and looking back with a constrained gaze; he stood pawing the ground, his eyes fixed upon him as tears flowed down in rivulets.

At that time, when Chandaka had gradually reached the city, it was as if someone had entered an empty house; the groves, gardens, springs, and forests both inside and outside the city were all completely parched because the Bodhisattva had departed.
All the inhabitants of the city, both great and small, not seeing the Bodhisattva but seeing only Chandaka, followed after him and asked:
"Where is Prince Siddhārtha now?"
Candaka replied, "The Prince has now abandoned the five desires and dwells alone in the mountain forests.
Having heard this, the multitude marveled at such an unprecedented event; each person looked at the others and shed tears, saying to one another:
"We shall follow the Great Prince and dwell in those mountain forests. Why is this?
Separated from the Noble Prince, what would we have to live for? The city and its palaces will become desolate and devoid of all that is delightful."

At that time, Chandaka led Kaṇṭhaka, carrying with him the necklaces, the priceless jeweled crown, and all the ornaments, as they entered the royal palace; the sound of the horse’s neighing was heard throughout the inner quarters.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and the ladies of the inner palace all gathered together and said to one another:
"The sound of Kaṇṭhaka is now not far off; could it be that the Prince is returning to the palace?"

At that time, after Chandaka had entered the palace gate, his maternal aunt, the queen, and all the court ladies, longing to see him, rushed toward the gate in competition. Seeing only Chandaka and not the Bodhisattva, they wept together and asked Chandaka:
"Where is the Prince now? Why have you returned alone?"
Chanda replied, "The Prince has renounced the five desires for the sake of seeking the Way; he is currently in those mountain forests wearing dyed robes and having shaved off his hair and beard."
Having heard these words, Mahāprajāpatī was overcome with grief and distress beyond measure; she wailed aloud and rebuked Chandaka, saying:

"What wrong have I done to you that you have taken my noble son and sent him away to those mountain forests? There, fierce beasts and venomous insects are most terrifying; how will he rely upon anything now as he goes alone?"
Chanda replied,
"The Prince entrusted me with the horse-king and all the precious regalia, urging me to return quickly, fearing that the Queen might otherwise give way to grief and distress."

At that time, the various court ladies within the palace, due to the causes and conditions of their lustful passions, were deeply attached with craving; their bodies and minds were afflicted with suffering and distress as they wept and choked with grief.
Mahāprajāpatī, with tears in her mouth, said: "Alas, Prince!

Your body was originally anointed with sandalwood, its majestic virtue and radiance so great; how is it that you now wither away in the mountains and wilds? How can you endure this suffering as mosquitoes and gadflies bite your skin?"
Alas, Prince!
When you were at home, you wore garments of *kauśeya* silk; how is it that you now wear such coarse and tattered clothing?
Alas, Prince!
"When you were at home, you partook of a hundred varieties of harmoniously blended, fragrant, and pure delicacies; how can you now eat this tasteless, coarse, and rough food?
Alas, Prince!"
"When you were at home, there was nothing upon which you sat or lay—whether rugs or cushions—that was not fine and soft; how is it that you can now endure lying upon thorns and brambles?
Alas, Prince!"

When you were at home, even those of wealth and high status served you with all their hearts, fearing they might offend you; how then could a person of such poverty and low station dare to deceive you today?
"Alas, Prince!

When you were at home, you were constantly entertained by beautiful maidens and indulged at will in the five desires; how is it that you now abandon yourself to the mountain forests to wander and dwell alone?"
Mahāprajāpatī, weeping and lamenting with various words of grief and distress, rose from the ground and asked Chandaka again:
"When my son was about to depart, what instructions did he give you?"
"Where is my son’s hair now? And who shaved it?
Canda, weeping and unable to restrain himself, replied to the lady:

"The Prince entrusted me with this message: 'When you arrive at the palace, prostrate yourself before my mother and entreat her most earnestly not to harbor any grief, saying: [He spoke as follows:]...
"I shall soon attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; we shall meet again.
Having said this, he took his precious sword and shaved off his own hair, casting it into the void; the devas caught it and returned with it to offer worship.
Mahāprajāpatī wept again and spoke these words: "Alas, Prince!
Your hair was very long, soft, and deep blue-black; from each pore it grew in a single curl. You were fit to wear a royal crown and receive the throne—why have you now cut it off and cast it away?"
"Alas, Prince!

Your two arms are muscular and long, your ankles do not protrude, and your gait is as dignified and elegant as that of a lion king. Your eyes are like blue lotuses, your body is of a true golden color, and your voice is deep and resonant like a drum or thunder. How could a person such as this endure the practice of the Way?"
‘Examining this place, it must be destined for a holy king; this person of sublime virtue should be its sovereign.
He then spoke in verse:
“If one says this ground is no place of merit, Then such a person of supreme virtue should not be born here.”
"Having manifested this body of rare and wondrous merit, he shall surely become a holy king for the world.
At that time, Yaśodharā raised her voice in mournful weeping and rebuked Chandaka, saying: "Chandaka!"
"When the Prince departed, I was fast asleep and heavy with drowsiness that night; I neither perceived nor knew [of his going].
Where did you take the Prince and leave him? How far has he gone now, and why have you returned alone?"
"Chanda! You have brought me no benefit; you are my enemy who has harmed me. You have now fully completed your evil deeds, so do not weep in vain."
"Chanda! This horse’s neighing was usually heard for several li; why was it so silent on that night? Today, his mournful cries only increase my sorrow."
"Both you and Kaṇṭhaka have acted unskillfully, leaving me without a master and the city empty and desolate—all because of this Kaṇṭhaka and you, Chandaka.
Thereupon, Chandaka wept in sorrow and said to Yaśodharā:
"Queen, you should not now scold and revile Kaṇṭhaka, nor should you hold me responsible; neither I nor Kaṇṭhaka were at fault from the beginning."

Why is this? When Kaṇṭhaka departed, it was not without signs of distress; he neighed mournfully, stamped the ground, and moved neither forward nor back. His whinnying resounded for half a yojana, and the sound of his hooves was heard for one krośa; yet, solely through the supernatural power of the devas, the queen was not made aware of it.
"What fault or transgression have Kaṇṭhaka and I committed?

Your Majesty previously issued a strict command that all those in attendance must apply themselves with great care to protect the Prince; yet now, the guards at all the city gates and the sentries are all overcome by sleep and lack any awareness."

When the Crown Prince first went forth, he was like the sun rising in the heavens, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the entire world. During his journey, I led the way before him; at the moment of his initial departure, I assisted him by opening all the city gates. At that time, Kanthaka’s hooves did not touch the ground. His shaving of the hair and its casting into the air, as well as the exchange of garments—these various deeds were all performed through the supernatural power of the devas.
At that time, Yaśodharā, overwhelmed by intense anguish, suddenly collapsed to the ground. Shedding tears, she said:
"Alas, alas! Why has the Prince abandoned me and departed?
Have you not heard the Vedic discourses which state that in ancient times there were kings who entered deep mountains, taking their queens with them to practice the holy life together?"
"Why, Chanda, have you abandoned me today alone?
If the Prince were practicing various austerities for the sake of being born in heaven, it would be to seek celestial maidens."
"But why must those celestial maidens be sought for, that you should abandon the royal throne and forsake us? Chanda!

It is not my wish to be born alone in heaven, nor do I seek the exquisite pleasures of the human world; I only pray that wherever my lord may be born, I shall always be his wife, so that we may once again enjoy such supreme rewards as we did before."
Having spoken these words, he wept in sorrow and said again: "Chanda!

Where is my lord now, that I am thus left without cause as one who is alone and widowed? From this day forward, I shall wear no fine clothes nor eat choice foods; the use of perfumes, flowers, and necklaces for my body is forever ended; though I remain at home, I shall always maintain the thought of dwelling in the mountain forests."
Yaśodharā rebuked Chandaka with thousands of words, but Chandaka stepped forward and admonished her, saying:
"Great Queen!
Do not give rise to such bitter grief and anguish."
Why is this so? When the Prince went forth, the various devas followed and escorted him.

The Heavenly King of the East and the Lord of the Gandharvas; the Heavenly King of the South and the Lord of the Kumbhāṇḍas; the Heavenly King of the West and the Lord of the Great Nāgas; the Heavenly King of the North and the Lord of the Yakṣas—all of them were clad in adamantine armor. Some held bows and swords, some carried spears and halberds; some led the way before him, while others followed behind. Brahmā, Śakra, and the gods of the sun and moon all brought their retinues along. The sons of the gods from the desire realm transformed themselves into the bodies of māṇavas, and countless billions of celestial youths and divine maidens were filled with great joy, scattering exquisite celestial flowers upon the Prince.

The Crown Prince observed this and neither grasped nor rejected it; he felt no greed and was not elated, remaining like space, unobstructed by anything. I can hardly describe each of these details in full.
At that time, King Śuddhodana heard the sound of wailing from within the palace from afar and emerged from his own quarters in great haste.

Then, Chandaka, carrying the Bodhisattva’s precious crown, pearl necklace, and parasol, led Kaṇṭhaka to the King's presence and reported everything in detail, prostrating himself with his head at the King's feet.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having beheld the Bodhisattva’s various ornaments and having heard the words spoken by Chandaka, cried out in a loud voice, saying: "Alas! Alas!"
"My beloved son has suddenly turned his back on me; where has he gone now?
she cried, collapsing and rolling about in wailing lamentation.

At that time, the cries of grief from all the inhabitants of Kapilavastu shook heaven and earth. The Śākya kinsmen were each filled with sorrowful longing, unable to sustain themselves; they looked at one another with streaming tears and all came forward to offer consolation, supporting the King and helping him to sit.
Although the King briefly regained consciousness, he lapsed back into unconsciousness after a short while; regaining his senses after a long time, he rebuked Chandaka, saying:
"Where have you abandoned my son?"
Chanda, terrified and trembling, addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
The Prince has renounced the five desires and is untainted by the world; though I urged him with earnest and repeated admonitions, he had no intention of turning back, and spoke thus to me:"
"Do not admonish me; I have no further need for any sensual pleasures now. I wish to renounce the throne and find joy in these mountain forests.
When King Śuddhodana heard Chandaka speak these words once more, he wept in deep distress and said to Chandaka:

"I am now at my end, devoid of all power and vigor; my limbs are broken like a withered stump, or like a great tree stripped of its branches and leaves. My enemies may well treat me with contempt, for I am now alone and utterly powerless."
Alas, my son!
O most excellent of men, why have you abandoned your home and departed against my wishes?
Alas, my son!

His various marks were fully perfected and adorned with a hundred merits; within each mark, every excellence was completely present. While the court ladies slept and remained unaware, he suddenly emerged.
Alas, my son!
You were so skillful and possessed of great wisdom; while you were within the palace, I had no sorrow, but now that you have abandoned me and departed, I am left with no further support.
Alas, my son!

Born into a noble lineage, he was always held in high esteem by the multitude; yet he renounced his precious throne and all his retinue from the four quarters, departing alone like a white elephant breaking through great timbers.

"When my son departed, all the city gates were difficult to open and difficult to close; when they were opened or closed, their sound resounded far and wide. Why then was it that no one heard them this night?"
"Surely it must be that the celestial deities have caused this silence. Alas, my son!

You have renounced the precious throne as if discarding phlegm or spittle. I previously built for you palaces for the three seasons to suit the cold and the heat; why have you abandoned them all at once and departed? Why do you delight in the wilderness, dwelling among the mountains and forests, content to be a companion to birds and beasts?"
From this day forward, the various deities who protect the city shall all abandon this city and depart.
Alas, my son!
My heart of love and affection penetrates to my very marrow; for what reason have you abandoned me to enter the mountain forests?
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought of the Bodhisattva day and night without ceasing, wishing to restrain him and bring him back. He further recalled the prophecy made by the seer in the past:

"If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; the seven treasures will appear spontaneously, and he shall rule over the four continents, endowed with a thousand sons who are handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing all enemies.
If he leaves the household life, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and transform and enlighten the ten directions."
"Knowing for certain that my son will most certainly not return, he summoned his great ministers and addressed them, saying: 'Gentlemen, you all have children at home;

you enjoy one another's company and find comfort before your eyes, yet you do not consider my grief. I have an only son of extraordinary marks and holy wisdom, who was destined to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents. Now, having suddenly departed for the deep mountains and remote valleys—places of extreme peril and no human habitation—who shall know of his hunger, thirst, cold, or heat?'"
"You, my ministers, should select five of your sons and grandsons to follow and attend upon him; if any among you return midway, I shall exterminate your five clans.
The ministers, receiving the decree, immediately selected five men and entered the mountains to seek and serve him.
At that time, the five men pursued him but could not catch up; they thought to themselves:
"This is a man who has transcended the world; he travels without choosing his path—what fixed way could there be for him?"
"If I were to return, I would surely destroy my own clan; it would be better to select a suitable place to dwell and live there as I please.
Thereupon, the five Bhadrakas fled into the mountain forests.

Chapter Sixteen: King Bimbisāra Exhorts [the Bodhisattva] to Accept Worldly Benefits At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Candaka, having received the Bodhisattva’s instructions, comforted the Great King, Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and the Śākya clansmen, causing them to be free from sorrow and affliction.”

Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he shaved off his hair and beard and went to a hunter, where he traded a garment of *kauśeya* silk for the pure dharma-robes of a *kāṣāya*. Thereupon, he proceeded to the place of the female ascetic, the brahmin Bhīlū.
At that time, the woman invited the Bodhisattva to partake of a vegetarian feast on the following day.
Having accepted the invitation, he next went to the place of the female ascetic, the brahmin woman Padmā.
At that time, the woman also invited the Bodhisattva to partake of a vegetarian feast on the following day.
Having accepted her invitation, he proceeded to the dwelling of the brahmacārin seer Revata.
At that time, that seer also invited the Bodhisattva to partake of a vegetarian feast the following day.
Having accepted the invitation, he went again to the place of the two seers, Prabhāsa and Dānta; those seers likewise invited the Bodhisattva to partake of a vegetarian feast the following day.
"O bhikṣus!
The Bodhisattva proceeded in due order to the city of Vaiśālī.
Beside the city was a seer named Ārāḍa, who, together with three hundred disciples, was constantly teaching them the concentration of the sphere of nothingness."
At that time, the seer saw the Bodhisattva from afar and, struck with wonder, said to his disciples:
"You should behold this most excellent of men.
The disciples addressed the seer, saying:
"I see this person whose appearance is upright and handsome, such as has never been seen before;
from where has he come? Bhikṣus! At that time, I asked Ārāḍa:
"Can the Dharma you have realized be heard?
Now that I wish to practice it, I pray that you will explain it to me.
The seer replied:
"Gautama! The Dharma I have realized is profound and subtle; if there are those capable of learning it, I shall proclaim it for them so that they may practice it.
If there are sons of good family with pure faith who receive my instruction, they shall all achieve the subtle concentration of the sphere of nothingness."
“O bhikṣus! Having heard what the rishi said, I thought to myself:

‘I now possess diligence, mindfulness, concentration, aspiration, faith, and wisdom; if I dwell alone in a secluded place, constantly and diligently practicing with a mind free from negligence, I shall certainly realize the Dharma attained by that rishi.’”
Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort without weariness, and after a short time, he had attained realization in all respects.
Having attained meditative concentration, he went to where the seer was and spoke these words:
"Great Seer!..."
“You have realized only this; are there any other dharmas?
The seer replied, “Gautama!
"I have attained only this; there is no other dharma.
The Bodhisattva replied, "Such a dharma as this I have already realized through direct personal experience."
The seer said:
"What I have realized, you too are able to realize; it is fitting that I and you should dwell together and instruct disciples. O bhikṣus!
At that time, the rishi treated me with the utmost respect; he offered me the most excellent and subtle of offerings and, among all his disciples, made me his sole companion.
“Monks! At that time, I reflected:
‘The words of the seers are not capable of ending suffering; what dharma can serve as the cause for liberation from suffering?’”

At that very time, he departed from the city of Vaiśālī and traveled by stages until he reached the great city of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha. Entering Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, he stayed alone in a certain place, constantly guarded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas. At dawn, having dressed and taken up his alms-bowl, he entered Rājagṛha through the Hot Springs Gate to beg for food in succession.

His gait was dignified and graceful, his faculties were serene, and he gazed five cubits ahead with a mind free from distraction. When the people of the city saw the Bodhisattva approaching, they were struck with wonder and all spoke thus:
"Who is this person?"
"Is this a mountain deity, or is it Brahmā, or is it Śakra, or is it one of the Four Heavenly Kings?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The pure body of the Bodhisattva possesses immeasurable radiance."
Fully endowed with dignified deportment, his mind was tranquil and exceedingly supple.
Residing on Vulture Peak Mountain, he maintained the dharma of one who has gone forth;
then, at the time of dawn, having put on his robes and taken up his alms bowl, he departed.
Having disciplined body and mind, he entered the city to beg for alms.
His body was like a mass of molten gold, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
whether men or women were by the roadside, none could gaze upon him without weariness.
When the residents within the city saw this superior person arrive, they all conceived a sense of wonder;
they rushed forward in competition to gaze upon him, exclaiming, "This man is most extraordinary! From where has he come today?"
There were many court ladies who all ascended the exquisite pavilions;
from within their windows and balconies, they gazed out without ceasing for even a moment.
The streets were completely filled, yet the marketplaces were entirely empty.
Abandoning their respective tasks, they all came together to wait upon the Bodhisattva.
Someone hurriedly went to inform King Bimbisāra:
"A Brahmā has now arrived, entering the city to beg for alms."
Again, others spoke thus:
"Perhaps he is Śakra, Lord of the Devas, or one from the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, or Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens."
"The Four Heavenly Kings, the sun and moon,
or perhaps Rāhu and others, Vairūḍhaka, and the various hosts of Vimala gods.
Again, another addressed the king, saying:
"This is the deity of Mount Ling; Great King, you should know that you have now attained great benefit.
When the king heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy;
he ascended the high tower himself and gazed from afar upon the body of the Bodhisattva.
His marks and signs were exceedingly dignified and majestic, like a mass of pure gold;
the King therefore commanded his attendants to offer food to the Bodhisattva and to seek out his dwelling, following him to observe him.
The messenger followed the Bodhisattva and saw him go to Vulture Peak;
returning, he informed the Great King and related in detail all that he had witnessed.
Having heard these matters, the King’s sense of rare wonder increased all the more.
At that time at dawn, he prepared his carriage and went in person to pay his respects.
From afar, he beheld within the rocky crags a light and form of supreme purity;
its majestic appearance was most solemn and beautiful, as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Having cleared away all attendants, he proceeded on foot.
Prostrating at the Bodhisattva’s feet and having offered various greetings,
he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"From where has the Great Being come?
Where is his native land and village?
Who are his father and mother?"
Are you a brahmin, or are you a kṣatriya?
Or perhaps one of the sages and saints?
O Benevolent One, speak according to the truth.
The Bodhisattva replied to the king, saying:
"My father is King Śuddhodana.
He resides at the foot of the Snowy Mountains; his city is named Kapilavastu."
"The people are exceedingly peaceful and happy; seeking the unsurpassed path, I have therefore now gone forth.
The King bowed his head deeply and said:
"You are now in the prime of youth, with a most handsome countenance;
you ought to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses—why then do you go begging?
I shall relinquish this kingdom and rule it together with you."
Now that we have fortunately met, my heart is filled with great joy;
I wish to become your close friend and share the royal throne together.
Why do you delight in dwelling alone in the empty mountains and wild forests?
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with gentle words and phrases,
slowly replied to the Great King:
"Because I seek the tranquility of nirvana, I have no desire for any worldly honors or positions."
Having renounced it all to go forth into homelessness, how much less could one harbor greedy envy for a royal kingdom?
With the great ocean as his palace, would he ever again look upon a cow’s footprint with longing?
And give rise to a mind of attachment?
The five desires have boundless faults; they can cause one to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. The wise should keep far away from them.
Abandon it like mucus or spittle;
before long you will fall. It is also like clouds in the sky, vanishing and perishing in an instant, tossed and driven by the swift wind.
It never pauses for even a moment.
If one becomes attached to the five desires, one immediately loses the bliss of liberation.
What wise person would seek out the cause of great suffering?
The fire of craving blazes most fiercely; once it has been obtained, one never again reaches satiety.
Having obtained it, one must then suffer the great anguish of separation from what is beloved.
The supreme fruit among human beings—
even if all people in the world were to receive these two kinds of rewards, their minds would still not know contentment;
having obtained this, they would seek yet more.
Driven by thirst, one drinks salt water; the five desires are just like this.
Seeking them without ceasing, one remains forever within birth and death, revolving eternally without end.
One must purify and restrain the sense faculties and realize the untainted Noble Path;
only then is one called "contented.
Impermanent and lacking solidity, the nine orifices are constantly overflowing.
The multitude of sufferings act as a mechanical device;
yet, without giving rise to craving or attachment, I have gone forth from home now for the sake of seeking the bliss of nirvana.
Bimbisāra said: "Excellent, O Great Guide!
I was formerly your subject; you are a prince of royal lineage, yet you were able to renounce the glory of the five desires."
If I now urge you toward worldly benefit, you will surely incur immeasurable sin;
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will pity me and forgive my transgression.
Within this very realm, may you realize the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
"May you not forsake me; I shall obtain great benefit.
Thereupon, rising from his seat, he prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of followers, he returned to his own palace.
“The Bodhisattva has tamed his mind and serves as a refuge for the world;
wherever he goes or stays, he benefits all beings. He shall now proceed to the Nairañjanā River.
Chapter 17: On Asceticism The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “... [as above] ...”
“Near Rājagṛha there was a seer named Udraka, son of Māra, who, together with seven hundred disciples, constantly taught the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva saw that the rishi was highly learned and wise among the assembly, and was revered by all; he thought to himself:
"If I do not go to his place and engage in ascetic practices identical to his, how can I reveal the faults in the various meditative concentrations he practices?"
I now employ skillful means to cause them to know for themselves that what they have been practicing is not ultimate;
furthermore, I wish to reveal and manifest my own meditative concentration and wisdom to benefit all, so as to inspire a sense of wonder in this assembly.
Having formed this thought, he went to the place where the rishi was and spoke these words:
"Venerable one! Who is your teacher?
And what is the dharma that you practice?"
The rishi replied, "I originally had no teacher; I attained awakening spontaneously.
The Bodhisattva said to him:
"I have now come specifically to seek what you have realized; I pray that you will expound it for me, and I shall practice it accordingly.
The seer said, "I shall expound it for you according to your wishes."

At that time, having received those instructions, the Bodhisattva practiced with focused diligence in a secluded place. Due to the causes and conditions of his long-standing cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he immediately attained hundreds of thousands of worldly samādhis; in accordance with those various concentrations, all their distinct and manifold characteristics manifested before him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva arose from his concentration and said to the rishi,
"Beyond this concentration, what further dharma is there?
The rishi replied:
"This is the most supreme; there is no other dharma beyond it.
The Bodhisattva reflected thus:

"I possess faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and could quickly realize that rishi’s dharma; yet what he has attained is not the true path, not the dharma of disenchantment, not the dharma of a śramaṇa, not the dharma of enlightenment, and not the dharma of nirvāṇa."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Bodhisattva, wishing to cause those seers to abandon their heterodox paths, spoke of the matters mentioned above.
At that time, the five Bhadravargas, who had previously practiced the holy life under them, secretly deliberated among themselves, saying:”

"We have studied for a long time and are still unable to fathom the depth of that samādhi; how is it that the Prince, in such a short time, has already been able to realize the Dharma of the Great Sage, yet finding it not yet ultimate, seeks something even more excellent?"
"For this reason, he will certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
When he attains that path, we five shall also have our share.
Having formed this thought, they immediately left the rishi and returned to follow the Bodhisattva.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva departed from the city of Rājagṛha and, together with the five Bhadravargas, traveled by stages toward the Nairañjanā River and Mount Gayā; there, at the summit of the mountain, he spread grass beneath a tree and sat down."
He reflected thus:

"Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in this world, those who are negligent in body and mind, dwelling in greed and following the heat of affliction, though they practice asceticism, remain very far from the Path.
It is like a person who, seeking fire, takes wet wood and places it in water, then drills it to seek a spark; could such a person ever succeed in obtaining fire?"
"If a person dwells in greed and other such passions, they cannot realize the transcendent, supreme wisdom despite practicing asceticism;
it is just the same in this case. He further thought:

"Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world, if they restrain their bodies and do not act upon greed, yet their minds still harbor attachment to sense objects, they remain far from the Path even though they cultivate ascetic practices."

For example, suppose there is a person who, seeking fire, takes wet wood and places it on dry land, then drills it with a fire-drill in hopes of obtaining fire; would this person be able to obtain fire?

Furthermore, if there is another person whose mind has not yet become tranquil due to the arising of craving and other such afflictions, they will likewise be unable to realize supramundane, superior wisdom despite practicing ascetic austerities.
"Furthermore, he thought:

'Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in this world, those who guard their body and mind, remain free from greed and desire, eliminate all feverish afflictions, and practice the most supreme tranquility and asceticism, are able to realize supramundane, superior wisdom.
It is like a person seeking fire who takes dry wood, places it on dry ground, and drills it; one should know that such a person will certainly obtain fire.'"

Furthermore, if there is another person who does not dwell in sensual desire, whose body and mind are tranquil, and who diligently practices asceticism, they will likewise be able to realize the supreme wisdom that transcends the world.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "After the Bodhisattva had left Mount Gayā, he traveled by stages until he reached the eastern side of the Uruvilvā pond. There he beheld the Nairañjanā River; its waters were clear, cool, and swirling in bright eddies. Its banks were level and even, and the trees grew in lush profusion. All manner of flowers and fruits flourished in brilliant splendor, lovely to behold. Along the riverbanks, villages and towns were everywhere abundant; houses stood close together and the population was flourishing."

At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually arrived at a certain place—tranquil, secluded, and vast, free from mounds or ruins; neither too near nor too far, neither too high nor too low—and he thought to himself:
"To dwell in this place now would be easy for settling the spirit; since ancient times, many who have practiced the holy path have resided here."
He further thought:

"I have now appeared in this world of five turbidities and see those inferior beings, such as the various non-Buddhists, who are attached to the view of self and practice various ascetic penances; shrouded by ignorance, they vainly seek [the truth], tormenting their own bodies and minds in an attempt to attain liberation."
That is to say: some carry a vessel and wander about begging for food;
some take only a single handful of food to sustain themselves for a day;
and some do not beg for food, but accept whatever is offered by others.
Some do not accept invitations but must go themselves to beg in order to seek liberation.
Some constantly eat the roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of plants; or they eat lotus roots, wild animal dung, bran-water, rice-washings, or oil dregs.
Others do not eat sugar, ghee, honey, strong wine, sweet or sour delicacies, or any such flavorful foods in their quest for liberation.
Some beg for food from one household, or two, three, or even up to seven;
some eat once every day, or once every two days, or even once every half-month or month, seeking liberation through such means.
Some have food that increases or decreases according to the waxing and waning of the moon, whether consumed gradually or all at once, and in greater or lesser amounts;
some eat only a single handful or up to seven handfuls per day;
and some eat only a single grain of wheat, a single seed of hemp, or a single grain of rice per day.
Some seek liberation by drinking only pure water;
some, known as "divine names," starve themselves to death, believing that they will be reborn among gods or humans according to their own wishes;

some spin the feathers of owls to make clothing, or wear tree bark, or wear the hides of oxen and sheep, rags from the dustheap, or coarse woolen blankets; some wear only one garment up to seven garments, or wear black or red as their clothing, or again, go naked.
Some carry three staffs in their hands, while others string together skulls in pursuit of liberation.
Some bathe once a day, some twice a day, up to seven times a day, or never bathe at all;
some smear themselves with ashes, while others smear themselves with ink.
Some smear themselves with excrement and soil, or wear withered flowers;
some scorch their bodies with the five heats, smoke their noses, or throw themselves from high cliffs; they constantly stand on one leg, gazing upward at the sun and moon;

some lie upon woven rafters, thorns, ashes, dung, shards, stones, wooden planks, or pestles in pursuit of liberation; others utter the sounds of *oṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *sūda*, and *svāhā*, upholding incantations and reciting the Vedas in search of liberation.

Or they may rely upon various Brahma kings, Śakra, Maheśvara, Tuka, Nārāyaṇa, Kumāra, Kātyāyana, Mātali, the eight Vasus, the two Aśvins, Vaiśravaṇa, Varuṇa, Ārici, Caṇḍāla, Gandharvas, Asuras, Garuḍas, Mahoragas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, Kumbhāṇḍas, and other celestial spirits and deities in their quest for liberation.

Some take refuge in earth, water, fire, wind, and space; in mountains, rivers, ponds, streams, ravines, and the great ocean; in forests, trees, creeping vines, grasses, burial mounds, and crossroads; or in places where cattle are raised and among the stalls of butchers; or they serve swords, blades, wheels, spears, and all manner of weapons in their quest for liberation.
Because these non-Buddhists fear birth and death, they diligently seek liberation and practice asceticism, yet it yields no benefit whatsoever.
They take refuge in that which is not a place of refuge, and perceive auspiciousness in that which is not auspicious.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
'I now wish to subdue the heterodox teachers by manifesting a rare and wondrous feat, so as to cause all devas and humans to give rise to a pure mind.'"
Furthermore, he wishes to cause those who would destroy causes and conditions to understand the retribution of karma;
he also wishes to manifest his great majestic power through merit and wisdom, and to analyze the distinct characteristics of various meditative concentrations;
and he further wishes to manifest the power of his great courage and diligence.

Thereupon, he sat cross-legged at that spot; his actions of body, speech, and mind were tranquil and unmoving. When he first concentrated his mind, he focused single-mindedly on one object, regulating his inhalation and exhalation until the heat pervaded his entire body. Sweat flowed from his armpits and moisture dripped from his forehead like falling raindrops; yet he endured this suffering without succumbing to exhaustion, giving rise instead to a heart of courageous and diligent effort.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva regulated his inhalation and exhalation until a great sound issued from within both ears, like the sound of wind being drawn into a bellows; yet, undergoing such painful matters, he did not give rise to weariness."
"O bhikṣus!

At that time, I cut off the inhalation and exhalation through my ears, nose, and mouth; the internal wind struck the crown of my head and produced a great sound, like a strong man brandishing a sharp blade to split open the skull bone. Although I experienced such suffering, I did not give rise to a mind of exhaustion or retreat."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, all of the Bodhisattva’s inhalations and exhalations ceased. The internal wind became powerful within his two flanks, swirling and turning with a loud resonance, like a butcher using a knife to carve an ox; yet he endured this painful ordeal without any weariness."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At that time, because internal winds were stirred within him, the Bodhisattva experienced a pervasive heat and distress throughout his body, just as if a person of weak strength were subjected to a great mass of fire and his entire body were scorched.”
Experiencing this extreme suffering, he further increased his heart of courageous and diligent effort, thinking to himself:

"I now abide in that Immovable Samādhi; my actions of body, speech, and mind have all attained right reception (*samāpatti*). Entering the fourth dhyāna, I am far removed from joy and pleasure; having dispelled conceptualization, there is no fluctuation. Like space, it pervades all things and cannot be altered; this concentration is named *Aspharaṇa*."
At that time, the Bodhisattva practiced such extreme asceticisms as these.
O Bhikṣus! The Bodhisattva further had this thought:
"Among those in the world, whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, who regard the practice of fasting as asceticism, I now wish to surpass them by eating only a single grain of barley each day."

"Monks, you should know! In the past, when I was eating only a single grain of barley, my body became emaciated like an *aśvattha* tree; my flesh was wasted away so that my ribs were visible like the rafters of a dilapidated house, and my vertebrae were exposed in succession like the nodes of a bamboo cane. My eyes were sunken like stars at the bottom of a well, and the crown of my head was withered and shriveled like a dried gourd. The ground where I sat bore the marks of a horse's hoof, and my skin was so wrinkled it looked like the surface of a sliced melon. When I raised my hand to brush away dust, the hair on my body fell off as it was scorched; when I rubbed my belly with my hand, I touched my backbone."

Furthermore, eating only a single grain of rice or even a single sesame seed, his body became emaciated ten times more than before; his complexion was like a mass of ink or dead ashes. When people from the villages of the four directions came to see him, they all sighed in lamentation, saying:
"Why does the Prince of the Śākya clan subject himself to such suffering?"
"Where now is that upright and beautiful form? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"During the six years of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practice, he never allowed his four modes of deportment to degenerate. In the intense heat of midsummer, he did not seek coolness; in the bitter cold of deep winter, he did not seek thick warmth. Even when mosquitoes and gadflies bit his body, he did not brush them away. Sitting in the full lotus posture with body and mind unmoving, he neither yawned nor sneezed."

Cowherd boys would often come to see me, playfully poking my nose with grass stalks, or poking my mouth or my ears; at those times, my body and mind remained unmoved. I was constantly venerated by devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, and I was able to lead twelve lakṣas of heavenly beings to abide upon the path of the Three Vehicles.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "In the past,
when the Bodhisattva Had renounced his throne and left the household life,
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, He contemplated various skillful means."
“I have emerged from this world of turbid evil, born here in Jambudvīpa,
where there are many people of false views who destroy the Dharma and follow heterodox paths.
These fools seek liberation by inflicting suffering upon their own bodies and minds.”
Though they fear the causes of birth and death, they remain perpetually deluded regarding the fruit of liberation.
Some rush into masses of fire, throw themselves from high cliffs,
scorch their bodies with the five heats, or destroy themselves by smearing themselves with ashes.
In daily life, he takes but a single handful of food, using only the meager amount to sustain his life.
He begs for alms at the doors of others, accepting them only when the host is pleased;
yet if the host’s countenance shows even a slight trace of stinginess, he will go without food for the entire day.
Sometimes hearing the sound of a pestle and mortar, or the barking of a dog, he would immediately stop and not go out to beg; even when called, he would not accept.
As for ghee, oil, fine delicacies, milk, curd, sugar, and the like—
They abstain from all [refined foods], eating only coarse and unpalatable fare:
bran-water and oil-cakes, deer-dung and lotus roots,
as well as various flowers and leaves of grasses and trees, seeking thereby liberation.
Some consume only pure water; some eat but a single sesame seed daily, or restrict themselves to a single grain of rice;
some even starve themselves to death in their quest for liberation.
Rags from dust heaps and bird feathers, tree bark, animal hides,
and various other coarse garments;
even those who wear only the seven robes, or some who remain constantly naked.
Seeking liberation amidst thorns,
ashes, and dust; seeking liberation among wooden boards, pestles, tiles, and stones.
Some stand on one foot, with hair disheveled or tied in a topknot,
turning in circles with the sun in their quest for liberation.
Others constantly pay homage to the sun and moon, to rivers, oceans, and mountains.
Like trees and forests on a high plateau, these various non-Buddhists seek liberation;
yet they diligently practice useless hardships,
clinging to false karmas, firmly grasping them without ever relinquishing them.
Such people with false views shall fall into evil realms after death.
For their sake, in the past, for six years,
I manifested the subduing of them by diligently practicing great asceticism.
There are those ignorant people who, seeing the false asceticism of non-Buddhists,
mistakenly take it for the true Dharma; they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and,
in order to bring them to maturity, diligently practice great austerities themselves.
He then chose a secluded place and sat in the full-lotus posture in samādhi;
during this time of restricting his food, he consumed but one grain of hemp and one grain of rice per day.
He did not seek warmth when walking in the cold, nor did he seek coolness when dwelling in the heat.
He did not chase away mosquitoes or gadflies, nor did he avoid the wind and rain.
When cowherd boys came to look at him, they playfully pierced him with blades of grass and thorns through his ears,
nose, and mouth, using blades of grass, wood, tiles, and stones.
Though they strike and hurl things at my body, they cannot cause me harm; I endure it all.
Nor do I give rise to exhaustion, even regarding tears, saliva, excrement, urine, and the like.
All impurities have been severed; only skin and bone remain.
Blood and flesh are completely withered and dry;
the body is exceedingly emaciated, like an aśoka tree, abiding in the ānāpāna-samādhi.
With body and mind tranquil and unmoving, Yet not relishing the bliss of dhyāna,
They give rise to the heart of great compassion And universally for the sake of all sentient beings,
Practice such a samādhi.
By practicing this samādhi, one swiftly attains Buddhahood, Extinguishing the hosts of non-Buddhists and subduing all heterodox teachers.
To those who do not believe in Bodhi— such great Bodhi—
Difficult to encounter even in immeasurable kalpas,
for the sake of these multitudes of people, he entered the Anāpāna-samādhi.
There were twelve lakṣas of gods and humans present.
Abiding on the paths of the three vehicles,
they constantly, day and night, made offerings to the bodies of the bodhisattvas;
each of them made a great vow, wishing to abide in the *nāva-samādhi*.
"Benefiting all sentient beings, His mind is like empty space.
Chapter 18: Departure for the Nairañjanā River The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities for six years, Māra Pāpīyān constantly followed him, seeking to find his faults but being unable to do so. Becoming weary and disheartened, he withdrew in dejection."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Is a forest and wilds of profound purity;
To the east he gazes upon the Nairañjanā River, And to the west he rests by the Piṇḍapātra Pond.”
First giving rise to the mind of diligence, he came seeking the ground of tranquility;
seeing that place to be exceedingly secluded and vast, he stayed there to eliminate the afflictions.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān arrived at the Bodhisattva’s abode.
Deceitfully employing gentle words, he spoke to the Bodhisattva:
"All sentient beings in the world cherish their own lives;
yet now your body is withered and parched—of a thousand deaths, not one shall remain whole."
One should practice the method of fire-worship, for it will surely yield a great fruit;
one ought not to needlessly sacrifice their life merely to be pitied by others.
The nature of the mind is inherently difficult to subdue, and the afflictions are not easily severed.
"Who can realize Bodhi? Why do you wish to torment yourself?
The Bodhisattva addressed Pāpīyān, speaking these words:
"Dullness, intoxication, greed, hatred, and delusion—these are your kinsmen."
Having brought you here, I shall destroy your roots of goodness together with you.
I seek no worldly blessings; do not disturb me with these things.
I now have nothing to fear, for death is my ultimate limit.
Vowing to seek liberation, with a resolve never to turn back,
though there be various pains and afflictions, my mind remains ever tranquil.
Abiding in this firm concentration, with diligence, aspiration, and the like, [I shall proceed].
I would rather die guarding my wisdom than live without it.
Like a man of righteous valor who perishes in the decisive struggle for victory,
I would not be like a cowardly weakling who seeks to remain alive only to be controlled by others.
Therefore, I shall now destroy your armies:
first, the army of craving; second, the army of sorrow;
third, the army of hunger and thirst; fourth, the army of attachment.
The fifth is the army of torpor and drowsiness; the sixth is the army of fear;
the seventh is the army of doubt and regret; the eighth is the army of anger and concealment;
the ninth is the army of grief and affliction, along with self-praise and the disparagement of others.
"False claims of offerings and the like—
such multitudes of armies are your retinue, capable of crushing and subduing gods and humans.
I now dwell constantly within them, with right mindfulness, right awareness, and so forth."
"O Pāpīyān, I shall extinguish you, just as water douses an unbaked clay vessel.
When the Bodhisattva spoke these words, Māra immediately withdrew in defeat.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Regarding all śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas of the past, present, and future who, while practicing asceticism, afflict their bodies and minds and undergo pain and distress—one should know that such people merely torment themselves and derive no benefit whatsoever."
He further thought:

"I have now practiced this most extreme austerity, yet I am unable to realize the transcendent, supreme wisdom. Thus I know that asceticism is not the cause of Bodhi, nor is it the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, or the cultivation of the path. There must certainly be another method by which one may attain the eradication of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Again, he thought to himself:

"In the past, within the garden of my father the king, beneath a Jambu tree, I cultivated and attained the first dhyāna. At that time, my body and mind were filled with joy and bliss; in this manner, I even attained the fourth dhyāna. Reflecting upon what I previously realized, these are the causes of Bodhi and will surely be able to eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death."
The Bodhisattva further reflected:

"I now possess this emaciated body, which is incapable of receiving the Way. If I were to use my power of supernatural faculties and the power of wisdom to restore my body and proceed toward the site of enlightenment, would that not fail to accomplish such a task? It would neither be an act of compassion for all sentient beings, nor would it be the method by which the Buddhas realize bodhi.
Therefore, I should now receive fine food to empower my body; only then will I be able to proceed to the site of enlightenment."
At that time, there were certain devas who always delighted in practicing asceticism; knowing that the Bodhisattva wished to eat fine food, they said to him:

"Venerable One, do not accept this fine food. We shall now employ skillful means and our supernatural powers to restore your physical strength to its original state, so that it will be no different from having eaten."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"It has indeed been a long time since I have eaten, and the fourfold assembly of followers all know that I am practicing asceticism.
If I were to refrain from eating by means of the power of those devas, it would constitute a falsehood."
When the five Bhadravargīyas heard that the Bodhisattva intended to partake of fine food, they all thought to themselves:

"If even through such ascetic practices the śramaṇa Gautama could not attain the transcendent, supreme wisdom, how much less now, when he wishes to eat fine food and dwell in pleasure? This man of no wisdom has fallen away from his meditative concentration."
He then left the Bodhisattva and went to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in Vārāṇasī.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Since the Bodhisattva began his ascetic practices, there was a village headman in the hamlet of Uruvilvā named Senāpati who had ten daughters; these ten maidens, together with the five Bhadravargas, had constantly provided the Bodhisattva with offerings of hemp and wheat.”

At that time, when the women learned that the Bodhisattva had abandoned his ascetic practices, they immediately prepared various kinds of food and drink to offer him. Before many days had passed, his physical appearance became radiant and joyful; thereupon, the people spoke to one another again, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses a majestic and dignified form and great merit."

Among the ten maidens, the youngest was named Sujātā. Formerly, during the time of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, she constantly provided food and drink to eight hundred Brahmins, making this vow: "By the merit of providing sustenance to these Brahmins, may it benefit the Bodhisattva, enabling him to quickly achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Bodhisattva again had this thought:
'For six years I have practiced with diligent austerity, and my robes have become worn and tattered.'"
