"In the Śītavana charnel ground, he saw some old, tattered discarded rags (pāṃśukūla). As he was about to take them, the Earth Deity addressed the Space Deity, saying:
'How marvelous! How marvelous!'"
"The Prince of the Śākya clan has renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and taken up these discarded robes of refuse.

When the deities of the void heard these words, they informed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; thus it was passed on in succession until, within a single thought-moment, the news reached as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, holding a worn garment in his hand, spoke these words:
"Where is there water to wash this garment?
Then, a certain deva appeared before the Bodhisattva and, pointing to the ground with his finger, caused a pond to appear instantly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"Where is there a stone with which I may wash these rag-robes?
Then Śakra-devānām-indra immediately placed a square stone in the middle of the pond; seeing the stone, the Bodhisattva took it up and used it to wash his robes.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I shall wash these old garments for you, O Honored One; I pray only that you grant me permission.
However, the Bodhisattva, wishing to ensure that future communities of bhikṣus would not have others wash their old garments, washed them himself and did not give them to Śakra.
Having finished washing his clothes, he entered the pond to bathe.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān transformed the bank of the pond, making it exceedingly high and steep.

On the bank of the pond was a tree named Asana; at that moment, the tree deity pressed down the tree until it bent low, allowing the Bodhisattva to grasp a branch and reach the bank. There, beneath that tree, he put on his old garments.
At that time, a Śuddhāvāsa deva named Vimalaprabha brought a saffron robe of the proper measure for a śramaṇa to offer to the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva had accepted the robe, he put on his saṃghāṭī at dawn and entered the village to beg for food. The deity of that settlement, during the night before, had said to Sujāta:
"You have always provided great offerings of food for that pure person; today, having abandoned his ascetic practices, he will partake of fine food."
You previously made this vow:
"Once that person has accepted my food, may they swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Now is precisely the time; you should prepare it with all haste.

When the maiden Sujātā had heard the words of the deity, she immediately took a thousand head of milch cows and milked them seven times. She boiled the milk, taking only the most refined and pure portion from the top and placing it in a new vessel; she then cooked it with fragrant non-glutinous rice to make a congee.
While it was being cooked, auspicious signs such as a thousand-spoked wheel and a *pundarīka* lotus appeared upon the surface of the milk gruel.
When the maiden Sujātā saw these signs, she reflected to herself:
"What auspicious omen is this?"
At that time, a seer said to Sujātā, "If anyone should eat this milk-rice porridge, they will surely attain unsurpassed bodhi.

Then, having finished cooking the milk-rice porridge, Sujātā swept and cleansed her dwelling until it was utterly pure; she arranged a magnificent seat with various offerings and addressed the maiden Uttarā, saying:
"You should go and invite the brahmin to come with you.

Having received these instructions, the maiden Uttara set out toward the east; she saw only the Bodhisattva and did not see the brahmin. She traveled south, west, and north, yet in each direction she saw only the Bodhisattva and never the brahmin. It was exactly the same everywhere.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas concealed the body of the brahmin so that the maiden Uttara could never see him again.
Upon her return, Uttara said to Janavasabha:
"In the place where I went, I saw only the śramaṇa Gautama; I no longer saw any other brahmins."
The maiden Sujātā said:
"This is most excellent; it is for his sake that I have prepared this milk-gruel. You should go at once and invite him on my behalf."
The maiden Uttarā went to where the Bodhisattva was, prostrated herself at his feet, and spoke thus:
"Sujātā has sent me to invite the Noble One.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva went to her location and sat upon an excellent seat; thereupon, the maiden Sujātā took a golden bowl filled with milk-rice and presented it to him as an offering.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva reflected:
"By eating this milk-rice, I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He then spoke again to Sujātā:
"I have finished eating; to whom should I give this golden bowl?
The girl Sujātā replied, "I pray that you accept this bowl and use it as you please, O Venerable One."

At that time, the Bodhisattva took up the milk-rice porridge, departed from the village of Uruvilvā, went to the Nairañjanā River, set the bowl upon the bank, shaved off his beard and hair, and entered the river to bathe.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Bodhisattva bathed, hundreds of thousands of devas scattered celestial incense and flowers until they filled the river.

When the Bodhisattva had finished bathing, they vied with one another to collect this water and carry it back to their celestial palaces. Sudhanu took the hair and beard that had been shaved off and erected a stūpa to make offerings to them.”
Once the Bodhisattva had emerged from the riverbank, he reflected:
"On what seat shall I partake of this exquisite food?
Thereupon, the Naga Queen of the river held forth a noble seat that surged up from the earth; she arranged it in a pure place and invited the Bodhisattva to sit.

Once the Bodhisattva had sat down and consumed that milk gruel, his physical marks and signs were restored to their original state. He then cast the golden bowl into the river; at that time, the Dragon King was filled with great joy, retrieved the golden bowl, and made offerings to it within his palace.

Then Śakra Devānām Indra immediately transformed his form into that of a garuḍa, seized the golden bowl from that nāga king, and returned to his own palace where he erected a stūpa to make offerings to it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat; the Naga Queen took back the noble seat she had offered and returned to her own palace, where she erected a stupa to make offerings to it.
O Bhikṣus!

"By the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom, having consumed the milk gruel, his thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, as well as his fathom-wide halo, became increasingly radiant. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When practicing austerities for six years, My body was exceedingly emaciated;
Without the power of the devas, I could not have proceeded to that site of enlightenment."
Out of compassion for sentient beings, And in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas,
One must partake of fine food Before realizing great Bodhi.
In the past, there was a woman Who practiced virtue and was named Sujātā.
For six years the Buddha practiced austerities, extensively bestowing gifts upon a multitude of eight hundred.
At midnight he heard the words of the heavens; at dawn he milked the cows.
Having refined the milk of a thousand cows, he prepared a gruel which he held forth as an offering.
Having put on his robes, the Bodhisattva went on foot to her house;
he accepted the milk-rice from her and proceeded toward the Nairañjanā River.
For immeasurable kalpas, the Bodhisattva had extensively cultivated all manner of virtuous deeds.
Body and mind both tranquil, his every movement exceedingly gentle and refined.
Reaching the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he was surrounded by devas and nāgas;
the Bodhisattva entered the river to bathe, while the devas scattered fragrant flowers.
As he was about to ascend the riverbank, a deity approached and lowered a jeweled tree;
a virtuous woman offered a golden bowl, and a nāga queen presented a wondrous couch.
Walking with the gait of a lion, he proceeded toward the seat of enlightenment.
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Seven;
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Nineteen: Approaching the Site of Enlightenment At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Bodhisattva had bathed his body and partaken of the milk gruel; his physical strength was now fully restored. Just as he was about to proceed to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree—the ground of sixteen merits—in order to subdue those demonic adversaries, he walked toward the west with the marks of a Great Man.”
That is to say, he proceeds slowly and with composure; his deportment is as beautiful as a rainbow as he walks;
his elegant gait is leisurely and dignified as he moves as majestically as Mount Sumeru; he does not walk with haste, nor does he walk too slowly;
he does not walk with heaviness, nor does he walk with frivolity; he does not walk with turbidity or confusion, being free from defilement.
He walks with pure conduct, faultless conduct, conduct free from delusion, and conduct free from attachment;
he walks like a lion king, like a dragon king, and like Nārāyaṇa;
he walks without touching the ground, marked by the seal of the thousand-spoked wheel, and his toes are webbed with nails as red as [copper].
He walks with the ground reflecting like copper; he walks while shaking the great earth; he walks while emitting a great sound like the clashing of mountains;
he walks while natural pits, hollows, and mounds become level and even;

he walks while the radiance from beneath his feet illuminates sentient beings who have committed offenses, leading them to rebirth in the happy realms; and he walks while lotus flowers spring up at every place his feet tread.
He proceeded by following in the footsteps of the Buddhas of the past as they ascended the lion throne; he proceeded with a mind like a vajra, indestructible;
he proceeded closing off all evil destinies and opening the gates of all wholesome paths; he proceeded to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
he proceeded to extinguish the power of Māra; he proceeded to crush all heterodox doctrines; he proceeded to eliminate...
He proceeds having severed the cataracts of ignorance; he proceeds having cut off the wings of birth and death;
he proceeds eclipsing Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the Sovereign King of Devas; he proceeds as the sole honored one in the trichiliocosm;
he proceeds having personally realized the noble path without awakening through another; and he proceeds on the verge of realizing all-knowledge.
He practices, practicing in association with mindfulness and wisdom; he practices with the desire to eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death;
he proceeds toward Nirvana, the city of tranquility, free from defilement, deathless, and fearless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva proceeded with right mindfulness toward the Bodhi tree, gazing directly ahead as he walked; at that moment, there were such immeasurable displays of majestic deportment.

Then wind-gods and rain-gods came from the Nairañjanā River to the Bodhi tree, sweeping and sprinkling everywhere until it was entirely pure and adorned, and they rained down immeasurable, most excellent fragrant flowers that completely covered the ground.

In this trichiliocosm, all trees, great and small, bowed their branches toward the Bodhi tree; likewise, all mountains, including Mount Sumeru and others, both large and small, lowered their peaks toward the Bodhi tree.

The various sons of the gods of the desire realm each scattered diverse, subtle, and exquisite fragrant flowers; each exquisite flower was one *krośa* in length and breadth, forming a floral platform. Furthermore, they manifested a broad road, vast and far-reaching without end, with railings made of the seven treasures on both sides of the road, all most magnificent and beautiful, their height and depth equal to seven *tāla* trees, adorned everywhere with banners and canopies made of various jewels.
Furthermore, he manifested seven-jeweled tāla trees, with golden cords draped between each tree; upon these cords were suspended precious bells, interspersed with bright pearls and lapis lazuli.

Between those two trees there were ponds made of the seven treasures; within those ponds, golden sand was spread everywhere and fragrant water filled them to the brim, with blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), red lotuses (*padma*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*)—such flowers as these completely filling the ponds.

The four sides of that pond were adorned with stairways made of the seven precious gems; surrounding these stairways, kalaviṅkas, wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and jīvañjīvakas emitted harmonious and elegant sounds.

There were eighty-four thousand celestial maidens who sprinkled various fragrant waters upon the road ahead, and there were another eighty-four thousand celestial maidens who scattered various heavenly flowers.

Beneath each tree, moreover, there were exquisite platforms made of various jewels. Upon each of these platforms were eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, all of whom held precious vessels filled with the finest sandalwood and aloeswood incense. Furthermore, five thousand celestial maidens performed divine music, singing and dancing in praise, producing harmonious and elegant sounds.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When the Bodhisattva approached the Bodhi tree, his body emitted immeasurable light in all directions, and boundless lands were shaken throughout. Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas played celestial music, raining down various heavenly flowers from the midst of the sky, and also raining down immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial garments."
Furthermore, immeasurable elephants, horses, oxen, and other animals surrounded the Bodhisattva, letting out roars whose sounds were harmonious and pleasant.

There were also immeasurable parrots, śārikas, kokilas, kalaviṅkas, wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, emeralds, and jīvamjīvakas, all of which flew about in circles, emitting melodious and elegant sounds.
"When the Bodhisattva proceeded toward the site of enlightenment, there were such immeasurable, rare, and auspicious signs as these.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When the Bodhisattva was about to sit upon the seat of enlightenment, on that night, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the trichiliocosm, addressed the assembly of Brahmās, saying:"
"O Virtuous One, you should know!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dons the armor of diligence; with wisdom firm and the mind free from weariness, they accomplish all bodhisattva practices, penetrate all gates of the pāramitās, attain great mastery in all bodhisattva stages, and obtain the pure intentions of all bodhisattvas."

He fully understands the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings; he dwells in the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and transcends all demonic realms. He is able to personally awaken to all wholesome dharmas, attaining enlightenment not through others. Protected by the great supernormal powers of all Tathāgatas, he shall expound the path of liberation for sentient beings, act as a great caravan leader for them, and crush and subdue all the hosts of Māra’s armies.
Within this trichiliocosm, the Buddha alone is supreme as the Great King of Physicians, who compiles the medicine of the Dharma to rescue sentient beings from suffering;
he is the Great Dharma King, who illuminates the ten directions with the light of wisdom and erects the great banner of the Dharma.
They are not defiled by the eight worldly concerns, just as a lotus flower is unstained by water;
they are able to accumulate immeasurable and true Dharma-treasures, just as the great ocean contains all manner of rare jewels.
Equal toward enemies and kin, they abide as immovable as Mount Sumeru; their minds are pure, like a maṇi jewel free from all defilement; they have attained great sovereignty over the trichiliocosm.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) with such immeasurable merits as these: for the purpose of subduing all demonic adversaries; for the purpose of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for the purpose of perfecting the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; for the purpose of turning the wheel of the true Dharma; for the purpose of letting out the great lion’s roar; for the purpose of bestowing the great rain of Dharma so that all sentient beings may attain fulfillment; for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to obtain the pure eye of Dharma; for the purpose of causing all non-Buddhist paths to cease their disputations; for the purpose of bringing his original vows to fulfillment; and for the purpose of attaining mastery over all phenomena.
"O virtuous ones!
You should resolve to go there, approach him, and make offerings.
Then he spoke these verses:
“Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, Possessing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
As well as meditative concentration, wisdom, and supernormal powers, He has now realized nirvana.”
If you wish to distance yourself from the three evil realms, And leave behind the eight difficult conditions,
To receive the retribution of sublime celestial bliss, And even attain nirvana,
You should hold superior offerings And make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
Having practiced austerities for six years, he was about to proceed to the site of enlightenment.
The Lord of the Trichiliocosm, Śakra, Brahmā, and the sun and moon—none could equal him;
all who beheld him were filled with joy.
Having subdued all the hosts of Māras, he shall surely attain perfect enlightenment;
his physical marks are the thirty-two, most excellently adorning him;
his Brahma-voice is exceedingly clear and penetrating, and his mind is pure, free from all faults.
Some may have the aspiration to be reborn in the Brahma world;
some may have the aspiration to realize the fruit of a śrāvaka;
and some may have the aspiration to become a pratyekabuddha.
“Or there may be those who, desiring with joyful aspiration, shall attain the unsurpassed fruit—
such persons as these should make offerings to the Teacher.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

At that time, for the sake of making offerings to the Bodhisattva, the Great Brahmā King, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the entire trichiliocosm to become completely pure. He removed all saline wastelands, potsherds, rubble, and thorns; the ground became as level as the palm of a hand, free from mounds or ruins, and was adorned with treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and pearls.

Furthermore, auspicious grasses sprang up throughout the trichiliocosm, greenish-blue, curling to the right, soft and lovely like *kalantaka* cloth. Moreover, the great oceans were transformed into level ground, yet they did not disturb the fish, turtles, crocodiles, alligators, or other aquatic creatures. All the Brahma Kings, Śakras, and World-Protecting Four Kings from the lands of the ten directions beheld this trichiliocosm thus adorned and purified; each, from their own realm, adorned it and offered worship from afar.

Furthermore, all the bodhisattvas from the infinite lands of the ten directions, for the sake of making offerings, presented extraordinary and superior offerings surpassing those of humans and devas within their respective home countries; they all perceived boundless worlds as being like a single buddha-field, and even in the dark and obscure places between the Mount Sumerus and Iron Ring Mountains where the majestic light of the sun and moon cannot reach, they all saw the bodhisattva’s radiance shining everywhere.

“There are sixteen devaputras who protect this site of enlightenment; all these devaputras have realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Their names are:

Devaputra Parākrama, Devaputra Anabhibhūta, Devaputra Dāna, Devaputra Priya, Devaputra Vīrya, Devaputra Susthita, Devaputra Dharaṇīdhara, Devaputra Prabhākara, Devaputra Vimala, Devaputra Dharmeśvara, Devaputra Dharmadhvaja, Devaputra Śubhakārī, Devaputra Anāvaraṇa, Devaputra Mahāvyūha, Devaputra Śīlagandhavimala, and Devaputra Padmaprabha.”

These and other devaputras each transformed an area of forty thousand and eighty yojanas, extensively arranging immeasurable precious ornaments. On all four sides of that ground were sevenfold rows of jeweled paths; along each jeweled path were lined up precious tāla trees, with golden cords interlacing between every tree, from which hung various jeweled bells and which were covered by jeweled nets.
Jāmbūnada gold formed lotus flowers that covered the ground, each flower being adorned with the seven treasures.
Furthermore, various kinds of sublime celestial incense were burned, and all the wondrous trees existing among humans and devas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appeared therein;
likewise, all the excellent and wondrous fragrant flowers from the waters and lands of all worlds in the ten directions appeared therein.

Furthermore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions each manifest, within their own native lands, immeasurable provisions, vast adornments, and the bodhimaṇḍa of merit and wisdom; all such diverse activities are likewise manifested within this very bodhimaṇḍa.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When the sixteen sons of gods beheld such miraculous signs of supernatural power and various adornments, they leaped for joy with great delight. Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others, seeing this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), marveled at its unprecedented nature. Each of them regarded their own palaces as if they were burial mounds, and all offered immeasurable praises of his merit.”
Furthermore, there were four tree-guardian spirits of the Bodhi tree:

the first was named Vairatāyana, the second Sumanas, the third Ucchuṣmā, and the fourth Indradhvaja. Each, by means of their supernatural powers, transformed the Bodhi tree so that it became eighty *tāla* trees in height, breadth, and magnificence; its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were lush and flourishing, upright and lovely, with a splendor beyond compare that brought joy to all who saw it, surpassing even the Pārijātaka and Kovidāra trees in Śakra’s Nandana Grove.
The place where a Bodhisattva sits to attain enlightenment is the very center of the trichiliocosm; the ground beneath this tree is composed entirely of diamond and is indestructible.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “When the Bodhisattva was about to proceed to the Bodhi tree, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated boundless and immeasurable worlds. All sentient beings in the hells were freed from suffering; all sentient beings among the hungry ghosts were fully satiated; sentient beings among the animals turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness; those with impaired faculties all attained their restoration; those afflicted by illness all attained healing; those filled with fear all attained peace and joy; those imprisoned as criminals all attained release; the destitute all obtained wealth and treasures; those afflicted by afflictions (*kleśa*) all attained liberation; those suffering from hunger and thirst all obtained food and drink; those who were pregnant all escaped their perils; and those who were emaciated and weak all became robust and healthy.”
At that time, not a single sentient being was oppressed by greed, hatred, or delusion; neither humans nor devas died, nor did they undergo rebirth from a womb.

At that time, all sentient beings felt mutual compassion and benevolence toward one another, regarding each other as fathers, mothers, elder sisters, younger sisters, elder brothers, or younger brothers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The torments of suffering in hell all come to rest;
The beasts of prey that devour one another each give rise to a heart of loving-kindness."
The eight difficulties are all closed off, and the three evil realms are entirely empty and still;
wherever the light shines, all receive subtle and wondrous bliss.
Those whose eyes, ears, noses, tongues, and other faculties are incomplete—
All shall attain full perfection.
Those troubled by afflictions shall obtain great peace and happiness;
the poor and lowly shall attain wealth and honor, and those suffering from illness shall find complete recovery.
Those imprisoned obtain liberation;
all are free from anger and contention, and they successively give rise to hearts of loving-kindness, like parents who cherish their children.
The Bodhisattva’s net of radiant light pervades the ten directions.
Universally illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it eclipses boundless lands.
The Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains,
and all other mountains likewise cease to appear, transforming entirely into a single buddha-field.
Composed of various jewels, their adornments are most exquisite;
because they are illuminated by light, everything is as clear as looking into the palm of one's hand.
Such arrays of ornaments are for the purpose of making offerings to the Bodhisattva.
The deity who protects the site of enlightenment has sixteen sons of heaven,
each with a face eighty yojanas in extent, appearing in various ornaments.
The Bodhisattva, of great majestic power, likewise has a face eighty yojanas in extent.
He also manifests infinite lands, each one adorned and pure.
When the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, behold such sights,
they return their thoughts to their own original palaces and conceive the perception of them as tombs.
All gave rise to a sense of wonder and praised his various merits in verse:
"Excellent! His merit is inconceivable; It has brought forth such a fruit as this.
It is not merely through body, speech, and mind That such adornments have been produced."
By the power of his original vows, all things are accomplished;
according to the karma of all sentient beings, they all attain fulfillment.
The four guardians of enlightenment adorn the Bodhi tree.
Surpassing the Nandana Grove and the exquisite groves of Śakra,
this deity’s adornments are so upright and exceedingly lovely that all gods and humans praise them without end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The pure radiance of the Bodhisattva shines universally throughout the world, extinguishing the afflictions of all sentient beings; those who encounter this light all give rise to joy.”
This light also shone upon the palace of the Nāga King Kali; at that time, encountering this radiance, the Nāga King spoke these verses among the assembly of nāgas:
"The three Buddhas of the past have all already appeared, Their wisdom-light is of a true golden color.
Now, beholding again this stainless light, It is certain that a Buddha has arisen in the world."
That light is pure, surpassing the sun and moon; it is not like fireflies, candles, stars, or lightning, nor can it be reached by the majestic radiance of Brahmā, Śakra, or the asuras.
Because of my past karma of unwholesome deeds, the palace where I dwell is perpetually dark;
hot sand rains down constantly to scorch my body, and I reflect that I have long endured such suffering.
Suddenly encountering a radiance like the shining sun, body and mind become cool and filled with universal joy;
those practitioners who have cultivated for billions of eons shall now surely sit at the site of enlightenment.
Together with you and all our kinsmen, we offer robes, incense, flowers, and music,
as well as various articles of adornment, to the benefactor of the world.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, the Dragon King, together with his retinue, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as he looked toward the four quarters. He beheld the Bodhisattva’s physical form, majestic and towering like Mount Sumeru. Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits all surrounded him; their hearts were filled with great joy, and they prostrated themselves at his feet in reverent worship. They immediately offered various kinds of fragrant flowers, garments, and necklaces, performing many musical performances to honor the Bodhisattva.
With palms joined and bodies bowed, they praised him in verse: 'Your face is pure like the full moon, Great Teacher of the world.'
In the past, when I encountered various Buddhas, their auspicious signs were all like this;
now that the Honored One has defeated Māra, he shall surely realize Bodhi.
In former kalpas, he extensively practiced both internal and external giving.
Observing the precepts and practicing patience, Exertion, meditation, and wisdom, Skillful means,
great compassion, Vow-power, joy, equanimity, and so forth—
By means of these various merits, One shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
All the various groves bend their branches to pay homage to the Buddha-tree;
a thousand auspicious vases surround it in the void.
Flocks of birds emit harmonious cries, fluttering and wheeling in flight as they vie with one another to follow after it.
The color of your body is the light of true gold, Illuminating the ten directions;
Suffering and affliction cease in the evil realms, And the world is graced with happiness.
O Honored One, within the three realms, You shall surely be the Great Teacher.
The Brahma King and Śakra, along with all the sons of the gods of the desire and form realms,
have all abandoned their exquisite pleasures to come and offer worship;
surely you, O Honored One, shall now become the Great Physician-King in this world.
Wherever he treads, lotus flowers rise with each step;
this Honored One in the world must surely be one worthy of offerings.
As the Teacher sits at the site of enlightenment, surrounded by immeasurable koṭis [of beings],
All the hosts of Māra’s armies shall be utterly subdued by themselves.
The sun and moon may fall, and Mount Sumeru may crumble,
yet until enlightenment is attained, one can never be moved.
“May I and my retinue, having cast off this dragon body, adorn ourselves with merit and proceed to the seat of enlightenment.

Having spoken these verses, the Dragon Queen named Golden Light, surrounded respectfully by immeasurable dragon maidens, held various jeweled parasols, garments, necklaces, and exquisite celestial flowers; she further carried precious vessels filled with renowned incenses and played various musical instruments while reciting these sublime verses to praise the Bodhisattva:
“‘I prostrate now to him who is able to sever greed, hatred, and delusion, all the faults and afflictions of the world,
and who has crossed the ocean of birth and death.’”
The Honored One is the Great King of Physicians, Skilled at extracting the arrows of affliction;
Sentient beings who have not yet been tamed— He shall surely tame them.
Sentient beings dwelling in this world Are constantly shrouded by afflictions.
May the World-Honored One, with the sun of wisdom, Shine upon them so that they may find relief.
The world has been without refuge; Now it shall have a refuge.
And from the midst of the void, Various kinds of clothing and food shall rain down.
All the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, Have given rise to hearts of joy;
O Great Teacher of Eloquence, We pray that you will swiftly sit at the site of enlightenment.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra’s enemies, You shall surely attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Just like the Buddhas of the past, Who realized the Dharma of Bodhi;
Having practiced for immeasurable eons To benefit all living beings—
I pray that you will swiftly sit at the site of enlightenment And realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:
‘Upon what seat did the Buddhas of antiquity sit when they realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?’”
While he was reflecting thus, he immediately knew that all past Buddhas had sat upon pure grass and attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, a devaputra from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, knowing the Bodhisattva’s thought, addressed him, saying: "So it is, so it is!"
"All Buddhas of the past who sought to realize bodhi sat upon pure grass.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected to himself:
"Who can provide me with such pure grass?"

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and stood to the right of the Bodhisattva, neither too close nor too far, holding the grass. That grass was a deep azure like the tail of a peacock; it was soft and lovely like Kāśika cloth, curling to the right with a fragrant scent.
At that time, having seen the transformed person holding this wondrous grass and gradually approaching him, the Bodhisattva asked slowly:
"What is your name?
The person replied:
"I am named Śrī. The Bodhisattva reflected:

"I now desire to seek auspiciousness for myself, and I further desire that others may also attain auspiciousness. Since one named Śrī stands before me, I shall certainly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, when the Bodhisattva wished to seek pure grass from the transformed person and uttered these words,
his Brahma-voice was subtle and exquisite— namely, a voice of truth, a perfectly regular voice, a clear and resonant voice, a harmonious and moist voice,
a flowing and beautiful voice, a voice that skillfully guides, a voice without stammering, a voice without harshness, and a voice without breakage.
The voice is soft, gentle and refined, analytical, agreeable to the ear, pleasing to the mind;
it is like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, like the voice of the jīvajīvaka bird,
like the sound of deep thunder, like the sound of ocean waves, like the sound of a mountain collapsing, like the voice of celestial praise, and like the voice of Brahmā.
It was like the roar of a lion, like the voice of a dragon king, like the cry of an elephant king; it was neither hurried nor sluggish,
a voice of liberation, a voice free from attachment, a voice based on meaning, a voice appropriate to the occasion,
a voice proclaiming eight thousand koṭis of dharma-gates, in accordance with all things.
The sound of the Buddha-dharma.
With this exquisite voice, the bodhisattva spoke to the transformed beings, saying:
"O worthy ones!..."
"Can you provide me with some pure grass?
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"O Auspicious One, at this very moment, You should quickly bestow pure grass."
I shall sit upon this grass and subdue that host of Māras;
once I have realized the Dharma of tranquility, I shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
For the sake of Bodhi, I have practiced for immeasurable kalpas.
Through the powers of generosity, ethical discipline, diligence, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
through liberation and the resolve of intention;
and through merit and supernormal knowledges—by virtue of having cultivated all such practices, one now attains the fruit of perfection.
If you offer me pure grass, you shall obtain immeasurable merit;
because of this offering of pure grass, you will surely become a Guide.
Hearing these words, Śrīghoṣa felt great joy in his heart.
Holding pure and exquisite grass in his hands, he stood before the Bodhisattva and,
with a heart full of joy, addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"If by the gift of this grass you are able to attain great enlightenment,"
"I would be fortunate to first receive the Bodhi [teaching], and only thereafter accept the pure grass.
The Bodhisattva replied to Śiva:
"It is not merely by bestowing pure grass that one attains Great Bodhi;"
One must cultivate immeasurable virtues before receiving the prediction of the Buddhas.
Śrī, you should know this: awakening is not bestowed in vain;
yet awakening can indeed be bestowed in vain.
I shall bestow enlightenment upon all sentient beings.
Know this, Śrī, that once I have realized enlightenment, I will distribute it throughout all worlds; you should [abide] within my presence.
Having heard and received the nectar-like Dharma,
he proceeded toward the site of enlightenment; as he raised his foot to take a step,
the earth shook violently.
All the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others gave rise to hearts of joy, and with respectful palms joined, they said:
"The Bodhisattva shall now surely subdue the hosts of Māras;
he will certainly obtain the Dharma of Ambrosia and realize the Unsurpassed Way."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When the Bodhisattva was proceeding toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), immeasurable bodhisattvas and hosts of devas each adorned a bodhi tree. There were eighty-four thousand such bodhi trees, and for each one they made a vow that the Bodhisattva would sit beneath it and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
As for those bodhi trees, some were exceptionally lofty and sublime, measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas in height and composed entirely of flowers;
some were exceptionally lofty and sublime, measuring two billion yojanas in height and composed entirely of fragrance;
and some were exceptionally lofty and sublime, measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas in height and composed entirely of sandalwood.
There were some bodhi trees, lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary, five hundred million yojanas in height, composed entirely of silken fabrics;
some bodhi trees, lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary, ten billion yojanas in height, composed entirely of precious jewels;
and some bodhi trees, lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary, one hundred billion yojanas in height, composed entirely of the seven treasures.

Thus, beneath each of these eighty-four thousand bodhi trees, lion thrones were spread according to their respective colors and types: some lion thrones were adorned with flowers, some were adorned with incense, some were adorned with sandalwood, some were adorned with precious jewels, and some were adorned with various kinds of gems.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested the act of taking grass and spreading it everywhere like a lion king—endowed with power, firm in diligence, free from all faults, noble, sovereign, awakened by wisdom, and possessing great renown. Having subdued the hosts of Māras and crushed the various non-Buddhists, and being fully possessed of such manifold merits, he was about to realize bodhi. Facing east, he sat cross-legged upon the pure grass, straightening his body and fixing his mindfulness, and made this great vow:
'If I do not now realize Unsurpassed Great Bodhi, I shall never rise from this seat.'"
"I would rather let this body shatter than ever rise from this seat.
At that time, the Bodhisattva ascended the seat of enlightenment and immediately realized the Samādhi of the Great Array of the Play of Vast and Universal Spiritual Powers.
Having attained this samādhi, they each manifested their bodies sitting upon those lion thrones, every single body adorned with a multitude of wondrous marks and signs.
The other bodhisattvas, as well as the devas and humans, each thought that the bodhisattva was sitting on his throne alone.

Furthermore, by the power of meditative concentration, they are able to cause those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal kingdom, the world of King Yama, as well as all humans and devas, to see the Bodhisattva seated upon the seat of enlightenment.
Chapter 20: Adorning the Bodhimaṇḍa. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"At that time, when the Bodhisattva sat at the bodhimaṇḍa, the devas of the six desire realms, fearing there might be obstacles or difficulties, immediately took their places with reverence to the east. Likewise, in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, there were immeasurable devas who all stood with reverence."

At that time, the Bodhisattva emitted a great radiance; this light was named "Developing Bodhisattva Wisdom" and it shone everywhere throughout all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, pervading the entire realm of empty space.
At that time, in the eastern world-system there was a land named Vimalā, and its Buddha was named Vimalaprabha.

Therein was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vilasitavyūha; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva transformed all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space, into a single pure lapis lazuli site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All sentient beings of the five destinies within those Buddha-fields pointed to one another in succession and said to each other:
"Who is this person whose playful exercise of supernormal powers and majestic splendor of physical form are so magnificent?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested transformed bodhisattvas before each and every being and spoke these verses:
“Capable of severing all defilements and turbidities, The habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, and delusion;
Their bodies illuminate the lands of the ten directions, Outshining all other lights.”
"Merit, wisdom, and samādhi, accumulated and further increased over many kalpas—
these are all the adornments that constitute the power of the most supreme Muni.
At that time, in a world in the southern direction, there was a land named Ratnavyūha, and its Buddha was named Prabhāsa.

There was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Prabhūtaratnacchattra who, having encountered this light, arrived at the site of enlightenment surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas; for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva held a single precious canopy that completely covered this site of enlightenment. Great Brahmā, Śakra Devānām Indra, and the Four World-Protecting Kings said to one another:
"By what karmic fruit has such a jewel-adorned canopy appeared?"
From within the jeweled canopy, a sublime verse emerged, saying:
“In the past, across billions of kalpas, He made offerings to the Buddhas of the three times;
Through practicing generosity with a compassionate heart, He has thus attained this adornment of marks.”
"Having achieved the power of Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher has received this retribution;
for the benefit of all beings, he sits upright at the site of enlightenment.
At that time, in the western world, there was a land named Campā, and its Buddha was named King of Blooming Flowers, Wisdom and Supernatural Power.

There was a bodhisattva mahāsattva there named Ratnajāla; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva took a magnificent and wondrous jeweled net and completely covered the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). The hosts of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings who had gathered from the ten directions said to one another:
"By what causes and conditions has this jeweled net been brought forth?"
From within the jeweled net, a sublime verse emerged, saying:
“Capable of being the cause of all jewels, The locus upon which all jewels depend,
To whom the three realms all turn for refuge— His fame pervades the ten directions.”
"Desiring to realize great enlightenment, Abiding in the pure Dharma, one attains Buddhahood through the power of diligence; Thus can one inspire such offerings.
At that time, in the northern world, there was a land named Vartana, and its Buddha was named Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named King of Adornment; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva caused the merit-adorned pavilions of the infinite lands in the ten directions to all appear within this site of enlightenment. The assembly of beings who had gathered there felt a sense of wonder, and all the humans and devas said to one another:
"By what causes and conditions have these exceptionally sublime and wondrous pavilions been manifested?"
From within the wondrous terrace, he uttered these sublime verses:
"Due to the fulfillment of the provisions of merit and wisdom throughout boundless kalpas of the past,
his body, speech, and mind were pure, endowed with shame, modesty, compassion, and loving-kindness."
"The Unsurpassed Honored One of Capable Benevolence, Possessing every excellence without exception, Now sits upon the seat of Bodhi; Therefore, he has obtained such merit as this.
At that time, in the world-system of the southeast, there was a land named King of Virtue (*Guṇarāja*), where the Buddha was named King of the Radiance of Merit (*Guṇaprabhāsarāja*).

In that world, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Guṇamati; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva manifested an immeasurable palace adorned with various jewels and merit. When the assembled devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others who had come there saw this unprecedented sight, they were struck with wonder and said to one another:
"By what causes and conditions has such an auspicious omen appeared?"
Within the pavilion, he spoke in verse:
"Born from a multitude of virtues, The one who possesses complete merit Is able to accomplish all virtues;
Gods and dragons alike pay him homage."
"The Ocean of Virtue has come to the site of enlightenment; the fragrance of his merit perfumes everywhere.
Now seated upon the Bodhi throne, he receives such offerings as these.
At that time, in the southwest there was a land named Producing Jewels, and its Buddha was named Jewel Banner.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Abhyudgataratna; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, stood before the Bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva manifested immeasurable, incalculable circles of light made of various jewels. When the devas therein saw this unprecedented sight, they conceived a sense of wonder and said to one another:
"By what power has such a multitude of jewel-lights been manifested?"
From within that halo, a sublime verse emerged, saying:
"With palaces made of various jewels, With flowers, fruits, and groves,
And with head, eyes, marrow, and brain, With the flesh of the body, and hands and feet."
"Through such various acts of giving and the accumulation of all these merits,
I have now realized enlightenment and am moved by such offerings as these.
At that time, in the world-system to the northwest, there was a land named Cloud, and its Buddha was named Cloud King.

In that [world-system], there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Cloud-Thunder-Voice; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva manifested clouds of agalloch incense and sandalwood incense, which pervaded the entire site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All the assemblies of devas gave rise to feelings of joy and wonder, and said to one another:
"By what causes and conditions has such a auspicious response appeared?"
From within that cloud of fragrance, a sublime verse emerged, saying:
“The Cloud of Dharma covers all, Universally raining down the rain of Dharma;
It extinguishes the afflictions of sentient beings, Causing them to attain nirvana.”
"With the powers of supernormal knowledges, meditative concentration, and the faculties, adorned with merit,
and having realized the nectar-like Bodhi, he therefore receives such offerings as these.
At that time, in the northeastern world-system, there was a land named Golden Net, and its Buddha was named Jewel Canopy Radiance.

There was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Golden Net Adornment; having encountered this light, he arrived at the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas, and stood before the bodhisattva to make offerings.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva manifested within the offerings brought by those assembled Bodhisattvas an immeasurable and boundless multitude of great Bodhisattvas. Each was adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence and held flower garlands while bowing their bodies in prostration. One by one, these Bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Throughout boundless kalpas of the past, With deep faith and supreme reverence, They have praised all the Tathāgatas With subtle and wondrous voices."
"Now you sit upon the seat of enlightenment; therefore, I prostrate to you.
By this act of praise, may I attain the unsurpassed fruit.
At that time, in a world below, there was a land named Universal Observation, and its Buddha was named Universal Vision.

In that world, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnagarbha; having encountered this light, he came to the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas and stood before the bodhisattva to make offerings.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva manifested vast and wondrous golden lotuses before each and every bodhisattva. Within each flower were celestial maidens, appearing from the waist up, upright and exquisitely beautiful, their bodies adorned with various precious ornaments. Holding diverse necklaces of gold and pearls, they bowed their heads in prostration.
Then the various humans and devas said to one another:
"By what causes and conditions have we obtained such exquisite and beautiful maidens?
These maidens then spoke in verse:
"From boundless kalpas in the past, I have prostrated to all the Tathāgatas,
the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, as well as my parents and my elders."
"Upright and honest, free from faults, endowed with all merits,
and possessing the perfection of pure precepts— all such as these should be respectfully saluted.
At that time, in the world above, there was a land named Viśiṣṭaguṇa, and its Buddha was named Guṇarāja.

There was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gaganagañja who, having encountered this light, arrived at the site of enlightenment surrounded by countless bodhisattvas; for the sake of making offerings, he stood before the bodhisattva.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva caused a rain to fall throughout the void upon all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions—things never before seen and never before heard: various flower garlands of many jewels, unguents, powdered incense, and burning incense; silken banners and garments, victory banners, pennants, and precious canopies; mani-jewels and various gems; gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, and agate; elephants, horses, chariots, carriages, and military retinues; flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and boys and girls.

At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protectors, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all living beings were able to see [this]; they gave rise to hearts of joy and were free from any fear or alarm.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When the Benefactor of All Worlds Wishes to realize unsurpassed bodhi,
The immeasurable bodhisattvas of the ten directions All assemble like clouds."
The matters concerning those Bodhisattvas who have come here, I shall now briefly explain by means of a simile.
Immeasurable Bodhisattvas come from the void, like the thundering roar of dense clouds;
each one holds precious necklaces, with bright pearls hanging down in great adornment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the void; Adorned with jeweled crowns and trailing braided locks, They carry aloft exquisite flower-adorned pedestals, And reach the site of the Bodhi tree.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Like the thundering roar of a lion,
Proclaiming emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, Until they reach the site of the Bodhi tree.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the void, their voices roaring like those of the king of oxen;
raining down unprecedented and exquisite flowers, they reach the site of the Bodhi tree.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the void, their beautiful voices like those of the peacock king;
with bodies radiating a thousandfold marks, they come to the site of the path of enlightenment.
Countless bodhisattvas come from the void, their radiance like that of the pure full moon;
with wondrous voices they offer praise for the immeasurable virtues of the bodhisattva.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Their radiance shining like the sun,
Outshining all the palaces of Māra, As they arrive at the site of enlightenment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the void, Their physical forms as beautiful and radiant as rainbows;
With the provisions of merit and wisdom all fully perfected, They reach the site of the Bodhi tree.
Countless bodhisattvas came from the void, their hands extending nets of mani-jewels and various precious gems;
they scattered mandārava and sumanā flowers, as well as pāriyātra and campaka blossoms,
and bearing such flower garlands, they arrived at the site of the Bodhi tree.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Shaking the great earth with their supernormal powers;
yet all sentient beings feel no alarm or fear, and there is not one who does not rejoice.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Taking up the great king of mountains, Sumeru, in their hands;
As if holding a garland of flowers, they feel no weight As they arrive at the site of the path of enlightenment.
Immeasurable Bodhisattvas come from the void, bearing upon their heads four great oceans of fragrant water;
they sprinkle them everywhere across the great earth, making it pure and adorned, as they arrive at the site of the Bodhi path.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, each holding a most excellent jewel canopy,
so that all bodhisattvas may behold them as they arrive at the site of enlightenment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, manifesting as Brahma kings dwelling in tranquil concentration;
from every single pore they expound the wondrous Dharma, preaching great compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, manifesting the subtle and wondrous forms of Śakra;
surrounded by all devas and humans, they arrive at the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍa.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, manifesting the forms of the World-Protectors;
surrounded by all devas and humans, each scatters celestial flowers and incense,
while with the exquisite voices of kinnaras and gandharvas, they praise the Bodhisattva.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas came from the void, each holding trees of fragrant and wondrous flowers;
their branches, leaves, blossoms, and fruits were everywhere adorned as they arrived at the site of enlightenment.
Upon the flower-pedestals of those trees were bodhisattvas, who emerged half-way from within the flowers;
all were endowed with the thirty-two marks of perfection, each holding various exquisite blossoms:
*kubjaka*, *padma*, *utpala*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the void, holding pure lotus ponds in their hands;
their bodies as vast as Mount Sumeru transform into exquisite and wondrous flower garlands,
which completely cover the trichiliocosm as they reach the site of the Bodhi tree.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, each manifesting the conflagration at the end of an eon within their eyes,
yet further displaying the formation of an eon therein; from every single joint of their entire bodies,
they produce the infinite teachings of all Buddhas, which all sentient beings are able to hear.
All who hear it sever their various cravings and proceed to the site of enlightenment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void; their forms are upright and most lovely, adorned with an array of precious jewels, and their voices are like those of the kinnaras.
All devas, humans, asuras, and others, never tire of seeing or hearing him.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas arrive from the sky, their bodies as solid as adamant,
shaking the great earth down to its watery foundations, until they reach the site of enlightenment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Their radiance shining like the sun and moon;
They extinguish the suffering of afflictions for sentient beings, And arrive at the site of the Bodhi path.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, their bodies all formed of various jewels;
pervading the boundless buddha-fields, they rain down a profusion of diverse precious flowers and fragrances,
causing all sentient beings to rejoice as they arrive at the site of enlightenment.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, each capable of upholding the four kinds of treasuries;
within every single pore of their bodies, they expound countless scriptures.
Endowed with eloquence and great wisdom, they awaken all sentient beings who are mired in ignorance and intoxication.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the void, Holding celestial drums as vast as Mount Sumeru;
Striking them forth, they produce wondrous and sublime sounds, Pervading billions of buddha-fields, Universally proclaiming to all humans and devas:
"In the Sahā world, the nectar of immortality rains down."
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Eight;
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 21: Subduing Māra At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that after the Bodhisattva had sat upon the seat of enlightenment, he reflected thus:"
"I shall now attain perfect enlightenment. Māra Pāpīyān, who dwells as the most honored and supreme among those in the desire realm, should be summoned here and subdued.

Furthermore, the various devas of the desire realm and all the retinues of Māra Pāpīyān, who have long accumulated roots of goodness, shall behold my lion-like play and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Having formed this thought, he emitted from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows a ray of light named "Subduing the Hostility of Māra. This light shone throughout the trichiliocosm and radiated alongside the palaces of Māra.
Within that radiance, Māra Pāpīyān heard these verses:
"In this world there is a most excellent and pure person, Who has fulfilled his practice over a long period of time.
This scion of the Śākya clan has renounced his royal throne; He now sits manifest at the site of enlightenment."
Your body is said to possess great valor; you should go beneath the tree to engage in a contest with him.
That man has already reached the further shore; having himself crossed over, he shall deliver others as well.
You should extinguish the three evil realms entirely without remainder, so that the worlds of humans and devas may become ever more abundant;
once they have attained enlightenment, your realm will soon be empty.
The darkness of ignorance and its companion, hatred, shall all be dispersed until nothing remains;
he will surely open wide the gate of the Deathless—what plan do you now intend to take?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When Māra Pāpīyān had heard these verses, he again saw thirty-two inauspicious signs in a dream:
first, he saw that his palace was entirely shrouded in darkness.”
Second, he saw sand, gravel, and dust flying everywhere within his palace.
Third, he saw his palaces in ruins, overgrown with thorns and filled with filth and excrement.
Fourth, he sees himself terrified and uneasy, running hither and thither.
Fifth, he sees his jeweled crown fall off and his hair become disheveled.
Sixth, he sees that the trees in his garden are devoid of flowers and fruit.
Seventh, he sees his own head split open and his brain flowing onto the ground.
Eighth, he sees his own mind burning with feverish distress.
Ninth, he sees the trees and branches in his garden withering and falling away.
Tenth, he sees that the ponds and wells have all run dry.
Eleventh, he sees that the parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and saṃjīvakas within his palace have their feathers and wings shattered and withered.
Twelfth, he saw that within the palace, the bells, drums, lutes, harps, flutes, pipes, and *konghou* lutes—various kinds of musical instruments—all lay broken and discarded upon the ground.
Thirteenth, he saw his kinsmen in a state of distress and grief, raising their hands and beating their heads as they stood there despondent.
Fourteenth, he saw himself falling beneath a bed, injuring his head and face.
Fifteenth, he saw his sons who possessed great power approach the site of enlightenment and prostrate before the Bodhisattva.
Sixteenth, he saw his daughters weeping and lamenting in distress.
Seventeenth, he saw his own body with its robes soiled and greasy.
Eighteenth, he saw his own body emaciated and haggard, with dust and dirt covering his head.
Nineteenth, he saw the towers, pavilions, windows, and doors all completely collapsed and ruined.
Twentieth, he saw the generals of his army—gods, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth—all with their heads severed and lying in a heap upon the ground.
Twenty-first, he saw his precious jewels and necklaces consumed by fire.

Twenty-second: He sees the Four Great Heavenly Kings of the desire realm, Śakra Devānām Indra, and even the gods up to those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, all standing before the Bodhisattva, gazing up at him with reverence.
Twenty-third: seeing oneself fighting against an enemy and drawing a sword that will not come forth;
twenty-fourth: seeing oneself as loathsome and emitting foul sounds.
Twenty-fifth, he sees those to his left and right, as well as his own kinsmen, all turning their backs in opposition and abandoning him to depart.
Twenty-sixth, he sees all auspicious jars shattered and destroyed.
Twenty-seventh, he saw the god Nara uttering inauspicious sounds.
Twenty-eighth, he saw the deity Ānanda proclaiming that there was no joy.
Twenty-ninth, he saw the void filled everywhere with darkness, smoke, and mist.
Thirty: He saw the guardian deities of the palace raise their voices and weep aloud.
Thirty-one: He saw that even in places of sovereignty, all were no longer at ease.
Thirty-two: He saw his own palace tremble and become unstable.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Māra Pāpīyān had awakened from his dream, his entire body trembled and his heart was filled with fear. He summoned his ministers and said to them:
'I heard a voice in the air saying:'"

“The Prince of the Śākya clan has left home to study the Way and practiced austerities for six years; he shall attain perfect enlightenment while seated upon the Bodhi throne. Should his Way be realized, it will surely empty my realm.”
"You and your military hosts should go to that place and subdue him.
He then spoke in verse:
"You shall lead a great host of troops To overcome the śramaṇa beneath the Bodhi tree."
If you all would love and respect me, quickly drive him away by engaging him in battle.
Only when his intent is emptied from my realm, making him a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka,
and he is not extinguished but forever severed [from his goal], will he become a Buddha in the world without ceasing.
At that time, the Minister of the Military, who was a counselor to King Māra Pāpīyān, addressed him in verse, saying:
"The four celestial kings over whom Your Majesty rules, As well as the eight classes of beings, the nāgas, and the spirits,
The gods of the desire and form realms, following Brahmā and Śakra— They all prostrate themselves and take refuge in him."
The King’s sons were of supreme wisdom, their valor and strength peerless in the world.
The King’s army extended for eighty yojanas; though yakṣas, rākṣasas, and various spirits dwelt near the King on his left and right, they always revered those who surpassed them.
All joined their palms with deep reverence, Privately offering incense and flowers as tribute.
Having observed these signs and circumstances, I knew for certain that this was the Bodhisattva, superior to the king’s army.
Where the king’s armies dwell, the owl and the jackal raise eerie cries;
beneath the Bodhi tree, all is profoundly pure, as auspicious birds and wondrous beasts offer harmonious songs.
Such auspicious signs as these are surely powerful; when I observe the Bodhisattva, who could possibly surpass him?
Furthermore, where the king’s army and its hosts dwell, sand, gravel, and dust rain down constantly;
yet beneath the Bodhi tree, the abode of the Sage, the heavens rain fragrant flowers that pile up in abundance.
The ground where the king’s army was stationed was uneven, filled with sand, gravel, tiles, and stones;
yet beneath the Bodhi tree, it was level and smooth, further adorned with the seven precious jewels.
If one sees such preceding signs as these, a person of wisdom must certainly return;
when such adornments are fully and universally present, the Bodhisattva will surely attain perfect enlightenment.
"Great King, if you do not follow your minister's counsel, what was seen in the dream will ultimately not prove false.
Your Majesty must not offend the seer; it is fitting that you withdraw your troops and return to your own place."
In ancient times, there was a king who, having offended a seer, caused an entire kingdom to be turned to ash by a curse.
In the past, there was a king named Śuddhodana who, having acted contrary to the will of the great seer Rāṣṭrapāla,
caused that land to suffer from a severe drought for many years, so that neither the forests nor the crops could flourish.
Does Your Majesty not hear the Vedic treatises, which state that one possessing the thirty-two marks will surely attain Buddhahood?
With the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, his light shines universally upon the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
how much more so, then, this host of armies of yours—how could he not subdue them?
The mark of the invisible crown transcends the heavens; all devas can never behold it.
By practicing, one shall attain that subtle and wondrous fruit, which the world has not heard until now.
Sumeru and all the other mountains alike bow their heads before the Bodhi tree;
through the cultivation of giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom over the course of many eons,
he was able to sit alone and defeat the king’s army— all this is due to the power of his cultivated roots of goodness.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, having heard those verses from the great minister, Pāpīyān’s mind became distressed and confused. He again summoned his thousand sons; five hundred of these sons, belonging to the pure faction, stood to the right of the Māra-king and took refuge in the Bodhisattva, while the other five hundred sons, belonging to the dark faction, stood to the left of the Māra-king and assisted him."
Thereupon, Pāpīyān addressed his sons, saying:
"You should all deliberate with one mind as to what stratagem can be used to subdue him.
A son of Māra on the right side named Śāstṛ spoke a verse before Pāpīyān:
"A sleeping dragon, a drunken elephant, and a lion king—these three beasts are so fierce and violent that they are difficult even to approach;
how much more so for one who possesses such power of meditative concentration—who could possibly offend that Great Muni?"
The son of Māra on the left, named Pāpabuddhi, also addressed Pāpīyas with these verses:
“If I gaze upon a person, that person is surely destroyed; Now that I look at this tree, the tree too is shattered.
Wherever my wrathful eyes are directed, nothing remains whole; It is like encountering the Lord of Death—survival is impossible.”
The son of Māra on the right side, named Surūpa, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:
"What need is there to destroy that which is inherently unstable? Trees are known for their fragility and can be broken at will.
Even if your wrathful glare were to cause Mount Sumeru to crumble, how could you possibly lift your eyes to gaze upon the Bodhisattva?"
Even if one could swim across the great ocean, Or even draw up the vast deep in a single breath—
Such things might indeed be possible, But no one can harbor malice toward a Bodhisattva.
The son of Māra on the left side, named Śatabhuja, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse, saying:
“I now possess a hundred arms upon this single body, Each one capable of discharging a hundred arrows.
Great King, go forth without any anxiety; What is the need to harm such a śramaṇa?”
The son of Māra on the right side, named Subuddhi, again addressed Pāpīyas with these verses:
"Even if each single hair of yours were to become an arm, And each one could discharge a hundred arrows,
Though you might consider this a supreme feat, How could it harm even a single hair of the Bodhisattva?"
Through the Sage’s power of concentration and supramundane compassion, Poisons, fires, and weapons cannot cause him harm.
Those who brandish swords and staves with malicious intent Are scattered into the air, where they all turn into flowers.
Though gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas possess great power,
they are ultimately restrained by patience, which can cause their majesty and might to become weak and inferior.
The son of Māra on the left, named Ugratejas, again addressed Pāpīyān with a verse:
"I can now enter the body of this bhikṣu And burn it away with fire until it is utterly extinguished,
Just as a mountain fire consumes dry wood, Leaving no trace of any forest thicket behind."
The son of Māra on the right side, named Sunetra, again addressed Pāpīyan with these verses:
"The world and Mount Sumeru may be consumed by fire, But the diamond-like wisdom is truly difficult to burn.
Mountains may shift, oceans may dry up, and the great earth may vanish, And the sun and moon may fall from the sky; [But this wisdom remains unshaken.]”
"To benefit sentient beings he sits beneath the tree of enlightenment; until he has realized Bodhi, he shall never move.
The son of Māra on the left, named Pride, again addressed Pāpīyān with these verses:
"I now stand here and, stroking them with my hand, shall cause the palaces of the sun and moon to shatter completely."
Furthermore, one could suck up those four great oceans until everything within them is completely emptied;
one might even hurl this śramaṇa into the sea waters—Great King, do not let this cause you such distress.
Without relying on an army, I shall subdue him; I alone can cause him to be extinguished.
Now I shall break down the Bodhi tree and seize the śramaṇa to hurl him in the ten directions.
The son of Māra on the right side, named Youshin (Possessing Faith), again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:

"Even if one were to shatter the three thousandfold world-system with force, and even if such great powers were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could not move a single hair of the Bodhisattva;
how could they possibly harm one possessed of wisdom?"
The son of Māra on the left side, named Bhīṣaṇa, again addressed Pāpīyān with this verse:
“Such a śramaṇa is not to be feared; he dwells alone without any followers.
We shall now terrify him so that he flees to the ten directions. O Great King, your army is powerful—why should you be afraid?”
The son of Māra on the right side, named Ekālambana-prajña, again addressed Pāpīyān with these verses:
"Do the sun, moon, and lion have armies? Does the majesty of a Wheel-Turning King not rely on hosts?
All Bodhisattvas possess no troops; With a single body and a single thought, they shatter the demonic host."
"The son of Māra on the left side, named Pāpārthika, again addressed Pāpīyān with a verse, saying:
'I pray that Your Majesty do not grieve; I shall now take up no weapons at all.
With my trunk, I will coil up that śramaṇa And dash him down here until he is crushed to pieces. "
The son of Māra on the right, named Guṇavyūha, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:
"The physical strength of that person is exceedingly firm, Like that of Nārāyaṇa, it cannot be destroyed;
How much more so when he wears patience as his armor And exerts diligence as his blade!"
Taking the three liberations as their vehicle, and further using wisdom as their charioteer,
Bodhisattvas, by the power of such merit, will surely be able to crush and subdue my demonic armies.
The son of Māra on the left side, named Avivartika, again addressed Pāpīyān with these verses:
"Just as a launched arrow does not return of its own accord, Just as a mountain fire driven by the wind is difficult to stop,
And just as a thunderbolt of diamond never turns back— So long as the Son of the Śākyas has not been defeated, he will never return."
The son of Māra on the right side, named Raticara, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:
"A whetted arrow hitting a stone does not proceed further; a blazing fire meeting water is surely extinguished;
when a thunderbolt strikes the ground, where can it go? If you see the Bodhisattva, you should take refuge in him."
Great King, one might as well exhaust the entirety of space, Or cause the minds of all sentient beings to become one,
Or perhaps bind the sun and moon with a cord— Such things as these may indeed be accomplished,
But the Bodhisattva seated at the Bodhi tree, Great King, you cannot shake or move him.
The son of Māra on the left side, named Asaṃvigna, again addressed Pāpīyas with a verse:
“If my eyes were to look with their poison, Mount Sumeru would collapse and the great ocean would dry up;
you should know that as soon as the Śramaṇa and the Tree of Enlightenment are beheld by them, they will all be reduced to ashes.”
The son of Māra on the right, named Sarvārthasiddha, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:
"Even if this trichiliocosm were entirely filled with fierce poisons,
If one were to gaze upon the treasury of merit, It could cause all those poisons to become non-poisonous."
How could any poisons exceed the three poisons? Yet these three poisons do not afflict his body or mind;
for the Bodhisattva is fundamentally identical to empty space. Great King, be careful not to go there lightly.
The son of Māra on the left, named Priyabaddha, again addressed Pāpīyas with a verse, saying:
“Adorned by tens of billions of celestial maidens, With the playing of hundreds of thousands of exquisite stringed songs,
Entice him to enter the Palace of Sovereignty, To indulge his desires so that he may remain forever attached.”
"By this, Great King, you shall attain mastery; I only pray that you do not grieve over this.
The son of Māra on the right side, named Dharmamati, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse, saying:
"What he delights in is not unrighteous; it is only liberation and the various dhyānas."
"For the sake of sentient beings, he delights in practicing loving-kindness, And has no greedy attachment to those five desires.
The son of Māra on the left, named Caṇḍāla, again addressed Pāpīyas with a verse, saying:
"Great King, have you not heard the words of your sons? Their voices roar and thunder, shattering everything!"
"And possessing valor, strength, and swiftness, He shall go quickly there to destroy the śramaṇa.
The son of Māra on the right side, named Siṃhanāda, again addressed Pāpīyān in verse:
"The jackals howl in the great marshes Only because they have not yet heard the lion’s roar."
If they were to hear but once this lion’s roar, they would naturally flee in all ten directions.
So it is with all these ignorant Māras: having not yet heard the lion’s roar among men, they vainly compete in debate without ceasing; yet once they have heard it, they shall all be extinguished.
The son of Māra on the left, named Evil Thought (Duṣcintita), again addressed Pāpīyas with a verse, saying:
"Do you not see my host of troops? I possess evil thoughts that can quickly achieve success.
If it were not for those in the world who lack wisdom, why would you not rise up at once and flee?"
The son of Māra on the right side, named Subuddhi, again addressed Pāpīyān with these verses:
"He is not ignorant nor lacking in power; it is you yourself who are foolish and devoid of superior capacity.
You do not yet understand his skillful means; he shall surely subdue you with wisdom."
We, the sons of Māra, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, though we are thus valiant and pervasive throughout the trichiliocosm, cannot move even a single hair of the Bodhisattva;
how much less could our evil thoughts alone cause him harm?
None can harbor evil thoughts toward him; you should show him respect and give rise to a pure mind.
He is the Dharma King of the three realms; you ought to retreat and not engage in battle.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the Māra King again commanded his daughters, saying:
'O you daughters!'"
"Let us go together to the foot of that Bodhi tree to entice this son of the Śākyas and destroy his pure conduct.
Thereupon, the demoness approached the Bodhi tree and stood before the Bodhisattva; with thirty-two kinds of artful words and seductive gestures, she attempted to allure the Bodhisattva:
first, she raised her eyebrows without speaking.
Second, they lift their robes and advance forward;
third, they lower their faces and smile;
fourth, they engage in mutual playful banter.
Fifth, as if filled with longing and attachment;
sixth, gazing at one another;
seventh, drawing the lips and mouth closed.
Eighth, casting amorous glances askance;
ninth, gazing intently with a coy expression;
tenth, mutually saluting one another.
11. Covering the head with a robe.
12. Pinching or poking one another.
13. Tilting the ears as if listening.
14. Stepping forward with a mincing gait;
15. Exposing the thighs and knees;
16. Or exposing the chest.
Seventeenth, they display signs of desire by recollecting past instances of affectionate play, laughter, and sleeping together.
Eighteenth, they may, as if before a mirror, take pride in their own physical charms and gestures.
19. Moving about and emitting light;
20. Alternately rejoicing and grieving;
21. Sometimes rising and sometimes sitting.
Twenty-second, at times they emit a breath that seems unassailable;
twenty-third, their applied perfumes are intensely fragrant;
twenty-fourth, they hold necklaces in their hands.
Twenty-five: she covers her neck and collar. Twenty-six:
she displays herself as if in a secluded place.
Twenty-seven: she walks back and forth while looking back at the Bodhisattva.
28. Opening and closing his eyes as if he were scrutinizing something;
29. Walking back and forth or moving straight ahead while feigning that he does not see;
30. Uttering sighs and lamentations regarding sensual desires.
31. With beautiful eyes, she gazes intently.
32. She moves with graceful steps and casts sidelong glances.
