Possessing such causes and conditions for seduction, she further disturbed and agitated the Bodhisattva with her songs and words, speaking in verse:
"In this season of early spring, mild and warm, when all the grasses, trees, and forests are in full bloom, a man of spirit should enjoy his pleasures while the time is right;
once one's prime years are cast away, they can hardly be regained."
Though you are upright and of beautiful countenance, the five desires of the world are likewise difficult to obtain;
since you may find delight in such a sublime environment, why do you take pleasure in those teachings of Bodhi?
We women have received this celestial retribution; our bodies are subtle and wondrous, all fit to behold.
Such a heavenly body as this cannot be sought after; you, O Benevolent One, should now receive the fruit of your own retribution.
If even the various seers still give rise to defilement upon seeing me, how could a human being possibly be free from a defiled mind?
What is the use of practicing that meditative concentration?
The Dharma of Bodhi is exceedingly remote.
At that time, having heard those seductive and delusive words, the Bodhisattva felt compassion in his heart and immediately transformed the demoness with these sublime verses:
"I observe that the five desires harbor many faults and afflictions; Because of them, one loses supernatural powers through defilement.
They are like a pit of fire or a vessel of poison, Yet sentient beings rush toward them without realizing it."
I have long since been free from all afflictions; having awakened my own mind, I now awaken others.
The five desires of the world burn sentient beings, just as a fierce fire consumes dry grass;
they are like flames and illusions, devoid of reality, and like foam and bubbles, which do not endure for long.
Like an infant playing amidst excrement, or like a fool grasping the head of a snake— all these lack any real nature;
this body is a false illusion born of karma.
The four elements and five aggregates are a provisional combination; bones and sinews entwine to exist for a brief moment.
What wise person should be attached to this?
It is only because of delusion that ordinary beings give rise to desire.
Thus have I known all these illusions; therefore, I do not cling to them.
Seeking ultimate, sovereign bliss, I shall now realize enlightenment herein.
I am already liberated from the world, like the wind in space, which is difficult to bind.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body was like molten gold and his face like the full moon. His profound mind was tranquil and settled, as immovable as Mount Sumeru; he was like a pure pearl free from blemish, like the newly risen sun illuminating the world, and like a lotus flower unstained by the mud. His mind was without attachment and neither increased nor diminished."
At that time, the demoness again addressed the Bodhisattva with gentle words, saying:

"Virtuous One, your moral character is most venerable and you are honored by gods and men; you ought to have attendants. The heavens have sent me here to serve you. We are young, our complexions like the *utpala* flower; we pray that day and night, whether rising or resting, we may remain close to your side."

The Bodhisattva replied: "In the past you possessed merit and have now obtained this celestial body; yet you do not contemplate impermanence and instead create such delusions. Though your physical form is beautiful, your mind is not upright. You are like a painted vase filled with various foul poisons; it will surely destroy itself in due course—what is there to pity?"
"You have acted unskillfully and have forgotten your own origin; you shall surely fall into the three evil realms, and it will be extremely difficult to escape them.
You have come here on purpose to disturb the virtuous work of others; you are but leather bags filled with excrement—impure things—and for what reason have you come?"
"Go away!
I do not delight in you.

Since those māra-maidens could not seduce the Bodhisattva by their charms, they scattered karnikāra flowers and campaka flowers over him, circumambulated him three times to the right, paid homage, and departed.
They returned to the abode of the Māra King and addressed him, saying: "Great King!
Since time immemorial, we have never before seen such a person as this, whose mind remains unmoved even upon beholding our forms within the realm of desire."
I am capable of enchanting and exhausting the human mind; it is like parched seedlings withered by the sun, or like fresh butter placed in the sunlight that naturally melts away.
"For what reason has this man come to such a state?
I only pray, Great King,
that you do not harbor resentment or enmity toward this person."
He then spoke in verse:
“His body is like a treasury of lotuses; His face is like the pure moon;
His radiance is like a fierce flame; His complexion is like a mountain of purple gold.”
Having cultivated right practice throughout hundreds of thousands of births, all vows have been fully accomplished;
having crossed over birth and death oneself, one is able to deliver others, rescuing and aiding sentient beings without weariness or fatigue.
Excellent! I pray that the King do not be angry with him; he is the most honored and supreme among gods and men, his eyes pure as a lotus flower.
With a joyful and smiling countenance, free from all attachment, even if Mount Sumeru were to crumble and the sun and moon should fall, such a person could never be shaken.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the son of Māra named Śuklapakṣa, the Guide, addressed his father, saying:

'The Bodhisattva is pure and transcends the three realms; his spiritual powers and supernormal abilities are such that none can withstand them. All the devas, nāgas, and spirits praise him in unison. He certainly cannot be defeated or humbled by Your Majesty; do not trouble yourself by committing evil deeds and inviting calamity upon yourself.'"
Thereupon Pāpīyān addressed his son, saying: "Ho!
You are foolish and small-minded, your wisdom shallow and inferior; you have never yet witnessed my supernatural powers and spiritual strength."
The guide spoke again:
"Great King!
I am truly ignorant and my wisdom is shallow and inferior; I do not wish for Your Majesty to enter into enmity with that son of the Śākyas."
Why is this so? If there are sentient beings who come with malicious intent wishing to harm them, they do not harbor resentment;
yet, if there are other sentient beings who come with a virtuous mind to make offerings to them, they do not feel elation. Abiding between these two extremes, they give rise to a mind of equanimity.

"O Great King! Suppose there were someone who could paint various forms and images upon the void—this would not be difficult. To carry Mount Sumeru in one's hands while walking about—this too would not be difficult. Suppose there were someone who could float across the great ocean—this too would not be difficult. To bind the winds of the four quarters—this too would not be difficult. Even to cause all sentient beings to become of one mind would not be difficult; but to seek to harm a Bodhisattva is exceedingly difficult."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas did not accept his son’s admonition; he went to the Bodhi tree and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"You should rise quickly and depart from this place; you will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world as the sovereign lord of the great earth."
"Do you not remember the prophecy of the sages of old that you would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
If you were to arise and accept the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, you would be a sovereign lord of unsurpassed majesty, ruling the kingdom according to the Dharma and presiding over all."

"This wilderness is most terrifying; being alone without a companion, I fear it will harm your body. You should quickly return to the palace and enjoy the five desires to your heart's content; enlightenment is difficult to attain, and you would merely exhaust yourself in vain."
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Pāpīyas:
"You should not speak in such a manner now."
My mind takes no pleasure in the affairs of the five desires; therefore, I have renounced the four quarters as well as the seven treasures. Pāpīyan!
It is like a person who, having already vomited up food, would they ever be able to take it back and eat it again?
I have now already abandoned such karmic retribution; I shall certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi and bring an end to the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, O Pāpīyān!
"I have now sat upon the Vajra-seat and shall realize Bodhi; you should depart at once.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān glared with fury and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Why do you sit here all alone now?"
"Do you not see my host of yakṣa armies?
He then drew his sharp sword and approached the Bodhisattva, saying these words:
"I shall strike you down with this sword; rise quickly and depart, do not remain seated!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Pāpīyas:
"Even if all sentient beings in the world were to become exactly like you, and they all came bearing swords and staves to harm me, I would never rise from this seat."

Pāpīyān! It might as well be that the waters of the four great oceans and this great earth are moved elsewhere, that the sun, moon, and stars fall from the sky, or that Sumeru, the king of mountains, be overturned; yet this body of mine can never be moved.
When Māra Pāpīyān heard these words, his evil mind blazed even more fiercely; he roared in fury with a voice like thunder and spoke to the yakṣas:

"You must quickly lift up mountain rocks and take up bows, crossbows, swords, wheels, spears, halberds, axes, battle-axes, lances, javelins, hooks, and tridents—all manner of weapons—and summon the venomous dragons to unleash black clouds, thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts."
At that time, the yakṣa general led his own division of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others,
transforming their forms into various shapes. He further arrayed the fourfold army—
elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry— some appearing like asuras, garuḍas, or mahoragas.
Measuring hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of types, a single body can manifest many bodies: some with animal heads and human bodies,
some with human heads and animal bodies, some without heads but possessing bodies,
some with half-faces, some with half-bodies, some with two heads and one body, some with one body and three heads, or again—
A single body with many heads; or again, having no face yet possessing a head; or again, having a face yet lacking a head;
or again, having no face yet possessing three heads; or again, having many heads yet lacking faces;
or again, having many faces yet lacking heads; or again, being without eyes; or having only one eye, two eyes, or three eyes, and so forth.
Some have many eyes, or perhaps no ears; some have only one ear, two ears, three ears, or even many ears;
some have no hands, or only one hand, two hands, three hands, or even many hands;
some have no feet, or only one foot, two feet, three feet, or even many feet; or...
Some have entire bodies appearing as nothing but skeletons; some have heads that are skulls while their bodies are plump with flesh;
some have only their heads covered in flesh while their bodies are skeletal; some have large bodies that are emaciated and without bellies;
others are slender and tall yet have abdomens that protrude sideways; some have long legs, large knees, and sharp fangs and claws; or they have massive faces.
They protrude from the sides; some have their heads before their chests, some have lips hanging down to the ground, some have their upper garments drawn up to cover their faces;
some emit black smoke from their bodies, some spit fierce flames from their mouths; some have their flesh and blood withered away until skin and bone are joined together;
some emit pus and blood from their bodies and drink or suck one another’s; others sever their own limbs and joints, which lie scattered in disorder.
They cast themselves down, or their eyes roll to the corners; their mouths and faces are distorted and askew, or their tongues are vast and wide, or shriveled like gravel;
they hold human heads, or seize the hands, feet, bones, flesh, liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach of the dead to devour them;
or they grasp venomous snakes to eat them, or use snakes to coil around themselves.
Their necks, or their hands, may hold a skull; they may wear a garland of skulls;
or again, their facial complexion may be entirely red, entirely white, entirely blue, or entirely yellow; or it may be half-yellow, half-blue, half-white, and half-red;
or it may have the color of smoke-soiled wood, or the color of dead ashes; or again, the hair on their bodies may be like needles.
Some emitted flames from their hair; some opened and closed their eyes; some spat white foam from their mouths.
Others manifested hundreds of thousands of faces upon their bodies, each face appearing most terrifying.
Some had black snakes emerge from their eyes, ears, noses, and mouths to devour them;

some drank molten copper, or swallowed iron balls; some walked with their hands, feet, elbows, and knees severed; some emitted smoke and flames from their bodies while elephant heads bore mountains upon them; some had disheveled hair and were naked; some wore garments of blue, yellow, red, or white; some were clad in the skins of lions, tigers, wolves, snakes, and leopards; some had fire blazing atop their heads and glared with eyes wide in fury as they clashed and struck one another crosswise, filling the void of space, while others on the ground exhibited such diverse and wondrous forms that they could not all be recorded.

"These devas and ghosts, some spread black clouds with thunder and lightning; some rain down sand, soil, tiles, and stones; some lift up great mountains; some release fierce fires; some spit out venomous snakes; some bare their claws; some brandish swords; some bend bows; some dance with spears; some swing battle-axes; some move their lips and jaws; some open their mouths as if to devour; some weep, some laugh; some fly, some run; some hide, some appear—roaring and shouting with evil sounds that shake and rend the air."

Thus, an immeasurable and boundless host of hundreds of thousands of millions of soldiers crowded and choked the area around the Bodhi tree; smoke and flames blazed and steamed, while a raging, violent wind struck with fury, shaking the mountains and overturning the rivers and seas, until the heavens and earth were shrouded in gloom and the stars lost their light.
When the hosts of Māra had assembled at the midnight hour, immeasurable assemblies of Śuddhāvāsa devas spoke these words:
"The Bodhisattva is now realizing great bodhi."
Again, another deity said:
"The hosts of Māra are flourishing; because of this, they might perhaps harm the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to those deities:
"I shall soon shatter the army of Māra and cause them all to retreat and scatter, just as a fierce wind blows away delicate flowers.
Thereupon, he sat upright in right mindfulness, unmoving, and regarded the hosts of Māra as the play of children.
Māra became even more enraged and increased his combat power;

however, through the Bodhisattva’s compassion, those who attempted to lift stones were unable to do so, while those who had already lifted them could not let them fall. Swords and spears brandished and hurled remained suspended in mid-air, and any that did fall to the ground were all shattered into pieces. The poisonous breath of the evil nāgas was transformed into fragrant breezes, and the torrential rain of sand, gravel, tiles, and stones was turned entirely into *kubjaka* flowers.

All those who drew their bows to shoot at the Bodhisattva found that their arrows, once fixed to the strings, could not be released; and even those that were released remained suspended in mid-air, with lotus flowers sprouting from their tips. The fierce intensity of the flames was transformed into five-colored *kubjaka* flowers.
"At that time, Pāpīyān’s anger and poisonous malice still did not cease; leaning upon his sword, he stepped forward and said to the Bodhisattva:
'You, Śākya bhikṣu, if you do not rise quickly from this seat, I shall kill you myself.'"
Thereupon, he galloped east and west, seeking to approach the Bodhisattva, but was unable to advance.
At that time, the eldest son of the Māra King came forward and embraced his father, saying these words:
"Great King!
"Now, since I am personally unable to kill that śramaṇa, to harbor such evil thoughts in vain will surely invite sin and retribution.
Having failed to accept this admonition, Māra fled toward the Bodhisattva.
At that time, a Śuddhāvāsa devaputra, standing in the air, spoke to Pāpīyas:
"You do not know your own measure; you wish to harm the Bodhisattva, but you shall ultimately fail, just as a fierce wind cannot shake Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains."
He then addressed Pāpīyān, speaking in verse:
"The natures of earth, water, fire, and wind may contravene solidity, moisture, and heat, But the resolve of a Bodhisattva is firm;
There shall never be a time of turning back."
In the past, you made a great vow: "May I forever leave behind all afflictions;
Regarding the disease of birth and death, I shall become a Great King of Physicians.
When many fall onto deviant paths, I shall open for them the eye of right view."
Sentient beings dwell in darkness; you shall kindle the lamp of wisdom.
Desiring to rescue them from the sea of birth and death, you can provide the boat and raft.
You are this Great Holy Lord, who is now opening the gate of liberation.
Patience is its trunk, and faith and diligence its flowers and leaves;
it produces the fruits of all great dharmas, which you ought not to destroy.
You are now bound by delusion, while he has already attained liberation.
I shall now destroy your afflictions; do not act as an obstacle.
Do not harbor evil thoughts toward this person again.
Having practiced the Dharma for immeasurable eons, it is now all brought to fulfillment.
"Just as the Buddhas of the past, Attained bodhi here.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the deity of the Bodhi tree reviled the Māra king with sixteen kinds of words, while the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens praised the Bodhisattva with immeasurable wondrous voices."
At that time, King Māra’s anger was still not appeased, and he spoke these words:
"Now this bhikṣu has attained the further shore; he shall teach immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to distance themselves from my realm."
They further roused the hosts of Māra to drive and coerce the Bodhisattva, yet they were unable to succeed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke to King Māra, saying:
"Māra Pāpīyān, you should listen attentively!
"I shall now sever your enmity here, extinguish your evil karma, eliminate your jealousy, and bring you to the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
you should turn your mind toward this and give rise to great joy."
He further addressed Pāpīyān:

"By means of a minor merit, you have now obtained this celestial retribution; whereas I, throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, have cultivated noble practices, and now I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Then Māra Pāpīyān said to the Bodhisattva:
"The good you have cultivated in the past is known to you; as for your accumulated merit, who would believe you?
At that time, the Bodhisattva slowly raised his right hand and pointed toward the great earth, speaking this verse:
"Upon what do all things depend for their growth? The great earth can serve as an impartial witness;
may it bear testimony for me: you should now observe this as I speak according to reality."

At that time, the Earth Goddess, her form exquisite and her body adorned with various necklaces of genuine pearls, rose up from the earth before the Bodhisattva. Bowing low in reverence, she held up a vase made of the seven precious gems, filled to the brim with fragrant flowers, and offered it as an act of worship. She addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"I serve as a witness that throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Bodhisattva cultivated the noble path and has now attained Buddhahood. Furthermore, this ground of mine is the very core of the diamond realm; while all other directions may shift, this ground remains unmoving."
When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great sound issued forth with eighteen characteristics.

At that time, the hosts of Māra all retreated and dispersed; they were bewildered and lost their bearings, falling headlong and in disarray as they fled hither and thither. The various forms they had previously manifested could no longer maintain their shapes. At that moment, the Māra king’s spirit was crushed and humiliated, and his majesty vanished; hearing the roar of the great earth, his heart was filled with terror, and he fell down in a swoon.
At that time, there was an earth spirit who sprinkled cold water upon the Māra King and addressed him, saying:
"O Māra Pāpīyān!
Arise and depart quickly! Various weapons and arms shall come here to harm you."
At that time, the eldest son of Māra prostrated himself before the Bodhisattva, touching his head to the Bodhisattva’s feet, and spoke these words:
“Great Sage!

Please grant my father leave to confess his transgressions. He is foolish, shallow, and inferior, like an infant devoid of wisdom; leading his hosts of māras, he sought to terrify the Great Sage, yet when I previously offered counsel, he would not accept my words.”
"Now I beg the Great Sage to forgive my father and grant him leniency; I only pray that the Great Sage will swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and countless sons of gods filled the void of space. Seeing the Bodhisattva destroy the hosts of Māra, they all rejoiced greatly and performed celestial music. They rained down *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, *mahāmañjūṣaka*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers. They scattered fine powdered sandalwood incense upon the Bodhisattva, and each praised the Bodhisattva with verses of eulogy.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, together with his retinue, retreated and dispersed, returning to his own palace. **Chapter 22: Attaining Perfect Enlightenment** The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "At that time, the Bodhisattva subdued the demonic enemy, destroyed their poisonous thorns, and erected the banner of the Dharma.

First, free from sensual desires and evil, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he entered the first dhyāna. With internal tranquility and a unified mind, suppressing directed and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, he entered the second dhyāna. Free from joy, dwelling in equanimity as described by the noble ones, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, and experiencing happiness with the body, he entered the third dhyāna. Free from both suffering and happiness, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, entering into pure mindfulness and equanimity, he entered the fourth dhyāna."

"At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt in right concentration; his mind was pure, luminous, and untainted, free from secondary afflictions, supple, harmonized, and unshakable. During the first watch of the night, he attained knowledge and clarity, and with a concentrated mind, he acquired the supernormal power of the divine eye."

The Bodhisattva then uses his divine eye to observe all sentient beings—how they die here and are reborn there, whether they possess beautiful or ugly forms, and whether they are superior or inferior, noble or lowly—as they proceed according to their karma, knowing all of this completely.

These sentient beings, based on their bodies, speech, and minds, commit various evil deeds and slander the noble ones; because of these karmas of wrong views, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the woeful realms.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva observes that sentient beings, by virtue of their body, speech, and mind, perform various wholesome karmas; because of these right views and karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens.

During the middle watch of the night, maintaining a single-minded concentration, he realized the knowledge of recollecting past lives; he clearly perceived the events of births and deaths experienced by himself and others in the past, fully knowing one birth, two births, and so on, up to ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, a hundred million births, a billion births, and even extending back through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of births, as well as through the kalpas of formation and destruction, and immeasurable, boundless kalpas of formation and destruction—all of which he recollected and knew.

Regarding each dwelling place—whether by name or clan, whether by physical appearance, food and drink, suffering or pleasure, birth or death—he fully understands all physical characteristics, dwellings, and activities, whether pertaining to himself or others.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:

"All sentient beings dwell within the perilous and evil realms of birth, old age, sickness, and death, unable to awaken; how can I cause them to fully understand the limits of the aggregates of suffering that consist of birth, old age, sickness, and death?"
He reflected thus:
"From what do this old age, sickness, and death arise?
Immediately he was able to know that they exist because of birth; because there is birth, there is old age, sickness, and death.
"What causes such birth to exist?
He immediately understood that it exists because of existence.
"What, in turn, causes such existence to exist?"
He immediately understands that it exists because of grasping (*upādāna*).
[He then asks: "In this way, from what does grasping arise?
He immediately understands that it exists because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"From what cause does such craving arise?
He immediately understood that it arises because of feeling (*vedanā*).
"From what cause does such feeling arise?"
Immediately he was able to know that it exists because of contact.
[He then thought: "From what, in turn, does such contact arise?
Immediately he was able to know that it exists because of the six sense bases.
“From what cause do these six sense bases arise?
He immediately knew that they arise from name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
“From what cause does this name-and-form arise?”
Immediately he was able to know that it exists because of consciousness.
[He asked: "In this way, by what does consciousness exist?
Immediately he was able to know that it exists because of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
"By what cause, furthermore, does such a practitioner come to exist? He immediately understands that it exists because of ignorance (*avidyā*).

At that time, the Bodhisattva knows that ignorance has volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as its cause; volitional formations have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their cause; consciousness has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its cause; name-and-form has the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as their cause; the six sense bases have contact (*sparśa*) as their cause; contact has feeling (*vedanā*) as its cause; feeling has craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its cause; craving has grasping (*upādāna*) as its cause; grasping has becoming (*bhava*) as its cause; becoming has birth (*jāti*) as its cause; and birth has old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair as its causes—arising through mutual causality.
He further reflected:
"In the absence of what does aging and death not exist?
Through the cessation of what does aging and death cease?"

Immediately he was able to know: because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; because name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; because birth ceases, old age and death cease; and because old age and death cease, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
He further reflected: "This is ignorance;
this is the cause of ignorance; this is the cessation of ignorance; this is the path leading to the cessation of ignorance—there is nothing else besides these.
This is volitional formations; this is the cause of volitional formations; this is the cessation of volitional formations; this is the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations."
This is consciousness, this is the cause of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness, and this is the path leading to the cessation of consciousness;
this is name-and-form, this is the cause of name-and-form, this is the cessation of name-and-form, and this is the path leading to the cessation of name-and-form;
this is the six sense bases, this is the cause of the six sense bases, this is the cessation of the six sense bases, and this is the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases.
This is contact, this is the cause of contact, this is the cessation of contact, and this is the path leading to the cessation of contact;
this is feeling, this is the cause of feeling, this is the cessation of feeling, and this is the path leading to the cessation of feeling;
this is craving, this is the cause of craving, this is the cessation of craving, and this is the path leading to the cessation of craving.
This is clinging, this is the cause of clinging, this is the cessation of clinging, and this is the path leading to the cessation of clinging;
this is existence, this is the cause of existence, this is the cessation of existence, and this is the path leading to the cessation of existence;
this is birth, this is the cause of birth, this is the cessation of birth, and this is the path leading to the cessation of birth.

This is old age and death; this is the cause of old age and death; this is the cessation of old age and death; this is the path leading to the cessation of old age and death; and this is sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
In this way, the arising of this great mass of suffering, up to its cessation, should be understood. This is suffering;
this is its origin; this is the cessation of the origin of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of the origin of suffering—this is how it should be known.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the latter part of the night, when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva—through the noble wisdom of a Buddha, a World-Honored One, a Tamer of Men—realized through a single moment of corresponding insight all that ought to be known, all that ought to be attained, all that ought to be awakened to, all that ought to be seen, and all that ought to be realized; he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, became perfectly enlightened, and was fully endowed with the three types of clear knowledge."
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, immeasurable sons of gods among the hosts of devas spoke thus:
'We should scatter fragrant flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata.'"
Furthermore, there was a devaputra who had previously witnessed a former Buddha attain perfect enlightenment; he spoke these words:
"You should not yet scatter flowers, for the Tathāgata shall manifest auspicious signs, just as all Buddhas of the past manifested auspicious signs when they attained perfect enlightenment."
"O monks! Knowing that the devaputra desired to see an auspicious sign, the Tathāgata rose into the air to the height of seven tala trees and, in accordance with what he had realized, spoke in verse:
'All afflictions have been completely severed; All outflows have been utterly exhausted.'"
"Never again shall they undergo rebirth; this is called reaching the end of suffering.

At that time, those devaputras gave rise to joy in their hearts and scattered exquisite celestial flowers everywhere over the Buddha. At that moment, the fragrant flowers were spread so thickly that they reached up to the knees.

The Tathāgata has distanced himself from the darkness of ignorance and the net of craving and views; he has dried up the river of afflictions, uprooted the thorns of poison, and untied all fetters. Having destroyed the banners of Māra, he has raised the supreme victory banner. He is able to skillfully establish all realms of sentient beings and bestow predictions upon them. Observing their faculties and natures, he knows the root of their maladies and administers the medicine of ambrosia as a Great King of Physicians. He causes all sentient beings to attain liberation and establishes them in the bliss of the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*. Abiding in the *tathāgatagarbha*, having untied the silken cords of bondage, they enter the city of wisdom and become one with the pure *dharmadhātu* of all Tathāgatas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All Tathāgatas, upon seeing me attain the Way, have all praised me, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
They all covered me with their precious parasols.

Those various precious parasols merged into a single canopy that completely covered the trichiliocosm of the ten directions. From within the precious canopy, wondrous light issued forth; this network of light shone everywhere throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds.
In that world, the assembly of bodhisattvas praised the Buddha’s virtues, speaking in verse:
"Just like that *pundarīka* lotus, which springs up from the earth,
blooming with great purity, untainted by the mud."
Arousing a heart of great compassion, Like clouds that pervade and fill all space,
You shall rain down the great Dharma rain, To moisten and satisfy all sentient beings.
It can cause the sprouts of all virtues To grow and flourish in every way.
"Those capable of receiving the teaching shall achieve the fruit of liberation.
At that time, the devas spoke in verse:
"The Lion among Men has subdued the hosts of Māra; with all meditative absorptions manifest before him, he has realized the Deathless."
Having attained the three knowledges and the ten powers, his majestic spiritual power vibrates throughout the ten directions.
Among the assembly of bodhisattvas who had previously come, those who made offerings to the Buddha out of love for the Dharma rose from their seats,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and praised the Tathāgata, saying these words:
"Has the World-Honored One not grown weary? We have personally witnessed the subduing of the hosts of Māra.
Excellent, O Great Man, Honored One of the Three Realms! May you now rain down the boundless rain of the Great Dharma."
The Buddhas of the ten directions all bestowed canopies, and further uttered the subtle and wondrous voice of the kalaviṅka bird:
"Just as the pure bodhi attained by me, so too is that which you have realized, O Venerable One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“The goddesses of the desire realm, seeing the Tathāgata seated upon the bodhi-seat, attaining omniscience with his great vows fulfilled, subduing the hosts of Māra and establishing the banner of victory, acting as the Great Physician King who skillfully heals all ailments—”

Like a lion king, he is free from all fear; pure and stainless, he has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Endowed with the three insights (*traividya*), he has transcended the four currents (*catuḥ-ogha*). Holding the single umbrella of the Dharma (*dharma-cchatra*), he protects the triple world and is called a *brāhmaṇa*. Having distanced himself from all defilements, he is called a *bhikṣu*; having removed the storehouse of ignorance (*avidyā-kośa*), he is called a *śramaṇa*. Free from all unwholesome states, he is called one who knows contentment; because he has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), he is called a valiant hero. Able to destroy the banner of Māra, he is called one of great power. Like a jewel island, all the jewels of the Dharma are filled within him.
Then the celestial maidens spoke these verses:
“Beneath this king of Bodhi trees, He has subdued the entire host of great Māras;
Abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru, His body and mind are firm and free from fear.”
The Honored One practiced generosity for many eons, Thus attaining the perfection of all things;
The Honored One practiced ethical conduct for many eons, Outshining the hosts of Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas;
The Honored One practiced patience for many eons, Thus attaining a body of true golden color.
Because the Honored One exerted diligent effort throughout many eons, He was able to subdue all demonic adversaries;
Because the Honored One cultivated meditative concentration throughout many eons, He has obtained such supreme offerings as these;
Because the Honored One practiced extensive learning throughout successive eons, He swiftly realized the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
The Honored One is able to subdue the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death, the afflictions, and the celestial māra;
having utterly extinguished all such māras, he is now free from sorrow and distress.
The God among Gods is most venerable, Worshipped by the humans and devas of the three realms;
Thus, for those who plant seeds in this field of merit, The blessings they obtain shall never perish.
The tuft of hair between the brows is supremely radiant, Universally illuminating all lands throughout the ten directions;
It eclipses all the suns and moons of the world, Benefiting and bringing relief to all sentient beings.
The physical form and color of the Tathāgata are most majestic and dignified; his marks and signs and countenance are exceedingly pure.
He is worthy of being the one to whom the three realms offer sustenance, universally benefiting all sentient beings.
With pure eyes, he surveys the ten directions, universally beholding the physical deeds of sentient beings;
with pure ears, he hears everything—the voices of devas and humans, and the sounds of the Buddha-dharma.
With the mark of the broad and long tongue, he proclaims the wondrous sound; those seeking liberation hear the nectar of immortality.
Though the armies of Māra rise up to cause harm, he feels no fear; when gods and humans offer worship, he is neither elated nor resentful.
He destroys the demonic enemies without exerting force, subduing them solely through a heart of loving-kindness;
free from defilement, attachment, and all faults, his body and mind are peaceful and unshakable.
Now there is the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and humans; All sentient beings receive his wholesome benefit.
Having heard the True Dharma, you should believe and accept it; May you swiftly, like the Honored One, attain Perfect Enlightenment.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Under the Bodhi tree, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he manifested the supernatural powers of a Buddha, sporting with sovereign mastery beyond all measure; were one to wish to describe them, even an entire kalpa would not suffice.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in brief verse:
"The entire earth is universally transformed, Level and even as the palm of a hand;
Exquisite lotus flowers well forth, Each and every one with a thousand petals."
Countless hosts of devas each rained down various exquisite flowers;
moreover, before the World-Honored One, they joined their palms and gazed up at him in reverence.
When the World-Honored One first attained Buddhahood, he performed all manner of supernatural powers.
Sumeru and all the kings of mountains, The grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—
All of them bowed their heads, Prostrating at the seat of enlightenment.
This is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Manifesting the play of supernatural powers.
From his body he emits hundreds of thousands of kinds of light that illuminate the ten directions;
reaching even the sentient beings in the three evil realms, it extinguishes their suffering and brings them peace and happiness.
At that time, among those in the eight states of no leisure, there is not a single sentient being [who does not receive this benefit].
Encompassing greed, hatred, delusion, and all other afflictions—
this is the Lion King’s play of great supernormal powers.
The sun, moon, mani-jewels, fire, lightning, and all such radiances [are surpassed by it].
By the radiance emitted by the Buddha, all else was eclipsed and no longer appeared.
Among the gods and the world of humans, none were able to see the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Seated upon the lion throne, he performed miraculous displays of supernatural power.
The Buddha pressed the earth with his finger, and it immediately shook in six ways.
He subdued the hosts of Māra’s army as easily as one restrains cotton wool;
King Māra, filled with grief and distress, drew figures on the ground with his staff.
This is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sporting in great supernormal powers.
*The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
*The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of the Central Indian Kingdom, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Three: Praise.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devaputras scattered exquisite celestial fragrant flowers over the Buddha and praised him with verses in accordance with the true merits of the World-Honored One, saying:
“The afflictions of sentient beings are darkness; Wisdom is able to eliminate them.
The reason the Tathāgata appears in the world Is to be the light for the world.”
Having subdued all the hosts of Māras, with merit fully perfected, you shall now rain down the great Dharma-rain to universally nourish all living beings.
You are the most supreme person in the world; in wisdom and power, none can surpass you.
Dwelling in the world without defilement or attachment, He is like a pure lotus flower.
Sentient beings dwell through the long night, Bound by the maladies of affliction;
The Buddha, as the Great King of Physicians, Treats them so that they may attain healing.
Now that the World-Honored One has appeared in the world, the eight difficulties are all void and still;
all humans and devas alike, having encountered the Buddha, receive peace and happiness.
If there are those who behold this supreme man among men, [they shall likewise find liberation].
Throughout a hundred kalpas, they shall not fall into the various evil realms.
If there are those who hear the Buddha’s subtle, wondrous, and profound Dharma,
they will swiftly eliminate the affliction of the defilements, and the aggregate of suffering will likewise be exhausted.
One shall attain the most excellent fruit, the bliss of liberation and nirvana;
among all the worlds, one shall become a Worthy One (Arhat).
If one encourages others to make offerings, one likewise obtains great benefit and merit.
"One shall obtain the most excellent and wondrous fruits, even unto Nirvana.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven had praised the Tathāgata, he joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side."

At that time, the Devaputra Samantaprabha again made offerings to the Tathāgata with various kinds of exquisite incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, scattered blossoms, banners, streamers, and precious parasols. He circumambulated the Buddha three times, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
"The Muni’s profound wisdom and voice are harmonious and beautiful; He has attained the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
Among all sounds, yours is the most supreme; Therefore, we now pay you homage."
Because he gives rise to loving-kindness toward all worlds, he acts as a lamp and a refuge;
able to extract the various poisoned arrows from sentient beings, he is further the Great King of Physicians for the world.
In the past, the Honored One encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; He gave rise to a heart of great compassion to moisten all beings.
The Honored One is like a pure lotus in the world, Untainted by the mud of the three realms.
His mind is firm and steadfast, incapable of being thwarted; As lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru, it is difficult to shake;
Furthermore, like a diamond, it cannot be destroyed, And is also like the pure, full moon of autumn.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the devaputra Samantaprabha had praised the Tathāgata, he joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side.

At that time, the devaputra Brahmakāyika covered the bodhimaṇḍa with a jeweled net adorned with immeasurable maṇis as an offering to the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and praised him with these verses:”
“The World-Honored One can uphold the light of clear wisdom, And possesses the thirty-two supreme marks;
His mindfulness, wisdom, and merit are all perfected, He is free from all fetters, afflictions, and evils.
Pure and stainless, he has severed the three poisons; Therefore, we now pay him homage.”
His fame is heard everywhere as he realizes the three vidyās; He bestows upon all sentient beings the three gates of liberation.
Purifying all turbid impurities, his mind is fully tamed; Arousing great compassion, he benefits the world.
With the three karmas stilled, he has emerged from the world; He eliminates the three doubts and remains free from attachment.
For the sake of all the world, you practice asceticism; You transform sentient beings through the Four Noble Truths.
Diligently cultivating wholesome deeds, you transcend all conditioned formations; Having attained liberation yourself, you shall deliver others.
The Māra King brought forth his hosts of demons, yet the Honored One subdued them all through compassion;
having attained the nectar-like path of Bodhi, we therefore take refuge in you all together.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the Brahmakāyika devaputra had thus praised the Buddha in various ways, he withdrew and stood to one side.

At that time, the son of Māra from the right side, belonging to the pure faction, approached the World-Honored One, offered a canopy of various exquisite jewels to the Tathāgata, and praised him with a verse, saying:”
"I personally saw the Tathāgata, sitting upright upon the seat of enlightenment;
though the armies of Māra were most fiercely arrayed, he remained transcendent and undaunted,
and in a single moment, he subdued them all without exception."
Since you possess such virtues, I now prostrate in homage to you,
the Unsurpassed Great Muni, who is perfectly complete in all respects;
though hosts of Māras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges exist, they have never been able to shake you.
For the sake of awakening, the Honored One practiced generosity throughout immeasurable eons;
relinquishing his wife, children, and others, as well as his own flesh, limbs, and hands,
he was without any stinginess in all things, and thus attained this supreme adornment.
The Honored One has made vast vows and attained the unsurpassed path;
he shall deliver all living beings, with concentration and wisdom as his armor and pure dharmas as his boat and raft.
Having fulfilled his noble aspirations, he now proceeds.
I shall now deliver all living beings.
Praising the Buddha’s manifold virtues, I vow that in a future life I may attain the unsurpassed path; furthermore, by this merit, [may I...]
"Having subdued all the hosts of Māra’s enemies, may you swiftly realize all-knowledge.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the pure son of Māra had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, he prostrated before the Tathāgata, circumambulated him with reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side."

At that time, the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), surrounded by countless sons of gods, came to the place where the Buddha was with reverence. Taking exquisite celestial flowers of Jāmbūnada gold, he scattered them over the Tathāgata and praised him in verse, saying:
"What the Tathāgata speaks is entirely true; There is nothing concealed and no confusion.
Far removed from the darkness of ignorance and the defilement of sin, He has realized the great Bodhi of the nectar of immortality."
His radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions; therefore, I now prostrate in homage.
The World-Honored One is compassionate toward all, skillfully discerning the faculties of beings and subduing the heterodox.
Possessing supreme wisdom and the ten powers, he is able to reveal the subtle and wondrous conduct of sentient beings.
Abiding in the void, he manifests spiritual transformations, Moving without hindrance as if treading upon the earth.
Beholding the vast craving within birth and death, He knows it to be but delusive suffering and abandons it;
Following the mental activities of devas and humans, He teaches and transforms them all, causing them to attain liberation.
Benefiting the ten directions like the light of the sun, And serving as eyes for those within the three realms,
He acts as a refuge for all the world; His mind has never given rise to attachment,
He sports with supernatural powers with mastery, And in this world, there is none equal to him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven had praised the Buddha, he, together with the host of devas, prostrated, circumambulated him, and withdrew to stand to one side.”

At that time, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, together with the hosts of devas, respectfully surrounded him and approached the Buddha’s presence. With various flower garlands, precious jewels, and silken banners, they made offerings to the Tathāgata and praised him in verse:
“The light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom Extinguishes the three impurities;
All afflictions have been severed, And all auspiciousness is fully accomplished.”
The various sentient beings of the world, Attached to false pride,
are now gathered by the Honored One And led to the path of ambrosia. Therefore,
he has transcended the world, Receiving the offerings of gods and humans.
Able to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he is called the Great King of Physicians.
Before the World-Honored One, the light of the sun, moon, mani-jewels, fire, Śakra,
Brahmā, and others— all these lights fail to appear.
Illuminated by wisdom, this place is entirely auspicious;
everything therein is rare and marvelous, and for this reason I now pay homage.
The World-Honored One knows the true meaning and likewise knows all false and illusory phenomena.
Within these two dharmas, there is nothing that is not spoken according to reality.
Your speech is most subtle and your mind is exceedingly gentle;
as the teacher of gods and humans, I now pay homage to you with my head bowed.
The Honored One possesses great wisdom, awakening all sentient beings;
through the three knowledges and eight liberations, he is able to eliminate their three poisons.
He skillfully discerns the faculties of the multitude—those who are capable of receiving the teaching and those who are not.
"According to each one's own inclinations, I now pay homage.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the Deva-king of Nirmāṇarati had spoken this verse, he, together with the host of devas, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side."

At that time, the King of Tuṣita Heaven, together with the host of devas, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, respectfully surrounding him. They covered the Buddha with various celestial, exquisite garments, jeweled nets, and precious parasols, and spoke these verses in praise:
“In the past, in the Tuṣita Palace, You extensively expounded the pure Dharma;
Your bequeathed teachings remain even now, And all the devas yearn for them with longing.”
Such an ocean of merit, acting as a bright lamp for the world,
whom those who behold never tire of seeing— I now pay homage to you.
As the Honored One passes away from that heaven, the eight difficulties are all extinguished.
Having sat at the site of enlightenment, the world has attained peace and happiness.
For the sake of all sentient beings, the Buddha gave rise to the great bodhicitta;
now that he has subdued the enemy Māra, he has realized the unsurpassed path.
"Please swiftly deliver those who have not yet been delivered, and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the King of the Tuṣita Heaven had spoken this verse, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side."

At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with the assembly of devas, respectfully surrounded him and approached the Buddha’s dwelling. With various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, banners, flags, and precious parasols, they made offerings to the Buddha and praised him in verse, saying:
“The Buddha is the Unsurpassed One; Who in the world could be his equal?”
Through morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, I now pay homage to you.
Observing the hosts of devas at this site of enlightenment,
they offer worship to the Venerable One with exquisite jeweled pavilions.
There is no other person or deity capable of receiving such offerings.
The Buddha has appeared in the world; having practiced asceticism for a long time, he has subdued the hosts of Māra and attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Having extinguished the darkness of ignorance, the light of wisdom illuminates the ten directions;
acting as the Dharma-eye for the world, he benefits all beings.
Even if one were to spend immeasurable eons praising the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [one could not exhaust his virtues].
"The merit of a single pore cannot be fully exhausted;
his fame pervades the ten directions—therefore, I now prostrate to him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
After the King of the Yāma Heaven had praised the Buddha, he was respectfully surrounded by the host of devas; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra, together with the Trāyastriṃśa devas and the various hosts of devas, respectfully surrounded him as they approached the Buddha’s dwelling. Having made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, streamers, canopies, incense, flowers, and robes, they prostrated to the Tathāgata and praised him in verse, saying:
“The merit of the Tathāgata is exceedingly pure; Body and mind are unmoving, like Mount Sumeru.”
The light of wisdom illuminates the ten directions, And his renown is heard everywhere throughout all worlds.
Because the World-Honored One, throughout many kalpas in the past, Made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas,
He has now subdued Māra and attained perfect enlightenment, Becoming worthy of the supreme offerings of devas and humans.
The Honored One is one of great learning, concentration, and wisdom; He opens the unsurpassed eye of the Dharma of knowledge.
I now take refuge in the Victorious Banner of the Śākyas, The Great Lord of the Dharma for all the world.
For many eons, for the sake of enlightenment, you have extensively practiced immeasurable asceticisms;
through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and skillful means, as well as diligence, wisdom, and the great merit of Brahmā.
Having already attained such merits as these, you now further possess the fruit of the ten powers.
When I beheld the Buddha seated at the Bodhi tree, the hosts of Māra sought to inflict harm;
though some among the devas were filled with anxiety and fear, the Tathāgata’s body and mind remained undisturbed.
When the World-Honored One lowered his hand, the demonic hosts thereupon all retreated and dispersed.
As the Buddhas of the past attained perfect enlightenment, so too has the Honored One now realized the Way;
in merit and wisdom, everything is without difference—he is the one worthy of offerings from humans and devas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After Śakra Devānām-indra had praised the Buddha with these verses, he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew, and stood to one side."

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their celestial maidens, all holding *campaka* flowers, *pāriśa* flowers, and various other fragrant blossoms, and performing celestial music, came to the place where the Buddha was. Having made offerings to the Buddha, they spoke these verses in praise:
“The Tathāgata’s beautiful voice Can delight the minds of all.
Through his virtuous conduct, diligence, and precepts, His mind is pure and he always smiles.”
Causing sentient beings to find joy and delight, I now prostrate to you.
By means of those subtle and wondrous words, you eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings,
bestow immeasurable happiness, and lead them to a pure mind free from transgression.
Having attained untainted wisdom, there is none in the world who can compare;
Equanimous and immovable, like Mount Sumeru,
He manifests in the world, like a lotus rising from the water.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the Four Heavenly Kings had praised the Buddha, they prostrated, circumambulated him, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the devas in the void likewise covered the sky with various fragrant flowers, precious parasols, banners, pennants, bells, and nets. They also emerged half-way from their bodies, each holding various precious jewels and necklaces to make offerings to the Tathāgata, praising him with these verses:”
"I always dwell in empty space, beholding all that is good and evil;
only the body of the Tathāgata is pure and free from all faults."
Furthermore, I see multitudes of bodhisattvas holding various jeweled terraces that fill the entirety of space, their number being beyond measure.
I also see multitudes of bodhisattvas making offerings to the Tathāgata.
They scattered those exquisite flowers until they filled the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, they saw hosts of bodhisattvas bringing immeasurable offerings:
flower garlands, various necklaces, parasols, and earrings.
The fragrance of the flowers is most abundant, entirely without confusion;
like streams returning to the great ocean, they gather like clouds throughout the void.
The Tathāgata accepts these offerings with a mind that is equal toward all.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the celestial hosts of the void had made offerings to the Buddha, they prostrated, circumambulated him, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, because the earth deities wished to make offerings to the Buddha, they swept the ground clean, sprinkled it with scented water, and scattered famous flowers until the entire Bodhimaṇḍa was completely pure. They further covered it above with jeweled canopies and then praised the Tathāgata with these verses:”
“The Tathāgata sits upon this great trichiliocosm; this is the firm adamantine seat.
Even if my flesh and blood were to wither away entirely, I shall not rise until I have attained bodhi.”
Had it not been for the Tathāgata’s power of supernormal faculties, this dwelling place of mine would have shattered;
seeing these multitudes of bodhisattvas who have come, we are now all at peace.
Because the World-Honored One has walked upon this ground, the trichiliocosm has been illuminated;
wherever the Buddha’s light reaches is a stūpa—how much more so this place where he attained enlightenment?
May all the lands under my rule, together with this, be used by the World-Honored One.
May these sons of the Buddhas and the śrāvakas, along with the merit of the Dharma they have taught,
cause all sentient beings alike to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“After the earth deity had spoken this verse, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined her palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Merchants Receiving Prophecy. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, immeasurable devas all praised the Tathāgata’s merits.

At that time, the World-Honored One gazed at the King of Bodhi Trees without blinking for even a moment; taking the joy of dhyāna as his food, he had no thought of other sustenance, and remained seated without rising for seven days."

Countless devaputras from the desire realm came to the place where the Buddha was, carrying ten thousand precious vases filled with scented water; furthermore, countless devaputras from the form realm also came to the place where the Buddha was, likewise carrying ten thousand precious vases filled with scented water, to bathe the Tathāgata and wash the Bodhi tree.

At that time, after the Tathāgata had finished his bath, there were again countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others who vied with one another to take the water used for the Tathāgata’s bath and sprinkle it upon their own bodies; they all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When the sons of the gods had finished bathing the Tathāgata, they returned together to their celestial palaces. The fragrance of the remaining water they carried did not fade; they perceived only the scent of the Buddha and no other scent. Their hearts were filled with joy at this unprecedented experience, and they all attained the stage of non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Samantakusuma who rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what samādhi does the World-Honored One abide, such that for seven days you remain in the full lotus posture with body and mind unmoving?”
"O bhikṣus! At that time, I said to the devaputra Samantakusuma:
'The Tathāgata dwells sustained by the food of the Samādhi of Joyful Delight; by the power of this concentration, he remains in the full lotus posture for seven days.'"
At that time, the Devaputra Samantakusuma spoke in verse before the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One’s feet bear the thousand-spoked wheel, As pure and radiant as a lotus flower;
Constantly honored by the jeweled crowns of all devas— Therefore, I now prostrate in worship.”
At that time, the devaputra, having prostrated to the Buddha, spoke again in verse to offer praise:
"Desiring to dispel the doubts of those gods and humans, he joyfully joined his palms and stepped forward to inquire."
The Tathāgata has descended to birth among the Śākyas, causing all those of the Śākya clan to rejoice;
he can extinguish the three poisons and all doubts—may he resolve the delusions of gods and men.
For what reason did the One Possessing the Ten Powers, having attained perfect enlightenment, gaze upon the King of Trees for seven days?
O Lion among Men with eyes like blue lotuses, why did you remain unmoving in the cross-legged posture while gazing at the tree?
All Buddhas are likewise thus; does the World-Honored One alone gaze upon the King of Trees?
Your countenance is dignified and serene, your speech is without duplicity, your teeth are white, even, and closely set, and your mouth is fragrant and pure.
For the sake of benefiting devas and humans, please speak according to reality so as to inspire joy in them.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the devaputra:
"That which you have asked shall now be explained in brief.
It is like the worldly custom of ascending the royal throne, where for seven days one must avoid moving from it."
Thus these Buddhas, as Kings of Dharma, Conform to worldly custom and do not move for seven days.
Just as a valiant general, having achieved victory, Immediately reflects upon the conquered host,
So too these Buddhas, having subdued the hosts of Māra, Remain in the full-lotus posture for seven days without rising.
The three poisons, the afflictions, and ego-conceit—these all cause harm to sentient beings.
All afflictions are the causes of outflows; I have eradicated them all in this place.
From this, the fire of untainted wisdom arises, Incinerating the three poisons until nothing remains;
By the power of my wisdom at this place, I decisively sever the firm net of birth and death.
Rightly knowing that the substance of the aggregates is entirely unreal, Arising solely from delusive confusion since beginningless time,
The two types of ignorance— the grasping at "I" and "mine"— Along with all false views, are completely extinguished.
The dense forest of all hindrances and the four inversions—these are all incinerated by the fire of wisdom and roots of goodness;
the garland of false perceptions born of conceptualization is obtained [only to be] entirely cast aside upon the attainment of bodhi.
The sixty-five kinds of perilous ignorance, The forty unwholesome states and thirty impurities,
The sixteen forms of negligence and the eighteen realms, The twenty-five states of existence, all without exception, And the twenty heavy defilements—
these he has entirely abandoned; As for the twenty-eight kinds of worldly fears, [He has likewise transcended them all.]
Through diligence in this place, I have transcended all such things.
I have realized the five hundred roars of the Tathāgata and attained a hundred thousand perfect dharmas.
The ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the branches and leaves of the tree of transgression along with its very root, [have been uprooted].
I take wisdom as my fire, and within it I burn everything away until nothing remains.
The accumulation of craving and doubt is like a surging river, its waters of various views ever full;
here, with the sun of wisdom, I expose them to its majestic radiance until they are utterly exhausted.
Deceit, falsehood, flattery, crookedness, stinginess, envy, and the like— this forest of afflictions and such faults—
I shall now burn them all away with the fire of wisdom until they are utterly extinguished.
Slandering the Brahmās and the Noble Ones gives rise to various sins; these roots are capable of causing one to fall into the evil realms.
I administer the medicine of wisdom to them, causing them to vomit it all up until nothing remains.
Furthermore, in this place, I have attained the multitude of virtues of concentration and wisdom;
the host of sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions has been eliminated entirely, leaving nothing behind.
Furthermore, in this place, I have realized the true principle.
The arrows of all fetters and the conceit of "I am"— I have extracted them without remainder.
Furthermore, in this very place, with the sharp sword of wisdom,
I have severed "I" and "mine," the very root of birth and death.
Just as Śakra, the Lord of Devas, destroyed the hosts of Asuras,
so too have I attained the eye of pure wisdom in this place;
yet all sentient beings are shrouded by the cataracts of ignorance.
With the medicine of wisdom, I wash it away so that it may be removed.
Furthermore, at this place, with the cool water of liberation,
I extinguish the fire and smoke of craving within the wood of that objective realm.
Furthermore, in this place, with the wind of great diligence,
I have dispelled the clouds of afflictions and the lightning of conceptual discrimination.
Moreover, in this place, I have attained the samādhi of loving-kindness.
Treasury of all great merits, subduing the armies of Māra;
furthermore, in this very place, I attained the concentration of wishlessness,
a treasury of all great merits, severing all afflictions.
Furthermore, in this place, I attained the concentration of emptiness,
a treasury of all great merits, and severed all conceptual discrimination.
Moreover, in this place, I attained the concentration of signlessness.
A treasury of great merits, extinguishing all conceptual proliferation;
furthermore, in this very place, I have attained the three doors of liberation,
and through the power of supernormal knowledges and wisdom, I have decisively severed the net of birth and death.
Furthermore, I have forever severed that [delusion]: the perception of permanence in the impermanent, the perception of pleasure in suffering, and the perception of self in what is non-self.
By the power of my diligence, I have crossed over the ocean of birth and death.
I have torn asunder the net of all cravings, like the makara fish;
I have awakened to this: that all greed, hatred, and the like are like a great mass of fire, which incinerates all moths that fly into it.
Throughout the long night, for immeasurable and boundless eons,
I have labored within the cycle of birth and death, wandering on without rest;
now I have found cessation, free from sorrow and free from fear.
That which I have awakened to, the non-Buddhists cannot awaken to;
it is the meaning of the nectar-like words, capable of removing sorrow, affliction, and the like.
I have entered the city of fearlessness, having eliminated all aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Afflictions such as craving are all extinguished, and I shall no longer receive a future body.
For the sake of enlightenment, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas,
I have extensively practiced manifold virtuous deeds, giving away my own body, flesh, hands, and feet.
With all merits fully perfected,
one therefore attains here the supreme nectar, the unsurpassed Great Enlightenment—
the true Dharma realized by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
According to the various classes of sentient beings, you expound the Dharma through differentiation;
I now do likewise, having attained such a wondrous Dharma.
In a single kṣaṇa, I am able to realize and know all worlds.
Arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is empty, quiescent, and devoid of anything existent;
like a city of Gandharvas, like a mirage in the sky.
The Dharma-eye I have attained perceives universally infinite lands.
Just as one might view an *āmra* fruit within the palm of one's hand,
so too have I attained samādhi and mastered all things;
recollecting immeasurable eons is like awakening from a dream.
The various devas and humans of the world Are scorched by inverted perceptions;
I, now, in this very place, Am able to understand them as they truly are.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have sought unsurpassed bodhi.
Practicing great loving-kindness, by virtue of cultivating a mind of loving-kindness,
one subdues the hosts of Māra.
Practicing great compassion, by virtue of cultivating a mind of compassion, [one subdues the hosts of Māra].
Having eliminated all afflictions and troubles,
one practices great sympathetic joy; by virtue of cultivating a joyful mind,
one realizes the unsurpassed path.
Seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I practiced great equanimity;
because I cultivated a mind of equanimity through its conditions, I realized the Dharma of the Deathless.
Just now, before Māra, I made such a vow.
If I do not attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall never rise from this seat.
With the wisdom of the vajra, I have extinguished ignorance and the like;
having obtained the ten powers, I now therefore rise from this seat.
What was not yet attained is now all attained; all outflows are completely exhausted;
the army of Māra is utterly shattered and dispersed; for this reason, I now rise from this seat.
The gateway of the five hindrances is entirely broken; the fangs of the three cravings are all removed.
Therefore, at this moment, he has finally released his cross-legged posture.
At that time, the Supreme Being rose from the Vajrāsana and sat again upon the precious throne,
where he received the ritual ablutions of the devas.
The devas, with precious jars filled to the brim with fragrant water,
bathed the body of the Buddha, the God among Gods. Thereupon, the hosts of devas,
together with the celestial maidens, [paid their respects].
They struck up celestial music to perform this offering:
"O you sons of the gods, you should know this:
for this reason, I shall not rise from this seat for seven days."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“For what reason did the Tathāgata, having first attained perfect enlightenment, not rise from his seat for seven days?
It was because he remained in this place to eradicate birth, old age, sickness, and death, which have no beginning and no end; thus, for seven days, he gazed at the tree and did not rise.”
In the second seven-day period, he walked back and forth in a circuit extending to the limits of the trichiliocosm.

In the third seven-day period, he gazed upon the site of enlightenment without blinking for even a moment, thinking: "It is here that I shall dwell to sever birth and death and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Upon reaching the fourth week, the Tathāgata walked back and forth nearby, taking the great ocean as his boundary.
At that time, Māra the King went to where the World-Honored One was and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
Having practiced with diligence and undergone ascetic austerities for immeasurable kalpas, you have finally attained Buddhahood;
now is the very time to enter parinirvāṇa.
We pray that the Tathāgata will enter nirvāṇa; we pray that the Sugata will enter nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said, “Pāpīyān!

It was because I originally made a vow to benefit all sentient beings that I sought great enlightenment; having diligently accumulated merit through hardships for immeasurable kalpas, how can you wish for me to enter nirvāṇa so quickly while all sentient beings have not yet obtained benefit and profit within my Dharma?”

Furthermore, while in this world the Three Jewels are not yet complete, sentient beings are not yet tamed, spiritual powers have not yet been manifested, the sublime Dharma has not yet been preached, and immeasurable bodhisattvas have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how can I enter into nirvana?
At that time, having heard these words, the Māra withdrew to sit on one side and, scratching the ground with his staff, thought to himself:
"From this day forward, this realm of desire shall no longer be mine."
His heart was filled with grief and distress.
At that time, the three daughters of the Māra King, seeing their father in sorrow and suffering, said to him:
"Great King, what is it that you are doing, that your heart gives rise to such extreme grief and suffering?"
"One who now vexes the Great King— pray tell me who this person is?
I shall entice him with desire as one restrains an elephant with a rope,
causing him to give rise to attachment so that I may lead him back to my own palace."
At that time, the Māra King spoke a verse in reply to his daughters:
“The person in this world who has left defilement behind cannot be restrained by the objects of craving, for he has transcended desire; therefore, I am distressed.”

"These demonesses had already assumed seductive forms to disturb the Bodhisattva when the Tathāgata was still a bodhisattva; yet through various illusions and deceptions, they were unable to gain any advantage. Because women’s afflictions of greed and attachment are so deep and heavy, these three women further transformed their appearances—one into the form of a young girl, one into the form of a young wife, and one into the form of a middle-aged wife—and came to where the Buddha was."
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, caused those three women to all become old matriarchs.
Thereupon, the three women returned to their father’s place and spoke these verses:
“The King speaks of one who has left desire behind, Whom the objects of greed cannot defile.”
I further manifested transformations to delude and confuse that śramaṇa.
Any person who saw me would vomit blood when their lust was aroused;
yet now, though my exquisite form is revealed, it does not disturb his mind.
"By means of his great supernormal powers, he has transformed me into an old woman.
I pray that Your Majesty, by your majestic power, will cause me to regain my original form.
At that time, the Māra King replied to the women:
"I do not see anyone, whether god or human, who can restrain the Buddha.
You should go in person to repent for your previous transgressions; only when he withdraws his supernormal powers will you be able to restore your original forms."
Thereupon, the demonesses went to where the Tathāgata was and spoke these verses:
"We were devoid of wisdom; We deluded the Tathāgata.
Not knowing what is a field and what is not a field, We failed to recognize the wholesome and the unwholesome."
"I now feel profound remorse, hoping that my transgressions may be extinguished.
I only pray that by the power of your compassion, you will restore me to my original form.
At that time, out of compassion, the Tathāgata immediately withdrew his supernormal powers, causing the demoness to return to her original state.
In the fifth week, he stayed at the abode of the Dragon King Mucilinda.

At that time, cold winds and torrential rain did not cease for seven days. The Dragon King, fearing in his heart that the wind and rain might harm the Tathāgata, emerged from his own palace and approached the Buddha’s dwelling. He shielded the Buddha with his body, coiling around him seven times, and used his heads as a canopy to cover the Buddha above.

Furthermore, from the four directions, immeasurable dragon kings all came to protect the Buddha; their dragon bodies were piled up like Mount Sumeru. These dragons, having received the Buddha’s majestic radiance, attained a peace and joy of body and mind such as they had never experienced before.
After seven days had passed, the wind and rain ceased. The various dragon kings prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and returned to their own palaces.

At that time, during the sixth seven-day period, the World-Honored One went to the foot of a nyagrodha tree near the Nairañjanā River; this place was frequented by many non-Buddhists, and the assembly of those non-Buddhists all came to pay their respects and inquire after the World-Honored One:
“During these seven days of wind and rain, were you not troubled, but dwelt in peace and comfort?”
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Tranquil and contented, Contemplating and realizing the Dharma,
Benefiting all sentient beings, With compassion for all."
"Far removed from the defilement of all sins, Unattached to the world, having forever severed the mind of *māna* (self-conceit)— This is the supreme peace and happiness.

At that time, during the seventh seven-day period, the World-Honored One went to the Bahuputraka Grove and sat cross-legged beneath a tree. Observing sentient beings who were oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death, he cried out in a loud voice:
"All sentient beings in the world are constantly scorched by the five desires;
one should always contemplate the relinquishing of craving, for through craving they only grow more intense."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, in the kingdom of Northern India, there were two brothers who were the leaders of a great caravan of merchants. One was named Tīrthika-puṇya and the other was named Puṇya. They were wise and discerning, thoroughly proficient in worldly affairs; their natures were harmonious and gentle, and they were skilled at leading others. Their trade and commerce brought them exceptional profits, and they were returning to their home country with five hundred wagons laden with precious treasures."

This caravan had two well-trained oxen, one named Sujāta and the other named Yaśas.
