They were skilled in recognizing the path ahead and knew how to discern safety and danger; they would guide the way by following the scent of blue lotuses (*utpala*) without the need for whips or blows, resorting to such methods only when the other oxen could not carry on.
When they reached the Milk Forest, the road was exceedingly level and straight; yet the oxen’s hooves struck the ground so hard that the wheels and axles were shattered.

At that time, five hundred chariots were stranded by the roadside, and even with two oxen leading them, they could not advance; though lashes and whips were applied, they still could not move forward.
At that time, the merchants were filled with fear and said to one another, "The two oxen do not move forward; there must surely be something terrifying ahead.
They immediately dispatched mounted riders carrying weapons to patrol the path ahead.
When the messenger returned, he said to the merchant leader, "I traveled the road ahead without any perils or difficulties; why then could even the two oxen not proceed?
At that moment, a forest-guarding deity suddenly manifested his form and spoke to the merchants:
"O merchants, do not harbor fear.
Having wandered through birth and death for a long night, you have now attained a great benefit. Why is this so?

"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has appeared in the world; having first attained perfect enlightenment, he has resided in this forest for forty-nine days without eating. You should bring various kinds of food and drink and offer them to him."

Then the two tamed oxen proceeded toward the Buddha, and the merchants followed after them. Before they had traveled far, they beheld from afar the Tathāgata, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his bodily radiance blazing like the sun first rising.
Having seen the Buddha, they all conceived a sense of rare and profound reverence and spoke thus:
"Is this the Brahma King? Is he Śakra Devendra? Is he one of the Four Heavenly Kings? Is he the Sun or Moon deity? Is he a mountain spirit? Or is he a river spirit?"

The World-Honored One then slightly raised his *kāṣāya* robe to show it to the merchants. Upon seeing this, the merchants immediately recognized that the Tathāgata was a renunciant; their hearts were filled with joy, and they said to one another, "The dharma of those who have left the household life is not to eat at improper times.
We ought to prepare various delicious foods—such as clarified butter, honey, sugarcane, and milk gruel—and offer them to him in a timely manner."
The merchants prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink, approached the Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times to the right, stood to one side, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Out of compassion for me, please accept this humble offering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, when the Tathāgata was about to accept the food of those merchants, he reflected thus:"
"All the Buddhas of the past have all carried alms bowls; with what vessel shall I now receive this food?
Having had this thought, the Four Heavenly Kings each brought a golden bowl and offered it to the Tathāgata, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will use this bowl of ours to accept the food of the merchants; out of compassion for us, may we obtain great peace and happiness throughout the long night."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"The dharma of renunciation does not permit the acceptance of such golden bowls as yours; even when they successively offered bowls made of the seven precious substances, he accepted none of them."
At that time, the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa said to the other heavenly kings:
"I recall that in the past there was a blue-bodied deva who brought four stone bowls and gave them to us."
Furthermore, there was a deva named Samantaprabha who came and said to me:
"Be careful not to use this stone bowl; you should instead make offerings to it, regarding it as a stūpa."
"Why is this? In the future, there will be a Buddha who appears in the world named Śākyamuni; you should offer this bowl to that Buddha.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa spoke to the other kings of the gods, saying:
"Since you wish to give the stone bowl, now is precisely the right time.

The Four Heavenly Kings each returned to their own palaces and, together with their retinues, took that stone bowl, filled it with celestial flowers, and anointed it with incense. They played various celestial music to make offerings to the stone bowl and came to the place where the Buddha was. Each offered his bowl to the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

We pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept us, receiving this stone bowl we offer and partaking of the food of the merchants; out of pity for us, may you cause us to obtain great peace and happiness throughout the long night and enable us to become vessels of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The Four Great Heavenly Kings have offered me these almsbowls out of pure faith; however, it is not fitting for me to accept and keep four bowls. If I were to accept only one and not the other three, those three kings would surely feel resentment. Therefore, I shall now accept all four bowls offered by the kings."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the alms bowl from Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Northern Quarter, and spoke these verses:
“You have offered an alms bowl to the Sugata; You shall become a vessel for the Supreme Vehicle.
I now accept your gift, Causing you to be endowed with mindfulness and wisdom.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the alms bowl from the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke these verses:
“By offering this bowl to the Tathāgata, Your mindfulness and wisdom shall increase;
In birth after birth you shall experience happiness, And swiftly realize the Bodhi of a Buddha.”

**Chapter 25: The Exhortation of Mahābrahmā** The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment, he dwelt alone in a certain place within the Veṇuvana forest, entering deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to observe the world. He reflected thus:

That which is called transcending the five aggregates and entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—being without location or activity, pure in its essential nature, neither grasping nor abandoning, and beyond comprehension; that which cannot be demonstrated, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and effortless; far removed from the six sense objects, not conceived by the mind, not expressible by speech, and impossible to hear; that which cannot be seen, free from all obstructions, detached from all mental clinging, reaching the ultimate state: it is emptiness, non-apprehension, and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*.
If I were to expound this Dharma for others, they would all be unable to comprehend it; their efforts would be in vain and yield no benefit. Therefore, I should remain silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I have attained the nectar-like Dharma of non-action, Profoundly deep, tranquil, and free from defilement.

This Dharma is far removed from verbal expression, Like space, it is free from all defilement;
Where thought and mental activity do not proceed— If one can know this, it is truly rare.
This nature of phenomena is free from words; who is able to awaken to and enter its underlying principle?
Only by making offerings to the Buddhas throughout many kalpas can one finally hear it and give rise to faith and understanding.
It cannot be said that it exists, nor that it does not exist; It is likewise neither non-existent nor existent.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas of practice, I had not yet attained ultimate *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.

All dharmas are empty by their very nature.
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain perfect enlightenment and become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."

Seeing all sentient beings dwelling in birth and death, unaware of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma,

Excellent, Sugata!

“World-Honored One!

If I were to expound this Dharma for others, they would all be unable to comprehend it; their efforts would be in vain and yield no benefit. Therefore, I should remain silent.

“There are those in the world whose faculties are mature and who are capable of being delivered; I pray only that the World-Honored One will arise from his meditative concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Brahmā, saying:

“I have realized a most profound and subtle Dharma—supremely tranquil, difficult to see and difficult to awaken to—which cannot be understood through discursive thought, but is known only by the Buddhas.”

That which is called transcending the five aggregates and entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); being without location or activity, its essential nature is pure; neither grasping nor abandoning, it is unknowable; it cannot be demonstrated, is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and effortless; it is far removed from the six sense objects, beyond the reckoning of the mind, and cannot be spoken by words or heard; it cannot be perceived, is free from all obstructions, and having abandoned all points of reference (*ālambana*), it reaches the ultimate state—emptiness, non-attainment, and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas, having heard these verses, were filled with great anxiety and distress; they then suddenly vanished from that place.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

may the Buddha’s great compassion not abandon his original vow.
Like the lion’s roar, like the thunder of heaven,
"For the sake of sentient beings, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his Buddha-eye, beheld all sentient beings—those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties; those in the group of the fixed in error, those in the group of the fixed in correctness, and those in the group of the undetermined.

"Monks! "O Bhikṣus! At that time, the Tathāgata, observing sentient beings of indeterminate disposition, gave rise to great compassion and spoke these words:

"If there are those with pure faith, they shall listen to and receive such a Dharma.

"O Bhikṣus!

Chapter Twenty-Six: Turning the Wheel of Dharma, Part One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When I formerly practiced austerities, they attended to me with reverence; I shall first turn the Wheel of the True Dharma for those five men. "I shall turn the unsurpassed, supreme Wheel of Dharma, which has never been turned before.
At that time, Ajātaśatru took his leave of the Buddha and traveled south.
The Tathāgata journeyed north, passing through the city of Gayā, where there was a dragon named Sudarśana who prepared a vegetarian feast the following day to invite the Tathāgata.

After the Tathāgata had finished his meal, he proceeded to the village of Rohitavastuka; next he went to the settlement of Tālaka; then he passed through the village of Sālaka. Traveling in this manner, he was everywhere honored with offerings of food and drink by elders and householders, proceeding in succession until he reached the banks of the Ganges.
At that time, the river waters surged and flowed level with the banks; wishing to cross, the World-Honored One asked the boatman, who replied, "Give me the fare, and I shall ferry you across."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the boatman,
saying, "I have no payment. The boatman said:
"If there is no price to be paid, we shall ultimately not ferry you across.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata soared through the air and reached the other shore.
When the boatman saw the Buddha manifesting such supernatural power, he reproached himself, saying:
"I possess no such knowledge; why then have I not crossed over like these noble ones?
With a mind filled with grief and distress, he fainted and fell to the ground. After a long while, he regained consciousness and went to King Bimbisāra to recount in detail what he had seen.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately commanded the boatmen:
"From this day forward, do not accept payment for ferrying śramaṇas across.
"O bhikṣus! [he said.]

The Tathāgata went to Vārāṇasī; at the time of dawn, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food and returned to his original place. Having finished his meal, he proceeded to the Deer Park.
At that time, the five Bhadravargīyas saw the World-Honored One from afar and said to one another:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is negligent and greedily attached;

he is unable to maintain the precepts. Desiring to sever the afflictions, he has already regressed and fallen away, losing his meditative concentration. Previously, when he practiced asceticism, he was still incapable of achieving anything; how much less so today, when he indulges in fine food and dwells in ease?"

"This indolent person is clearly not a vessel for the Path; we need no longer pay him respect or inquire after his well-being. Do not prepare a seat for him, do not provide water for washing his feet, and do not arrange any food or drink for him at all. We should not rise from our seats when he approaches, and if he wishes to sit, we should point to a low seat and have him take it."
Only Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya did not share the sentiments of the group.
At that time, as the World-Honored One gradually approached the place where the five men resided, the five all became uneasy, like birds in a cage being oppressed by fire.
"Monks, you should know!
Among the beings of the world, there are none who, upon seeing the Buddha, can remain sitting at ease.

At that time, the five men all violated their original agreement; unaware of it, they suddenly rose together to welcome the Buddha. Some spread out a seat, some provided water for washing his feet, some polished his shoes, and some held his robe. They all said:"
"Welcome, Elder Gautama!
Please be seated on this excellent seat.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had sat upon that seat, the five men prostrated before him, paid their respects, and stood to one side, addressing the Buddha:
“Venerable Gautama!
Your face and eyes are upright and handsome, your faculties are serene, and the radiance of your physical marks is like Jāmbūnada gold and the campaka flower, O Gautama!”
"Should you now realize the supramundane noble wisdom?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the five men:
"You should not address the Tathāgata as 'Elder,' for it will bring you no benefit throughout the long night."
He spoke again to the five men:

"I have already realized the Dharma of the Deathless; I now know the path leading toward the Deathless. I am the Buddha, endowed with all-knowledge; my mind is tranquil, untainted, and has attained mastery."

"You must come; I shall show you the Dharma and instruct you. You should listen and receive it, practicing according to what is taught. Then, in this very body, you will exhaust all outflows, dwell in liberation with clear wisdom, accomplish the holy life, complete what was to be done, and no longer undergo future existence."
He further addressed the five men:
"Formerly, you all resented me and spoke these words:
'The Elder Gautama is addicted to worldly pleasures; he does not steadfastly maintain the precepts, and his desire to sever the afflictions has already led him to fall back.'"
"Since we have just approached you and each of us feels uneasy, you should know that it is not appropriate to address the Tathāgata as 'Elder'.
The five Bhadravargas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to become a śramaṇa within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣu!"

His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes appeared upon his body, whereby he became a śramaṇa. His hair and beard were of a length as if shaved seven days prior; his majestic deportment was as dignified as that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet to repent for his past transgressions, and regarding the Tathāgata as his Great Teacher, he gazed upon him with reverence, giving rise to a heart of joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the pond to bathe; having finished bathing, he sat in quiet meditation at another spot and reflected:
"Upon what seat did the Buddhas of the past turn the wheel of Dharma?"

While he was reflecting thus, suddenly a thousand jewel thrones emerged from the earth at that spot. At that time, the Tathāgata rose from his original seat, respectfully circumambulated the first three high thrones, and sat cross-legged upon the fourth throne.
Then the five Bhadravargas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat before him.
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance, and its light shone everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm. Within this web of light, he spoke these verses:"
"Descending from that Tuṣita Palace, he was born in the Lumbinī Garden;
Brahmā and Śakra both received and supported him, majestic and powerful as a lion."
Walking seven steps toward the ten directions, he was never once confused in mind;
then, with a Brahma-voice, he uttered these words:
"Among all things, I am now the most honored and the most supreme."
Having renounced the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, you shall bring benefit to sentient beings.
After six years of ascetic practice, you will proceed at once to the seat of enlightenment,
subdue the hosts of Māra, and swiftly attain the unsurpassed path.
The Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas entreated him to turn the wheel of Dharma;
out of compassion for all the world, he accepted their request in silence.
By the power of his firm vows, he proceeded toward the Deer Park.
At this place where the seer descended, he proclaimed the unsurpassed Dharma.
This Dharma is that which has been realized through cultivation over countless eons;
you who delight in hearing it should come quickly to listen and receive it.
A human or celestial body is difficult to obtain; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is extremely rare;
to hear the Dharma and give rise to faith is likewise difficult for such a person.
You have not been born into the eight states of no leisure; you have now attained a human or celestial body.
Having encountered the Buddha and heard the True Dharma, you have been able to develop pure faith.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have never before heard the True Dharma;
now that you have met with it, you should practice it well.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Within the net of light, such verses were spoken to awaken all the multitudes of humans and devas throughout the trichiliocosm: 'You should come quickly!'"
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, turns the Wheel of Dharma.
Upon hearing these words, the devas, nāgas, and others came from their respective palaces to the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, by means of supernatural power, the earth deities caused this site of enlightenment to be exactly seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth, adorned in various ways and entirely pure. The celestial deities of the void further used various banners, streamers, and precious canopies as ornaments. The sons of gods from the desire realm and the form realm brought eighty-four thousand precious lion-thrones and placed them within the site of enlightenment, each requesting to say:
“World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for me, please sit upon this seat and turn the wheel of the true Dharma. “O Bhikṣus!”

At that time, from the lands of the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—an immeasurable *koṭi* of bodhisattvas who had planted roots of virtue in the past arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined in reverence, entreated the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma.

All the Śakras, Brahmās, World-Protectors, and the immeasurable hosts of sons of gods throughout the trichiliocosm of the ten directions prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, entreated the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The entire assembly spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One,

out of compassion for all sentient beings and for their benefit and peace, will rain down the great Dharma rain, erect the great Dharma banner, blow the great Dharma conch, and beat the great Dharma drum."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Dharmacakra. He held a wheel made of various jewels with a thousand spokes; its adornment was so exquisite and magnificent that it could not be compared to anything else, and it emitted a thousand rays of light."
Furthermore, it was adorned with flower garlands, precious bells, exquisite silks, and immeasurable precious ornaments.

Due to the power of the Bodhisattva’s prior vows, this wheel appeared; it was used to make offerings to the Tathāgatas—the Buddhas of the past—all of whom turned the Wheel of Dharma only after such a wheel had arisen.
At that time, that bodhisattva took this wheel-treasure and offered it to the Tathāgata, speaking these verses:
“O Honored One, recall the past, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon you the prophecy:
‘You shall attain perfect awakening, and your name shall be Muni.’”
At that time, I too made this great vow:
"When the Teacher attains Buddhahood, I shall offer him this precious wheel-treasure.
May all humans and devas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattvas,"
Their number is immeasurable, and all have turned the wheel of Dharma.
Each, by their own supernatural power, brings various offerings— jeweled terraces,
flower canopies, and the like— which could not be fully described even in an entire kalpa.
"In this trichiliocosm, the devas, humans, asuras,
and the multitudes of nāgas and spirits— all with one mind, they entreated him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“The Tathāgata passed the first watch of the night in silence; during the middle watch, he comforted the great assembly, causing them to give rise to joy; when the final watch arrived, he called the five Bhadravargas and addressed them, saying:
‘You should know this!...’”
Those who have left the household life face two kinds of obstacles. What are these two?

The first is when the mind is attached to the realm of desire and cannot be detached from it; this is the conduct of inferior persons—ignorant, ordinary, and foolish—who are not noble. It is not consistent with reason, nor is it a cause for liberation, a cause for the departure from desire, a cause for supernormal powers, a cause for attaining Buddhahood, or a cause for nirvana.
Second is improper reflection, whereby one inflicts suffering upon oneself in pursuit of liberation; thus, one experiences the retribution of suffering in the past, present, and future.
Monks! You should abandon these two extremes. I shall now explain the Middle Way for you; you should listen attentively and constantly practice it with diligence.
What is called the Middle Way?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these eight factors are named the Middle Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are four noble truths.
What are the four?

That is to say: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Bhikkhus! What is called the noble truth of suffering?

That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging; these are called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?
It refers to craving, grasping, and becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking pleasure here and there; this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
What is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?
It refers to the total exhaustion of craving, clinging, existence, delight, and greed—the longing for superior pleasure; this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
What is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is the eightfold noble path, namely right view up to right concentration; this is what is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Again he addressed the bhikṣus:

“Regarding this Dharma of suffering, though I had not heard it from another before, through skillful conformity and correct reflection, there arose in me knowledge, the eye, clarity, fullness, wisdom, and light.”

"Monks! Thus, regarding this Dharma of the origination of suffering, though I had not heard it from another before, through skillful conformity and proper reflection, there arose in me knowledge, there arose vision, there arose clarity, there arose pervasiveness, there arose wisdom, and there arose light."

"Monks! Thus, regarding this Dharma of the arising, cessation, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, through my own diligent, thorough, and systematic reflection upon it—without having heard it from another—there arose in me knowledge, there arose vision, there arose clarity, there arose pervasive understanding, there arose wisdom, and there arose light."

"Monks! This path leading to the cessation of suffering, which I had not heard from another, arose through my own proper reflection in accordance with reality; it gave rise to knowledge, gave rise to vision, gave rise to clarity, gave rise to all-pervasive understanding, gave rise to wisdom, and gave rise to light."
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"Suffering should be known; its origin should be abandoned; its cessation should be realized; and the path should be cultivated. Regarding these four dharmas, which I had not heard from others before, through skillful conformity and reflection in accordance with reality, there arose in me knowledge, vision, clarity, pervasiveness, wisdom, and light."
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“I have already known suffering, already abandoned its origin, already realized its cessation, and already cultivated the path. Regarding these four dharmas, which I had not previously heard from another, through skillful conformity and reflection in accordance with reality, there arose in me knowledge, the eye, clarity, pervasiveness, wisdom, and light.”
"Furthermore, he addressed the bhikṣus:
'Before I had seen the Four Noble Truths and before I had attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, right knowledge had not yet arisen.

Once I had realized and seen the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, my mind attained liberation and my wisdom attained liberation; no longer subject to decline, I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through right knowledge.'"
"My births have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a Brahma-voice—a voice produced from the accomplishment of immeasurable merit, cultivated through the practice of truth over immeasurable kalpas, realized spontaneously without relying on a teacher—and uttered this wondrous sound, saying to Kauṇḍinya and the others:

"The eye is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span. It is like withered grass or a wall made of mixed earth—perilous, fragile, and unsubstantial. As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."

Kauṇḍinya! All dharmas arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature; they are free from permanence and free from annihilation, like empty space. Although there is neither an agent nor a recipient, the laws of good and evil do not perish.

Kauṇḍinya! Form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Through the causal condition of being moistened by the water of craving, manifold sufferings increase;
if one attains the Noble Path and realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty, one can then eternally extinguish such manifold sufferings.
Kauṇḍinya! Ignorance arises from that discrimination and improper reflection; there is no other cause for ignorance, yet this discrimination does not itself reach the state of ignorance.

Furthermore, conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; yet this ignorance does not reach the volitional formations. Continuing in this manner, conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact; conditioned by contact, feeling; conditioned by feeling, craving; conditioned by craving, clinging; conditioned by clinging, existence; conditioned by existence, birth; and conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise. These constitute the causes of the world, and there is nothing else that can serve as their cause.

Although all phenomena arise, their causes do not arrive; ultimately, these phenomena are devoid of self, person, sentient being, or experiencer. When this body is relinquished and one passes to those aggregates, if one contemplates according to reality without conceptual discrimination, ignorance is extinguished.

With the extinction of ignorance, volitional formations are extinguished; with the extinction of volitional formations, consciousness is extinguished; with the extinction of consciousness, name-and-form is extinguished; with the extinction of name-and-form, the six sense bases are extinguished; with the extinction of the six sense bases, contact is extinguished; with the extinction of contact, feeling is extinguished; with the extinction of feeling, craving is extinguished; with the extinction of craving, grasping is extinguished; with the extinction of grasping, existence is extinguished; with the extinction of existence, birth is extinguished; and with the extinction of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are extinguished.
If one can thus realize the causes and conditions regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, at that time one shall attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Such a profound and subtle Dharma as this cannot be realized by followers of other paths.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects for Ājñātakauṇḍinya three times, Kauṇḍinya and the others fully comprehended the causal conditions of all phenomena; their outflows were exhausted, their minds were liberated, and they became Arhats.

At that very time, the Three Jewels appeared: the Bhagavān as the Buddha Jewel, the turning of the Dharma wheel in three phases and twelve aspects as the Dharma Jewel, and the five Bhadrakas as the Saṃgha Jewel.

When the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, sixty koṭis of devas from the desire realm, eighty koṭis of devas from the form realm, and eighty-four thousand people all became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma with a sublime Brahma-voice; its sound reaches throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions. Those Tathāgatas each hear the sublime Brahma-sound of the three turnings and twelve aspects, and all see the World-Honored One dwelling in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī turning the wheel of Dharma.”
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions remained silent and did not preach the Dharma. The bodhisattvas from those lands each rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Why does the Tathāgata now remain silent and not preach the Dharma?
At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"You should know!

The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, throughout immeasurable kalpas, diligently accumulated merit with courageous and vigorous perseverance while practicing the bodhisattva path; having surpassed the practices of immeasurable bodhisattvas, he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the Sahā world, benefiting all beings by giving rise to great compassion and turning the wheel of Dharma.
"The Brahma-voice of that Buddha pervades the boundless lands of the ten directions; it is because I have now heard the sound of his preaching the Dharma that I remain silent.
When the assembly of bodhisattvas had heard the Buddha’s words, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow:
"May we, in the future, swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha and awaken sentient beings with the eye of untainted Dharma (*anāsrava-dharmacakṣus*), becoming equal to that Buddha."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is an immeasurable multitude of great bodhisattvas who have come; they wish to hear of all the merits associated with the Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly proclaim the nature of the Wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha addressed Maitreya and the other bodhisattvas, saying:
“Good son! The Wheel of Dharma is profoundly deep because it cannot be grasped;
the Wheel of Dharma is difficult to see because it is free from the two extremes.”
The Wheel of Dharma is difficult to awaken to, because it is free from both mental application and non-application;
the Wheel of Dharma is difficult to know, because it cannot be cognized by consciousness nor known by wisdom;
the Wheel of Dharma is unmixed.
Because one can only realize it by severing the two obscurations;
because the Wheel of Dharma is subtle and wondrous, being beyond all analogies;
and because the Wheel of Dharma is firm and solid, as it can only be entered through vajra-wisdom.
The Wheel of Dharma is difficult to obstruct, for it has no fundamental limit;
the Wheel of Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation, for it is detached from objective conditions;
the Wheel of Dharma is inexhaustible, for it is without decline or loss.
The Wheel of Dharma is all-pervasive, for it is like space. "Maitreya!

The Wheel of Dharma reveals that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, and without location. It is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; it reaches the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and ascends to the further shore. It is empty, signless, wishless, and effortless; its essence is pure, free from all craving, and it accords with suchness (*tathatā*), is identical to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and is equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). It is indestructible and uninterrupted, unattached and unimpeded. It skillfully enters dependent origination, transcends the two extremes, and does not abide in the middle. It cannot be shaken; it accords with the effortless practice of all Buddhas, neither advancing nor retreating, neither exiting nor entering, and is without attainment and beyond verbal expression."

The nature is solely one, yet it enters into all phenomena; this is non-duality, which cannot be established as a fixed entity. It returns to the primary meaning and enters the dharma of true reality (*dharmatā*). The dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is equal and transcends all calculation; the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. It is beyond analogy, equal to empty space, neither deviating from the extremes of annihilation or permanence nor destroying dependent origination. It is ultimately quiescent and without change, subduing all Māras and crushing all heterodox paths. It transcends birth and death to enter the realm of the Buddhas—the sphere traversed by noble wisdom, realized by *pratyekabuddhas*, and pursued by *bodhisattvas*—which all Buddhas praise!
All Tathāgatas equally possess such non-differentiated dharmas.
Maitreya,
the essential nature of the wheel of Dharma that they turn is thus.

If there is one who thus turns the wheel of Dharma, they are called a Buddha; they are called the Perfectly All-Knowing One (Samyaksaṃbuddha); they are called the Self-Awakened One; they are called the King of Dharma;
they are called the Guide; they are called the Great Guide; they are called the Caravan Leader; they are called the Sovereign;
they are called the Sovereign of Dharma; they are called the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma; they are called the Donor of Dharma; they are called the Great...

The donor is named "Perfection of Good Conduct," named "Satisfaction of Noble Intent," named "Speaker," named "Doer," named "Consoler," named "Bringer of Peace," named "Valiant One," named "Victor in Battle," named "Maker of Light," named "Dispeller of Darkness," named "Bearer of the Lamp," and named "Great King of Physicians."
Healing the world is called extracting the thorns of poison, called the wisdom that transcends obstructions,
called universal vision, called universal observation, called the universal eye, called Samantabhadra, called universal radiance,
called the universal gate, called sublime dignity, and called non-attachment.
Because it is like the great earth, it is called "equanimous"; because it is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, it is called "immovable";
because it accomplishes all merits and transcends the world, it is called "most venerable"; because it penetrates all phenomena, it is called "invisible from above" (anavalokitamūrdha);
because it transcends the darkness of worldly afflictions, it is called "the bright lamp"; it is most profoundly deep.

It is called the "Great Ocean" because its bottom is difficult to fathom; it is called the "Treasure Repository" because it is fully endowed with the jewels of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*);
it is called "Untainted" because the mind is liberated through non-attachment and non-binding; it is called "Non-retrogressive" because it penetrates all phenomena;
it is called "Like the Wind" because it benefits sentient beings without discriminating among places; and it "incinerates all" [afflictions].
Because it burns away afflictions (*kleśa*), it is like fire; because it washes away all conceptual afflictions, it is like water;
because it is the sphere of unimpeded supernormal power and wisdom within the equal *dharmadhātu*—neither having a center nor a periphery—it is like space;
and because it removes the obstructions of all phenomena, it abides in unobstructed knowledge, transcending the range of the worldly eye.
Therefore, he is named "Pervading All Dharmadhātus"; because his body is unstained by any worldly realms, he is named "Supreme Person.
He is named "Immeasurable Wisdom," named "Teacher Who Expounds the World," named "Caitya," and named "Transcendent from the World."

He is named "Untainted by Worldly Dharmas," named "Victorious over the World," named "Sovereign of the World," named "Greatness of the World," named "Reliance of the World," named "One Who Has Reached the Further Shore of the World," named "Lamp of the World," named "Supreme of the World," named "Venerable of the World," named "Benefactor of the World," and named "Conformity."
He is known as the one by whom all worlds are fully understood; he is named the Lord of the World; he is named the Worthy One of the World;
he is named the Great Field of Merit; he is named the Most Supreme; he is named the Unequaled; he is named the Peerless; he is named the Ever-Right and Real;
he is named the One Abiding in the Equality of All Dharmas; he is named the Attainer of the Path; he is named the Revealer of the Path.
This is called the speaker of the Path; it is called transcending the realm of Māra;
it is called being able to subjugate Māra; it is called being born from birth-and-death to attain cool serenity; it is called departing from the darkness of ignorance;

it is called being free from doubt; it is called being free from afflictions; it is called being free from longing and seeking; it is called the removal of all delusions of view; it is called liberation.
He is named Pure; he is named Free from Greed; he is named Free from Hatred; he is named Free from Delusion; he is named One Who Has Exhausted the Outflows;
he is named Purity of Mind-Liberation; he is named Purity of Wisdom-Liberation; he is named Knowledge of Past Lives; he is named Great Naga;
he is named One Who Has Accomplished What Was to Be Done; he is named One Who Has Laid Down the Heavy Burden; he is named One Who Has Attained His Own Benefit; he is named Far-Going.
Being free from the fetters of birth and death is called the mind of right knowledge being well-liberated;

it is called having well-attained the further shore of mastery over all minds; it is called having attained the further shore of giving, the further shore of morality, the further shore of patience, the further shore of diligence, the further shore of meditative concentration, and the further shore of wisdom.

The perfection of wisdom is called the fulfillment of vows; it is called abiding in great loving-kindness, abiding in great compassion, abiding in great sympathetic joy, and abiding in great equanimity;
it is called diligent gathering of sentient beings, attaining unimpeded eloquence, acting as a great refuge for the world, great wisdom, and the practice of mindfulness, wisdom, and awakening.
Accomplishment is called attaining right mindfulness, right exertion, and the supernormal powers of the bases of psychic power;
it is called the five faculties, the five powers, and the factors of enlightenment;
it is called crossing the great ocean of birth and death, dwelling on the other shore, dwelling in tranquility, attaining the state of peace, and attaining the state of fearlessness.
He is named the Subduer of the Mara of Afflictions; he is named the Lion among Men; he is named Free from the Fear of Horripilation;
he is named Immaculate; he is named the Knower; he is named the Attainer of the Threefold Knowledge; he is named the One Who Has Crossed the Four Rivers.

He is called a Kṣatriya because he upholds the caityas; he is called a Brāhmaṇa because he is far removed from all defilements and stains; he is called a Bhikṣu because he has destroyed the storehouse of ignorance; he is called a Śramaṇa because he has transcended attachment; he is called a Purified One (Śuddha) because he has exhausted all outflows (āsrava); he is called a Greatly Powerful One (Mahābala) because he possesses the ten powers; he is called the Bhagavat because he has cultivated body, speech, and mind; and he is called the King of Kings because he is the Dharma King.
It is called the turning of the supreme wheel of Dharma; it is called benefiting sentient beings; it is called the unchanging and indestructible teaching of the Dharma;
it is called attaining the station of omniscience; it is called the accomplishment of the seven jewels of enlightenment;

it is called obtaining the realm of the jewels of all dharmas; it is called being gazed upon by the assembly; it is called the ability to subdue those who have not yet been subdued; it is called the virtuous...
He is able to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas;

he is named "Attainer of the Seven Purified Treasures," named "Accomplisher of All Happiness," named "Renouncer of Everything According to Every Wish," named "Bestower of Peace and Bliss upon All Sentient Beings," named "Holder of the Supreme Vajra Wisdom," named "Universal Eye," and named "One Who Sees All Dharmas Without Obstruction."
Samantabhadra performed great supernormal powers: the one named Expounding the Great Dharma, the one named Unsatiated by Any World,
the one named Radiance of Great Purity, the one named Intimate to All Worlds, the one named Knowing the Vessels of Sentient Beings, the one named Great Adornment,
the one named Surrounded by Learners and Non-learners, the one named Universal Illumination, and the one named...
Great Banner King, named Universal Radiance, named Great Light Shining Everywhere, named Unmixed in Response to All Interrogations,
named Non-discriminative, named Light Shining Universally, named the Luminous Field of the Prajñāpāramitā— Profound, Difficult to Know, Difficult to See,
and Difficult to Understand, named Great Brahmā, named Tranquil Majesty.

His deportment was named "Accomplishing All Supreme Practices," "Upholding Sublime Form," "Inexhaustible to Behold," "Tranquility of the Faculties," "Perfection of Provisions," "Attainment of Flexibility," "Attainment of Supreme Tranquil Flexibility," "Treasury of Subdued Faculties," "Like a Tamed Elephant King," and...
Like a pure pond;
because he is endowed with the thirty-two marks, he is named "Permanently Severing All Habitual Tendencies and Obstructions";

because his body is adorned with the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), he is named "Supreme and Unsurpassed Sublime Color"; and because he is a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) and a Charioteer of Men (*purūṣadamyasārathi*), he is named [the fourth].
Because he is fearless and fully perfected in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans;

because he has accomplished all tasks, his actions of body, speech, and mind are beyond reproach; because he has perfected the pure wisdom of all marks (lakṣaṇa), he is said to dwell in emptiness (śūnyatā-vihāra);
and because he is skillfully able to realize the equality of the nature of all dependent origination, he is said to dwell in signlessness (animitta-vihāra).
Because one is free from attachment regarding all wishes and desires, it is called the dwelling of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vihāra*);

because one has abandoned all objective spheres (*viṣaya*), it is called effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*); because it is the realm of wisdom characterized by the markless nature of the *tathatā*-dharmadhātu which is like space, it is called speech that is true, not false, and not otherwise;
and because one contemplates [all things] as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, or water [in a mirage].

Because it is like a mirror reflecting the resonance of the moon’s valley, it is called *śrāmaṇya*; because it tames sentient beings with every step raised and lowered, its movements do not pass in vain;
because it severs all ignorance, afflictions, and craving, it is the City of Dharma;
because it is the cause of *nirvāṇa*, seeing or hearing it brings benefit; and because it transcends the desire realm, it is called "emergence."

Because it transcends the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is called "the crushing of the banner of Māra"; because it transcends the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is called "the raising of the banner of wisdom.
Because it is the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body, it is called "the jewel of boundless merit that surpasses all worlds.
Because the flowers of wisdom bloom to achieve the fruit of liberation, it is called a "great tree," for it is difficult to encounter.
He is named Udumbara Flower because all that is sought according to one’s heart’s wishes is fully realized; he is named King of Maṇi Jewels because he accomplishes all karmic actions;
and he is named Webbed Hands and Feet because he has perfected all deeds.

Because he has firmly upheld and maintained the holy life (*brahmacarya*) throughout the long night without wavering, he is said to have the mark of being adorned with the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet.

Because throughout the long night he has provided offerings according to the Dharma to his parents, elders, and those worthy of offerings; because he has acted as a protector for the helpless and refrained from taking life, he is said to have long fingers and toes.

Having vowed not to kill throughout the long night, he expounds upon the merits of non-killing and exhorts all sentient beings to refrain from killing; because he protects and rescues all sentient beings, his hands and feet are soft and supple.

Throughout the long night, he made offerings to his parents and served those who were venerable and worthy of honor; with ghee and oil he moistened their bodies, personally anointing and massaging them with joy and without weariness—this is called having webbed hands and feet.
Because he was well able to gather in sentient beings through giving, kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation throughout the long night, his soles are flat and level.
Because he constantly increased the most excellent dharmas throughout the long night, the hairs of his body curl to the right and point upward.

Throughout the long night, he personally maintained, repaired, made offerings to, and swept the stūpas of the Tathāgata; upon hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, his hair stood on end and he conceived a sense of wonder. Furthermore, he expounded the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and because those who heard the Dharma conceived a sense of wonder, he was named "The Calf Like the King of the Eneya Deer."

Because he has, throughout the long night, heard the True Dharma, upheld it, recited it, and practiced according to its teaching; because he explains it for others and skillfully understands the meaning of profound phrases and meanings; because he acts as a refuge for sentient beings suffering from old age, illness, and death; and because he expounds the wondrous Dharma without giving rise to contempt—he is called "having the private parts concealed."

Because throughout the long night he has venerated śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas by giving them robes, manifested the virtues of the brahmacarya, displayed the ten wholesome paths of action, possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame, and taught others to practice with firm resolve—due to such deeds, his arms are long and well-proportioned.

Because throughout the long night he has not harmed sentient beings, and his actions of body, speech, and mind have been conjoined with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), his body is said to be like a *nyagrodha* tree.

Because throughout the long night he has always known the proper measure in eating—neither too much nor too little—and because he provides various medicinal decoctions to the sick, constantly gives rise to compassion for inferior sentient beings, repairs ruined stupas and constructs new ones, and bestows fearlessness upon those who are terrified, his body is said to be supple and lustrous.
Throughout the long night, they have made offerings to their parents, teachers, elders, and those worthy of offerings;

they have anointed their bodies with ghee and oil, provided them with warmth and coolness, bathed them, and burned incense for them; they have bestowed excellent dwellings, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites to bring them peace and security;
and they have sprinkled scented water and swept the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata, as well as...
Because they adorned Buddha-stūpas with incense, flowers, banners, streamers, and precious canopies, they were named "True Golden Color.

Throughout the long night, they did not harm or afflict sentient beings, constantly cultivating loving-kindness and patience, and exhorted all sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome paths of action.
They fashioned images of the Tathāgata and constructed stūpas and temples out of gold, or depicted the Tathāgata using golden pigments.
Because they have scattered powdered gold over Buddha images and stūpas, or adorned Buddha stūpas and Buddha images with banners,
streamers, and precious canopies, or bestowed clothing and food upon sentient beings,
each and every pore and each and every hair-follicle is entirely lustrous, distinct, and clearly manifest.
He has, throughout the long night, constantly associated with the wise, inquiring as to which dharmas are unwholesome and which dharmas are not unwholesome.
Which dharmas are to be cultivated?
Which dharmas are not to be cultivated?
Which dharma is supreme?
What dharmas are middling?
What dharmas are inferior?
One selects those that are wholesome and practices them; furthermore, because of sweeping and sprinkling the Buddha-stūpas, these are called the "seven high points."

Throughout the long night, he has made offerings to his parents, as well as to those worthy of offerings—śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—and to all whom one should honor. To the poor and lowly who have any desire or need, he has given according to their wishes: clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites. Furthermore, because he has cultivated gardens, ponds, groves, and wells to provide for those in need, it is said that the upper part of his body is like that of a lion.

Because throughout the long night he has constantly been able to provide offerings and pay respect to his parents and those worthy of offerings, and because he has never looked down upon or deceived the poor and lowly but has always given rise to compassion for them—due to such firm resolve and power that he does not abandon these practices—he is said to have "non-protruding ankle bones."

Because throughout the long night he has constantly examined his own faults without accusing others of their shortcomings, and because he has forever abandoned strife and conflict such that his physical, verbal, and mental actions are always pure, he is said to have shoulders that are level and full.

Throughout the long night, he has harbored a heart of reverence toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, welcoming them when they arrive and seeing them off when they depart; he is well-versed in all teachings and has attained fearlessness; he instructs those engaged in disputes so that they may cease their contention; furthermore, he teaches kings, ministers, officials, and all sentient beings to cultivate loyalty and filial piety. Because he causes them to practice wholesome deeds and increase the Buddha-dharma, he is named Siṃhahanu (Lion’s Jaw).

Throughout the long night, in accordance with the various desires of all sentient beings, he bestows everything upon them and comforts them with kind words, causing them all to rejoice; his power of aspiration is thus firm and steadfast—this is called "possessing forty teeth."

Because throughout the long night he refrained from double-tongued speech and strife, and because wherever there was strife he reconciled both sides so that each might be joyful, his teeth are called neither sparse nor missing.

Because throughout the long night he constantly cultivated wholesome deeds and remained far removed from unwholesome dharmas, and because he constantly bestowed milk, curd, and pure clothing upon sentient beings, smeared Buddha-stūpas with white clay as mortar, swept and wiped them clean, and made offerings of various white flowers to the stūpas—it is by virtue of such merits as these that his teeth are called white, even, and closely set.

Because the speech uttered throughout the long night causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy and happiness, because he does not seek out the faults of others but maintains an impartial mind, and because he exhorts all sentient beings to expound the True Dharma, he is said to have attained the supreme flavor among all flavors.

Throughout the long night, he does not afflict sentient beings; for those suffering from illness, he provides medical treatment according to their needs; and whatever fine foods they seek, he gives them as they wish without a single thought of stinginess—therefore, this is called the Brahma-voice.

Because throughout the long night he has refrained from false speech, harsh speech, and malicious speech; because he constantly dwells in the four Brahma-abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and because he preaches the Dharma to sentient beings with a gentle voice so that they all give rise to a heart of joy, his eyes are called deep blue in color.

Throughout the long night, he has always shown reverence toward his parents, teachers, and elders; he regards all sentient beings as if they were his only child; whenever anyone comes to him with a request, he constantly gives rise to compassion; and he exhorts all sentient beings to contemplate the images of the Buddha and its stūpas. For these reasons, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.

Because for a long night his mind has not been inferior and his intention is always vast; because he exhorts all sentient beings to cultivate the unsurpassed Dharma; because he remains free from frowning and is constantly smiling; and because he approaches virtuous friends first with words of comfort and encouragement—he is said to have a "vast tongue."

Because throughout the long night he has remained far removed from all faults of speech, constantly praising the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, and all Dharma-preachers; and because he has upheld, recited, transcribed, and explained the scriptures for others, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, he is named "The Uṣṇīṣa Whose Crown Cannot Be Seen."

Because throughout the long night he prostrated before his parents, various venerable ones, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; because he anointed their feet with fragrant oils and shaved their hair for them; and because he tied flower garlands upon the heads of all who came to him—therefore, he is named "The Pure Radiance of the Right-Spiraling Ūrṇā between the Eyebrows."
"Throughout the long night, they constantly keep their doors open for great giving, universally inviting all sentient beings to receive whatever they desire;
they also exhort sentient beings to practice such giving, draw near to virtuous friends without ever abandoning them,
seek the Dharma with reverence for their teachers without shrinking from hardship or weariness of mind, and [regard] the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas..."
Before the Tathāgatas, parents, and teachers and elders, they burn lamps with various fragrant oils and fashion exquisite,
upright images of the Tathāgata, adorning them with wonderful jewels. Furthermore,
they place white jewels between the eyebrows to manifest the marks and signs of a Tathāgata, exhorting all sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta and causing them to practice it.

Because of immeasurable virtuous practices, he is named "Attainer of Great Power," named "Accomplisher of Nārāyaṇa Strength," named "Accomplisher of the Tathāgata’s Fearless Power of Vow," named "One Whose Teaching of the Dharma is Unconfused," named "Awakened to the Ineffable," named "One Whose Power of Vow Can Cause All Sentient Beings to Understand According to Their Own Kind," and named "The Immeasurable."
Losing mindfulness is called having no divergent thoughts; it is called knowing the minds of all sentient beings as they truly are;

it is called relinquishment through non-analytical cessation; it is called the uninterrupted practice of desire-samādhi; it is called non-retrogression in vigor; it is called non-retrogression in mindfulness;
it is called non-retrogression in wisdom; it is called non-retrogression in liberation; and it is called non-retrogression in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Retreat" means emerging from wisdom; "all actions of body, speech, and mind follow the movement of wisdom";

it is called being unimpeded by the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the past, present, and future; it is called attaining unimpeded liberation (*asaṅga-vimokṣa*); it is called skillfully entering into the conduct of sentient beings;
it is called preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate; and it is called being well able to transcend the other shore of all characteristics of sound.

It is named "Skillfully Responding to All Diverse Sounds," named "Kalaviṅka Voice," named "Celestial Drum Sound," named "Celestial Music Sound," named "Earth Greatly Trembling Sound," named "Great Ocean King Sound," named "Great Dragon King Sound," named "Great Cloud Sound," and named "Sounds Accordant with the Various Classes of Sentient Beings."
He is named "The Unattached and Unimpeded One Who Inspires Joy in All Assemblies"; he is named "The One Honored by the Heavenly Kings Brahmā and Śakra";

he is named "The One Whom Asuras, Kiṃnaras, and Mahoragas Gaze Upon with Joyful Minds, Never for a Moment Ceasing to Behold Him"; he is named "The One Served by the Assembly of Śrāvakas"; and he is named "Bodhisattva."

He is revered and praised by the multitude; his preaching is called "teaching without expectation," his teaching of even a single word or phrase is called "never being in vain," and his preaching of the Dharma is called "timely."
"Maitreya!
I have now briefly explained the merits of the Tathāgata; were I to explain them in detail, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Without location and without conceptual proliferation, without arising and without cessation,
its essence is empty and tranquil— thus does he turn the wheel of Dharma.
Neither emerging nor entering, without cause and without marks.”
All phenomena are equal; thus he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Like dreams, illusions, and mirages, like the moon in water and echoes in a valley, they all lack intrinsic nature; thus he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Entering into the dharma of causes and conditions, neither annihilated nor eternal,
far removed from all evil views, he turns such a wheel of Dharma.
Far removed from non-existence, it is neither the Dharma nor the non-Dharma.
Fundamentally unborn and unceasing, he turns such a wheel of Dharma.
The reality-limit is not a reality-limit; true thusness is not true thusness.
Revealing the essential nature of all phenomena, he turns such a wheel of Dharma.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, And mind are all unreal;
Their nature is empty and without thought— Thus does he turn the wheel of Dharma.
By means of this wheel of Dharma, He awakens those who have not yet awakened.
The essential nature of all phenomena, I have personally realized for myself;
not awakened by another, I am called a "Self-Become One" (Svayambhū).
Having attained mastery over all dharmas, I am therefore called the Dharma King.
Knowing what is reasonable and knowing what is unreasonable, he is therefore called the Guide.
Teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate, he transforms and educates all living beings.
Being able to reach the further shore, he is therefore called the Teacher.
For those who have lost their way, you proclaim the Dharma of reality;
leading them to the further shore, you are thus called the Unsurpassed Teacher.
Through the four means of integration and wisdom, you universally gather all the worlds.
Having transcended the dense forest of birth and death, he is therefore called the Caravan Leader.
Being unimpeded regarding all phenomena, he is therefore called the Sovereign of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of the True Dharma, he is therefore called the Dharma King.
He is named the Great Teacher and the Upholder of the Dharma;
he is named the Unsurpassed Lord of the Dharma, and also named the Lord of Great Virtue.
He is also named the One Whose Vows and Precepts are Fulfilled, and also named the Bestower of Fearlessness; he is also named the One Who Reveals Nirvana.
It is also called "Able to Subjugate," also called "Able to Self-Liberate," and also called "Able to Awaken the Mind.
This is the great radiance of wisdom.
Universally illuminating all things, He shatters the darkness of ignorance and acts as the King of Physicians for the world.
Able to eliminate the disease of afflictions and skillfully extract the arrows of poison, He is named the Unsurpassed Guide.
Possessing the thirty-two marks, Complete with the eighty minor characteristics,
Every part of his body is subtle and wondrous, In accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
With the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, And the eighteen unique qualities—
The Great Vehicle’s Supreme Sage possesses such majestic power;
The unsurpassed wheel of the True Dharma and the Tathāgata’s supreme merits—
Were one to wish to explain them in detail, even an eon would not suffice to exhaust them.
The Buddha’s wisdom is without limit, as vast and expansive as empty space.
*Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Ten; *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Twelve.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlabhadra of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Two: Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
After the Tathāgata had finished converting the five men, he thought to himself:
"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa has great renown; together with five hundred disciples, he is served by kings and honored by ministers and commoners. I should go to him and instruct him in the True Dharma."
He immediately went to seek him out.
When Kāśyapa saw the Buddha, he stepped forward to greet him and inquire after his well-being:
"Are you dwelling in peace and security?"
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to Kāśyapa:
"Freedom from illness, contentment, tranquility, and pure faith—these constitute peace and security.
Kāśyapa then entreated the Buddha:
"The sun is already setting; I only wish that the Śramaṇa would deign to remain here, staying wherever he pleases.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "I wish to stay overnight in this stone chamber."
Kāśyapa said, "I do not begrudge it;
rather, there is a venomous dragon in my chamber, and I fear he might offend you.
This was repeated three times, and Kāśyapa replied:
"Rest within this middle space.

At that time, having washed his hands and feet, the Tathāgata entered the stone chamber, spread out his seat, and sat down. The dragon then became enraged and emitted smoke from its body; the Buddha also emitted smoke.
The dragon became even more violently enraged and emitted fire from its body; the Buddha also emitted fire. The two fires blazed together, burning the stone chamber.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw that the entire chamber was ablaze;
struck with alarm and lamenting, he thought: "This Great Śramaṇa is so handsome and noble, yet he did not heed my words and has been destroyed by fire."
He immediately ordered his disciples to each take a jar and draw water to extinguish the fire; however,
all the water in the jars was transformed into fire, leaving the master and his disciples even more terrified as they all said,
"The dragon-fire has killed this śramaṇa."
At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, subdued the venomous dragon and placed it within his alms bowl. The next morning, he emerged carrying the bowl containing the dragon.
Kāśyapa was greatly amazed at this unprecedented marvel and thought:
"Has this śramaṇa now brought the dragon back to life?"
"What is inside the vessel?
He saw that it was a venomous dragon.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I have already subdued him and caused him to receive the prohibitive precepts.
Kāśyapa was deeply ashamed and looked toward his disciples, saying,
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses supernatural power, he is not equal to me who has attained the path of an arhat."

At that time, the Tathāgata moved closer to where Kāśyapa resided, staying beneath a tree. During the night, the Four Great Heavenly Kings all came to listen to the Dharma; their radiance was so intense it was like great torches of fire. Seeing this at night, Kāśyapa thought the Buddha was performing fire rituals.
The next morning, he said to the Buddha,
"In the Dharma of the śramaṇas, is there also the practice of worshipping fire?
The Buddha replied:
"No," he replied.
"Last night, the Four Heavenly Kings came down to listen to the Dharma; that was their radiance.
Later, when Śakra descended to listen to the Dharma, his radiance became even more intense.
The next day, Kāśyapa asked again:
"Does the śramaṇa also worship fire?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so; this is Śakra coming to listen to the Dharma.
Later, when the Brahmā King descended to listen to the Dharma, his radiance became even more magnificent.
The next day, Kāśyapa asked again:
"Does the śramaṇa also serve the fire?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. This is simply the Brahma King who has come to listen to the Dharma.

Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples each maintained three sacrificial fires; when they wished to kindle them in the morning, the fires would not catch. They marveled at this and questioned their teacher.
The teacher said,
"This is because of what the śramaṇa has done.
They came together to question the Buddha.
"I have been tending my sacrificial fire, yet it will not ignite," he said.
The Buddha asked,
"Do you wish for it to ignite?"
"Let it be lit!
and the fire was immediately kindled.

Once it had been lit, Kāśyapa attempted to extinguish it but could not; even when his five hundred disciples assisted him in trying to extinguish it, they were likewise unable to do so. Each of them thought to himself:
"This must be the work of a śramaṇa.
Together they went to question the Buddha:
"The fire has already been ignited and now cannot be extinguished."
The Buddha said:
"Do you wish for them to be extinguished?
I shall cause them to attain extinction."
The fire was immediately extinguished.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the Śramaṇa [will accept my invitation]!"

"May you dwell here permanently to practice the holy life together with me; I shall command my household to provide for your needs, and every day at the proper time, I shall invite the Buddha and his company to come to my home for a meal."
The Buddha said, "You may go on ahead; I shall follow shortly.

As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha used his supernatural powers to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to take celestial fruits; he went east to Pūrvavideha to take āmalaka fruits; south to Jambudvīpa to take jambu fruits; west to Aparagoyānī to take harītakī fruits; and north to Uttarakuru to take naturally grown non-glutinous rice. He placed these in his alms bowl and returned through the air, arriving before Kāśyapa and sitting upon his bed.
Kāśyapa arrived later and asked the Buddha,
"By which path did you come, śramaṇa?
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"After you have departed, I shall go to the four quarters and up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to fetch these famous fruits and delicious rice; you may eat them.

At that time, the king, ministers, officials, and subordinate functionaries, as well as elders, householders, and brahmins of the kingdom of Magadha, were attending a seven-day assembly held by Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"The majesty and virtue of that great śramaṇa are towering and his marks and signs are unsurpassed; when the multitude see him, they will surely abandon me to serve him."
"It would be better if this śramaṇa did not come to my place for seven days.
Knowing his thought, the Buddha remained hidden and did not appear.
When the seven days had passed, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"The festival has concluded and there is a great abundance of leftover food; if that great śramaṇa comes now, I shall provide him with a meal.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, arrived there suddenly.
Kāśyapa was filled with surprise and asked,
"Why has the Tathāgata abandoned me for seven days?
The Buddha said:
"Because you previously gave rise to a thought, he did not appear; now that you have remembered him, he has returned.

At that time, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples were about to perform a fire sacrifice and were all splitting wood together. Each raised their axe, yet none could bring it down. Alarmed, they informed their teacher, who said:
"This is merely because of the doing of that Great Śramaṇa."
He immediately went to ask the Buddha, "My disciples were just now splitting firewood together; each raised their axe, yet none could bring it down.
The Buddha said:
"Cut it now! At these words, he immediately brought the axe down.
Once it had descended, the axe-head became stuck fast to the wood and could not be lifted.
He came again to question the Buddha, who said, "You may go;
it shall lift itself up. At that very moment, it was lifted up.

"The Nairañjanā River flows swiftly with the force of a rushing arrow; by his supernormal power, the Buddha caused the water to surge up above the height of a man, so that as he walked beneath it, dust rose with every step."

Kāśyapa looked from afar and, fearing that the Buddha might be drowning, immediately boarded a boat with his disciples to rescue him. Seeing the water surging up as the Buddha walked beneath it, with dust rising at every step, Kāśyapa called out to the Buddha:
"Śramaṇa!..."
"Would you like to board the boat?
The Buddha said,
"Very well!"
He then entered the water through the bottom of the boat, yet the boat remained without any leaks.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous, yet he is still not equal to me in the path of an arhat."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "You are not an arhat;
why do you act with such arrogance and claim to be an arhat?
Thereupon, Kāśyapa’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; filled with shame and trepidation, he prostrated himself.
"Now this Great Sage has indeed come to know my mind.
I only pray, O Great Sage!
May you accept me into your sublime Dharma and ordain me as a śramaṇa."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"Since you are an elder with many followers, and are one who is honored and revered by kings, ministers, and commoners, you should not disparage yourself now that you wish to study the Way; rather, you ought to deliberate upon this matter thoroughly with your disciples."
Kāśyapa said: "Excellent!
It shall be as the Holy One has instructed."
"However, it is not that my inner mind lacks resolve; I shall simply return and discuss this with my disciples.
Kāśyapa returned and gathered his disciples, saying:
"I have already gained faith and understanding in the Dharma of that śramaṇa; the path he has attained is the true and genuine one."
"I now take refuge; what is your intention?
The disciples replied, "We also wish to follow you in taking refuge."

At that time, Kāśyapa and his disciples removed their robes, took their fire-worship implements, and cast them all into the water. Together they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
“We and our disciples wish to become śramaṇas within the Noble Dharma.”
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he became a śramaṇa.

Kāśyapa’s two younger brothers—one named Nandika and the other named Gayā—each had two hundred and fifty disciples who previously resided by the water’s edge. Seeing the robes, ritual implements, and fire-worship paraphernalia of the various brahmins floating downstream, they were all struck with alarm and feared that their elder brother and his disciples had been harmed by someone.

He immediately set out with five hundred disciples, traveling upstream against the current. Seeing that his elder brother and the master’s disciples had all become śramaṇas, he was astonished and asked:

"My elder brother is now advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty; his wisdom is profound and far-reaching, and he is revered throughout the land. In my mind, I believed my brother had already attained arhatship. Why has he now abandoned his pure practice to emulate those śramaṇas? Is their path superior?"

Kāśyapa replied: "The Buddha-way is most excellent and its Dharma is unsurpassed. Since ancient times, I have never seen anyone whose spiritual powers and supernatural abilities equal those of the Buddha. His Dharma is pure and shall deliver immeasurable beings; he is able to teach and transform sentient beings through three matters:

first, the power of the Way and the transformations of supernatural abilities; second, wisdom that knows the minds of others; and third, skillfully understanding afflictions to prescribe medicine according to the illness."
Upon hearing this, the two younger brothers felt deep reverence in their hearts and looked toward their disciples,
asking, "What do you think?
The five hundred disciples spoke with one voice:
"We wish to follow the teacher's instruction.
They then all bowed their heads and requested to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus!
As soon as he spoke, their beards and hair fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they all became śramaṇas.

At that time, the Tathāgata, together with one thousand bhikṣus, went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and stayed beneath the trees in the forest. For the sake of his disciples, he at times manifested supernatural transformations, at times preached the Dharma, and at other times recited the precepts. Beholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, there was none who did not rejoice, and they all attained arhatship.

"At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī with the three brothers, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his two companions, as well as one thousand arhats, and arrived at the kingdom of Magadha."

At that time, King Bimbisāra had long heard that the Bodhisattva had attained the Way of Buddhahood; that his colossal body was sixteen feet tall and the color of purple-polished gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and fully possessed of the ten titles. He had realized knowledge and vision, accomplished the five eyes, and attained the six supernormal powers, such that Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings all served him.

"Now that you have entered my kingdom, my heart is filled with great joy. Originally, we made a mutual vow to attain Buddhahood together and deliver one another; you have not neglected me, but have followed my own wish.

He immediately issued an edict throughout the realm to cleanse and adorn the roads. The King mounted a precious chariot, with ministers and officials leading and following in front and behind, as a thousand carriages and ten thousand horsemen went out of the city to welcome the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One was near the city of Rājagṛha, sitting beneath a great tree in the Veṇuvana forest, surrounded by a community of one thousand bhikṣus. From afar, the king beheld the Buddha like the moon among the stars, like the sun first rising; he was like Śakra, and also resembled Brahmā dwelling in his celestial palace—majestic as a mountain of gold, towering and transcendent.

The king’s heart was filled with joy; he descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot. At a distance of five *vyāma*, he prostrated himself before the Buddha, announced his own name, and spoke these words:
"For a long time I have admired your venerable virtue, longing for you with deep reverence."
The Tathāgata then addressed the king with a Brahma-voice, consoling him and saying:
"Great King! Are the four great elements always at peace and secure?"
"Is it not exhausting to manage the affairs of men?
The King replied,
"By your protection, I have fortunately attained peace and security."
