At that time, King Bimbisāra and all his ministers and subjects, seeing Kāśyapa seated by the Buddha’s side, thought to themselves:
"Kāśyapa is an elder, a patriarch among the many seers; how could he have abandoned the Way to become a disciple of this Buddha?"
"Are you the teacher of the Buddha, or does the Buddha take you as his teacher?
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately addressed Kāśyapa with a verse:
“You have constantly made offerings to the mountains and rivers, Taking refuge in water, fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the various Brahmā deities;
Diligent and energetic from dawn until night, How long has it been since you began this service? Your mind has never known weariness or neglect.”
"The deities you worship—do they ever bestow blessings?
At that time, Kāśyapa replied in verse:
"Since I first began performing sacrifices, eighty years have already passed."
Wind, water, fire, and the Brahma heavens;
mountains, rivers, and the sun and moon—though one exerts constant diligence day and night, praying with an unwearied mind, ultimately nothing is gained;
only by meeting a Buddha does one find peace.
After these verses had been spoken, the king, his ministers, and the people of the land realized that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Arise; you should now manifest your arhat-like supernormal powers."

Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Kāśyapa immediately leaped into the air; fire issued from his upper body while water flowed from his lower body, or water issued from his upper body while his body remained unmoistened, or fire issued from his lower body while his body remained unscorched. He flew through the void, appearing and disappearing seven times; he entered the earth as if it were water and walked upon water as if it were solid ground, passing through Mount Sumeru without any obstruction.

Before the Buddha, he vanished from the ground in the west and appeared in the east; vanished in the east and appeared in the west; vanished in the south and appeared in the north; and vanished in the north and appeared in the south.
Having performed these transformations, he returned before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am your disciple; the Buddha is my teacher."
The king, along with his ministers and subjects, once again acknowledged that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"Great King!
Form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Form is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped; feeling is like a bubble on the water that cannot endure long; mental formations are like the core of a plantain tree, lacking any solidity; perception is like a dream, a false and illusory vision; and consciousness is like a magical illusion, arising from inversion. The three realms are unreal; all things are impermanent.
"Great King!
How long has it been since this country first came into existence?
The king replied:
"This kingdom has existed for more than seven hundred generations.
"Do you know all the kings who have ruled it?
He replied:
"I know only my father.
The Buddha said:
"In this world, all things are but momentary; only the Way can be relied upon. You should cultivate merit for the future and not let your life pass in vain."
"Great King, you should know this!

Just as when a person is born, although their body arises because of their parents, it is not the parents who bring about the retribution of that birth; rather, whether one is good or evil, beautiful or ugly, is the result of one's prior karma."

If one performs various wholesome deeds, after the end of life, one will be born among devas and humans or before the Buddhas of the ten directions; if one performs various unwholesome deeds, after the end of life, one will be born in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal. All phenomena arise when conditions converge and perish when conditions disperse.

"Great King, you should know this: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise."

"Great King! With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; and with the cessation of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease."
"Great King!

The twelve links of dependent origination are entirely level and traceless, like empty space; their differentiation is fundamentally non-existent, and one thereby attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

When this Dharma was spoken, eighty-four thousand devas and humans were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye, and an immeasurable multitude gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"At that time, King Bimbisāra attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; filled with joy, he invited the Buddha, vowing to receive the five precepts. The ministers, officials, and all the people within the kingdom likewise took refuge in the Buddha and received the five precepts."
Having received the precepts, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

You were able to renounce the status of a Wheel-Turning King to leave the household life and pursue the Way. In the past, I ventured to invite you first, vowing that when you attained the Way, I would be the first to receive your deliverance. Today, my long-held vow has been fulfilled; fortunately, by the grace of the Buddha, I have attained the tracks of the Path. Although state affairs are numerous and pressing, I shall henceforth attend upon you more closely."
The king and his ministers circumambulated the Buddha three times, took their leave, and departed.
Once the king had reached the palace, the ministers offered their congratulations:
"None of the kings of antiquity have ever seen a Buddha; only Your Majesty has encountered a Tathāgata."
The King was even more delighted and further consoled his ministers, saying:
"By virtue of your past merits, you have now fortunately encountered the appearance of a Buddha in this world.

He then issued a decree to the ladies of the harem, the court beauties, and all the people within the realm, commanding them to constantly cultivate the fasts and precepts and to fully uphold the Dharma.

At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom of Magadha named Kalandaka. Seeing that the Buddha had entered the country but no monastery yet existed, he offered his excellent bamboo grove to the Tathāgata. He came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, you possess great compassion and pity for all beings as if they were your own father or mother. Having renounced worldly glory, you have now attained Buddhahood; yet, as there is no monastery, I offer this bamboo grove to the Tathāgata."
The Buddha then offered prayers of blessing and accepted it, constantly dwelling within it together with the assembly of sages.

At that time, the people of the kingdom of Magadha were numerous and prosperous, indulging in worldly pleasures; they clamored, sang, and danced day and night without ceasing. When the Buddha entered the country and transformed them with his Dharma teachings, they all observed the precepts, cultivated their minds, and abandoned their worldly pleasures.

The Buddha had a disciple named Śrāvastī who entered the city for alms with dignified decorum; his gait was calm and composed, and among the passersby, there were none who did not rejoice upon seeing him.
At that time, Śāriputra saw this śramaṇa and thought to himself:

"I have studied the Way for a long time and am somewhat familiar with the rules of propriety, yet I have never seen such a person; he must surely possess extraordinary learning, for his deportment is so refined."
"Go and ask what path he practices.
Thereupon, Śāriputra asked the bhikṣu,
"Who is your teacher?"
"I wish to hear of his resolve.
At that time, the bhikṣu replied in verse:
"My Teacher possesses all the marks and signs; He is the most honored in the three realms.
The five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination do not abide in either emptiness or existence.
I am still young in years, and my studies are yet not profound;
it is impossible through mere words to describe the various merits of the Buddha.
Having spoken these verses, he addressed Śāriputra:
"The teacher whom I serve is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans; his accumulation of merit and cultivation of virtue cannot be fully described."
Descending from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in Jambudvīpa, at the moment of his birth, he was able to take seven steps in each of the ten directions and, raising his hand, proclaimed:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored; I alone am the most supreme. I shall deliver all beings from the suffering and afflictions of the three realms."
“Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all come to serve him; the merits of the Buddha cannot be fully described.
When Śāriputra heard these words, it was as if he had beheld the light of the sun after being in darkness, and he said to the bhikṣu:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"In my youth I was fond of learning; at eight years old I followed a teacher, and by the time I was sixteen, there was nothing I had not mastered, leading me to consider myself enlightened.
Now that I have encountered the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, he is truly my teacher. As for the Buddha of whom you speak, where is he now?"
The bhikṣu replied, "He is currently at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery.
Then Śāriputra, leading his disciples, went to where the Tathāgata was; having prostrated at his feet and offered greetings, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have dwelt for a long night constantly treading upon folly and delusion; fortunately, having encountered the Buddha, I pray that you will open the path of correctness for me, so that I may become a śramaṇa and achieve the precepts.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"

His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; his outflows were exhausted, his mind was liberated, and he attained arhatship.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I and my fellow student Mahāmaudgalyāyana have made a pact that when we attain the Way, we shall certainly inform one another.
Now I wish to go there; I pray that I may receive your holy sanction.
The Buddha said:
"It is time to know that this is the moment.
Then Śāriputra entered the city of Rājagṛha to seek out Maudgalyāyana, and from afar he saw Maudgalyāyana wandering through the streets and alleys with his disciples.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana observed that Śāriputra’s appearance had changed and asked him in turn:
"What extraordinary vision have you seen that your countenance and attire have come to this?
He replied:

"In learning, there is no fixed teacher; one follows wherever the Way resides. Having sought the Dharma for many years without encountering a Great Sage, I am now filled with universal joy at having met you. Therefore, I have come to seek you, wishing to share in the flavor of the Dharma."
Maudgalyāyana replied, "This is no small matter; we must deliberate upon it together.
Śāriputra said:
"I have previously practiced alongside you and have fully mastered everything you have learned; please do not speak of it further.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra, "Virtuous one, your wisdom has always surpassed mine; how could the teaching you now give be in error?"
Having spoken these words, he followed Śāriputra to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“I have been far removed from the Great Sage and submerged in afflictions; now that I am able to serve you in person, I pray that you will allow me to become a śramaṇa.”
He immediately cast aside his water jar, deer-skin garment, and staff.
The Buddha said, “Welcome!”

His hair and beard fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; his outflows were exhausted, his mind was liberated, and he attained arhatship.
At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and their two hundred and fifty disciples all left the household life and became arhats.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that his son had attained the Way six years prior, was filled with profound joy and an ever-increasing thirst for him. He spoke to Udāyin, saying:

"You should now go and invite the Buddha to return to the kingdom to inquire after his well-being. It has been twelve years since we were parted; my grief day and night has been beyond restraint, and to see him once more would be like being born again."

Having received the King’s instruction, Udāyin went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and fully related the King’s intention. He then beheld the various devas, including Brahmā and Śakra, all coming to take refuge, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to become a śramaṇa.”
The Buddha said,
"Welcome! His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa, attaining the path of arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected thus:

"I originally made a solemn vow with my father, the King, that once I had attained Buddhahood, I would return to my kingdom to deliver my parents; now that I have realized the Way of the Buddha, I have not violated my original vow."
He then said to the bhikṣu Udāyin:

"You should go there first and manifest your supernormal powers, performing the eighteen transformations so that they may know my Way has been perfected. If even a disciple is thus, how much more so the majestic virtue of a Buddha?"

Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Udāyin flew through the air and returned to his native land. Above the city of Kapilavastu, he manifested eighteen miraculous transformations in mid-air; the king, his ministers, and the common people were all struck with awe and alarm.
Then Udāyin spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata is most rare, Difficult to encounter;
Through diligent practice over immeasurable kalpas, He has compassionately pitied all sentient beings.”
Having practiced the path of a bodhisattva in the past, you have now fulfilled your vows;
seated beneath the Bodhi tree, you have subdued the great enemy, Māra.
You have destroyed the causes of birth and death and extinguished all afflictions.
Having already attained perfect enlightenment, he expounds the unsurpassed Dharma.
Originally, by the King’s command, I left the country to welcome the Prince;
I spoke of the King’s long-standing sorrowful thoughts, and my words were most piteous.
The Buddha looked back toward his native land, intending soon to see his kinsmen;
I, then receiving the Buddha’s command, set out to enter Kapilavastu.
Taking leave of the Buddha, I exercised my supernormal powers and suddenly arrived at the place of the Great King.
Manifesting various transformations, like pure lotus flowers,
the royal father beheld these divine miracles and his heart was filled with great terror.
He inquired from whence they came, for he had never before witnessed such transformations.
"The Prince originally renounced his kingdom to seek the Way and deliver sentient beings;
after enduring immeasurable eons of diligent suffering, he has now attained Buddhahood.
O King, do not be alarmed or fearful; you should instead gladden your heart."
"I have already crossed over birth and death, serving as a messenger for the Prince, the King’s son.
When the King heard his son’s inquiry, tears fell from him like stars in the rain.
'For twelve years now, my grief and longing have been without end.'"
"Suddenly hearing that the Auspicious One has arrived, it is as if a dead man has been restored to life.
My son has renounced the throne; what is the name of the path he has realized?
At that time, I replied to the King:
"Through diligent toil he attained the Way, and is titled the God among Gods,
the foremost in the three realms.
"When my son was at home, I built for him various seasonal palaces, carved and adorned with intricate paintings."
"Where do you dwell now?
I then replied to the king:
"The Buddha has attained the subtle and wondrous Dharma; wherever he dwells, there is no lack of peace."
He always dwells beneath the trees, where the devas come to make offerings.
"When my son was at home, he sat and slept upon spread mats and cushions, all fashioned with exquisite embroidery; they were soft and lustrous."
I then replied to the king:
"The Naga Queen offered a precious bed; yet the Buddha’s mind is free from likes and dislikes, never showing joy or resentment."
"Abounding with various delicacies and sweet flavors— such as those served for your current meals—
what kind of food have you prepared?
At that time, I replied to the king:
“Carrying my bowl, I go for alms; may the merit for the multitude neither increase nor decrease.
I offer prayers for those who give, wishing them peace and security in every lifetime.
When my son was at home, may he always sleep in peace.”
As the strings sang forth pure tones, you then arose from sleep.
At that time, I replied to the King:
"The Buddhas have no sleep; Śakra always holds this in his heart."
"The Brahma King has come to offer encouragement and assistance.
"When my son was at home, he bathed with fragrant water, and its sweet scent filled the entire room."
"What kind of incense do you use now?
I then replied to the king:
"The eight liberations and the three gates of deliverance are the bath that washes away all defilements."
The mind is tranquil, free from sorrow and affliction, like the pure void.
"When my son was at home, he was anointed and perfumed with various fragrances;
he was pure and free from dust and filth, his scent intense and sweet."
I then replied to the king:
"Taking the Way and its Virtue as fragrance, it pervades the ten directions and the eight difficult realms,
reaching everywhere without exception."
"Four kinds of exquisite jewel couches, layered with cushions and rugs,
where one may rest and rise in peace and joy.
At that time, I replied to the king:
"Taking the four dhyānas as his seat, with mastery over the mind through meditative concentration,
he is unstained by the mud of afflictions, pure like a lotus flower.
When my son lived at home, his military guards were most formidable."
"In their coming and going, they shall always be protected, and their eyes shall not behold any evils.
At that time, I replied to the King:
"The Bodhisattvas are infinite in number; together they constitute the assembly of disciples."
Attended respectfully by those on his left and right,
with elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and chariots, he traveled throughout the four directions,
wandering and observing at will.
At that time, I replied to the King:
"With the five supernormal powers as my side-horses, I fly through the air without obstruction;
I see clearly into all hearts and traverse beyond birth and death."
"When my son was at home, banners and feathered guards were arrayed;
men holding various weapons served as his vanguard and retinue.
At that time, I replied to the king:
Universally rescuing all from calamities and hardships, with kindness, wisdom, benevolence,
and reverence as their solemn guard;
with bells and drums leading the way before them, accompanied by various musical performances.
"Those who gaze upon it always fill the streets.
I then replied to the King:
"Having attained perfect enlightenment at the Tree of the Path, I delivered the five Bhadravargīyas."
Eighty-four thousand devas have all attained the Dharma-eye;
the ninety-six kinds of paths have been subdued and brought to take refuge.
He beats the drum of immortality, its sound penetrating the three thousandfold world-system.
All who received the instruction attained clear awakening, and everyone was filled with joy. [They asked:
"In which kingdom does our son, the King, reside?
How vast or narrow is his domain?"
"How many people are there to be transformed?
Will they all submit and take refuge?
"The Buddha leads the trichiliocosm, Transforming and guiding all sentient beings."
Throughout the ten directions, beyond all counting, there is none who does not receive benefit.
"When my son was at home, he assisted me in governing and transforming the people;
he exhorted them with ritual propriety, and they followed him in obedience, none daring to disobey."
The Buddha has awakened to the emptiness of all phenomena and abandoned the four inversions;
there is none who does not submit and take refuge in him, for his activity is quiescent and unconditioned.
In the Buddha-dharma there is neither love nor hatred, and he has attained complete penetration of all things.
The transformation reaches all sentient beings, such that none fail to receive benefit.
Suppose there were a person who possessed immeasurable heads,
and each head had immeasurable tongues, and each tongue possessed inexhaustible eloquence.
If people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to spend eons as countless as the sands of the Ganges extolling a single merit of the Buddha, they would still be unable to exhaust it;
how much less could I, who am like a firefly’s glow, ever manifest the radiance of the sun?
When King Śuddhodana heard this verse, he exclaimed:
"Excellent!
The words of the seer Asita are not false."
He asked Udāyin,
"Does the Buddha wish to come?
Udāyin replied:
"Seven days from now, the Tathāgata shall arrive.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he addressed his ministers, saying, "I shall welcome the Buddha, and the protocol for my retinue and procession shall follow that of a Cakravartin King."

I have first commanded the relevant authorities to level the roads, sprinkle the ground with fragrant water, and suspend silk banners and canopies; every kind of adornment shall be prepared as is appropriate, for I shall go forty *li* outside the city to welcome the Tathāgata.

Udāyin said, "I originally came at the Buddha's command to report to Your Majesty. Now I request that you convey the King’s intent to the Buddha: that for many years he has been filled with longing to behold the Tathāgata, and that the myriad subjects likewise all hope for his blessings and protection."
The king said:
"Excellent! I pray that you may see the Buddha quickly."
Then Udāyin returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The king and the people of the country are counting the days and measuring the time, longing to see the Buddha. I have already informed the king that in seven days from now, the World-Honored One shall arrive.”

At that time, after seven days had passed, the Tathāgata, together with his disciples, adjusted his robes and bowls and proceeded toward the city of Kapilavastu with dignified and orderly deportment. Hearing that the Buddha was returning to his native land, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings all came to escort him. Brahmā attended on his right, Śakra attended on his left, and the Four Kings and various devas escorted him in front and behind. Devas, nāgas, and spirits scattered flowers, incense, and music as offerings; jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies were arrayed along the roadside, and the heavens rained fragrant water to sprinkle upon the ground.

When the Tathāgata wished to set forth, he first manifested auspicious signs: the three thousandfold world systems of the ten directions shook in six ways; all withered trees sprouted flowers and leaves once more, and the dried-up streams and ravines naturally flowed with springs.

Having witnessed these auspicious omens, the King issued an edict to the Śākya clansmen, the great ministers, and the officials, commanding them to solemnly carry banners and canopies, burn incense, scatter flowers, and perform various musical performances to welcome the Buddha.

From afar, the king beheld the Buddha amidst the great assembly, like the moon among the stars, like the sun first rising, or like a tree in full bloom; his body was sixteen feet tall, majestic and resplendent. Having seen the Buddha, grief and joy welled up within him simultaneously, and bowing his head in prostration, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Having been separated for many years, we are now able to meet again.
The ministers, the hundred officials, and all the people bowed their heads in prostration and followed the Buddha into the city.

At that time, as the World-Honored One’s feet crossed the threshold, the earth shook violently; the heavens rained down exquisite flowers and musical instruments sounded of their own accord. The blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the lame were able to walk, the sick were healed, the mute were able to speak, the insane returned to sanity, the hunched straightened themselves, and the effects of poisons naturally vanished.

The cries of birds and beasts harmonized with one another, their voices clear and resonant; as rings and pendants struck against each other, they all produced flowing melodies. Precious treasures appeared spontaneously from hidden stores, and those with divergent hearts were all brought into harmony. All sentient beings were free from lust, anger, and delusion; looking at one another, they regarded each other as fathers, mothers, elder brothers, younger brothers, sons, or even as themselves. The hells were stilled, the hungry ghosts were satiated, and animals, casting off their bodies, were destined for rebirth among humans or in the heavens.

The Father King beheld the Buddha’s colossal body, sixteen feet in height, the color of purple-polished gold, like the moon among the stars and also like a mountain of gold, with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings all attending upon him.

Seeing that the bhikṣus—who had formerly been non-Buddhists and had long practiced austerities until their bodies were emaciated—were attending upon him like black crows beside a mountain of purple gold, they could not manifest the virtues of the Tathāgata. He then commanded five hundred men from the noble and wealthy Śākya clan, who were handsome in appearance, to be ordained as śramaṇas to serve at the Buddha’s side, so that he would be like a garuḍa atop Mount Sumeru, or like a maṇi jewel placed in a crystal vessel.
The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda also became a śramaṇa. Nanda’s attendant, named Upāli, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

A human body is difficult to obtain and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter. Even those of noble and high status have all abandoned worldly glory; as for me, my status is lowly and humble—what is there to crave or delight in? Only through the Buddha’s compassion, I pray that you will grant me deliverance and allow me to become a śramaṇa.”
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa; he then took a seat among the bhikṣus according to the established order.
Nanda arrived later and performed his prostrations in due order; however, upon reaching Upāli, he stopped and did not prostrate, thinking to himself:
"This man is a servant of my household; it is not proper for me to offer him salutation."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda, saying:

"The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean, which accommodates the hundred rivers; the four currents flow into it and all become of one taste. Regarding the precepts, whether one is senior or junior does not depend on nobility or meanness. Because the four great elements combine, they are conventionally designated as a 'body. Within this, there is emptiness and stillness, fundamentally devoid of a self. You should contemplate the noble Dharma and not give rise to arrogance."
At that time, Nanda cast aside his arrogance and, with a humble mind, paid homage to Upāli; thereupon, the great earth shook for him.

Then the Buddha entered the palace and sat upon the throne; the king, ministers, and commoners daily provided him with a hundred kinds of sweet delicacies, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, delivering countless beings.
Yaśodharā, taking Rāhula—who was already seven years old—came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and after gazing upon him and exchanging greetings, she addressed the Buddha, saying:

"It has been a long time since we ceased our attendance and neglected our offerings. All the Śākya kinsmen harbor doubts: 'The Prince has been away from the kingdom for twelve years; how could he have conceived and fathered Rāhula?'"
The Buddha told the King, his father, and the assembled ministers:
"Yaśodharā maintains her vows with such purity and integrity that she is without blemish; if you do not believe me, I shall now provide proof."
At that time, the World-Honored One transformed all the bhikṣus so that they were all like the Buddha, their marks and signs and radiance being equal and without distinction.
Then Yaśodharā took her finger-ring and gave it to Rāhula, saying to him:
"Give this to him who is your father."
Rāhula took the ring and went straight forward to present it to the Buddha.
The king and his ministers were all filled with joy and exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"Rāhula is truly a son of the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the king, who immediately attained the Way. The ministers, the myriad commoners, and the ladies of the inner palace all received the precepts and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring life. At that time, the kingdom was peaceful and secure, and the nations of the ten directions came to offer congratulations.
Chapter 27: Entrustment. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, Nanda, Sunanda, and others, saying:

"O you devas! From the time the Bodhisattva first descended from Tuṣita to be born in Jambudvīpa, until his renunciation, his subduing of Māra and his adversaries, and his turning of the Wheel of Dharma—[all this has been accomplished]."
They have all provided their assistance.

Now they further entreat me to benefit the world by expounding such a Great Adornment Sūtra, concerning the conduct of Bodhisattvas, the realm of the Tathāgatas, and the playful mastery of sovereign spiritual powers.
If you are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this to others, this Dharma-seal of mine shall increase and spread.

Should those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle hear this sutra being preached, they will surely experience great joy and encounter what they have never known before; they will give rise to a mind of firm diligence and seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Therefore, your merit shall be immeasurable and beyond calculation.
"If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this sutra, join their palms in faith and acceptance, such persons shall obtain eight kinds of merit."
What are the eight? First, being handsome and of excellent complexion;

second, possessing powerful and flourishing strength; third, having a mind that is awakened and thoroughly penetrating; fourth, attaining eloquence; fifth, obtaining all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); sixth, having clear and lucid wisdom (*prajñā*); seventh, the excellence of leaving the household life; and eighth, having a powerful and flourishing retinue.

"If there are good men or good women who wish and desire to hear such sutras as these, and who prepare a high seat for the Dharma-preacher, they shall, upon changing their bodies, obtain eight kinds of seats."
What are these eight? First, the seat of a householder;

second, the seat of a lay devotee; third, the seat of a wheel-turning monarch; fourth, the seat of a world-protector; fifth, the seat of Śakra; sixth, the seat of Brahmā; seventh, the place where a bodhisattva sits when attaining awakening; and eighth, the place where a Tathāgata sits when turning the wheel of the true Dharma.
"If there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sutra and extol and praise it, these people shall obtain eight kinds of pure speech.
What are the eight? "
First, their words and deeds correspond with one another, for they are free from contradiction and contention;
second, what they say subdues the assembly, for it is worthy of being followed and upheld;
third, what they say is gentle and supple, for it is not coarse or harsh.
Fourth, his speech is harmonious and pleasing because it gathers in and sustains sentient beings;
fifth, his voice is like that of the kalaviṅka bird because it brings joy and delight to sentient beings;
sixth, his voice is like a deep thunderclap because it subdues and overcomes those of external paths.
Seventh, he attains the Brahma-voice, for it transcends the world;
eighth, he attains the Buddha-voice, for it accords with the faculties of sentient beings.
"If there are good sons or good daughters who transcribe this sutra and circulate it in the four directions, such persons shall possess eight treasuries of merit."
What are the eight?
First is the treasury of mindfulness, because of the absence of forgetfulness;
second is the treasury of wisdom, because of being well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena.
Third is the treasury of wisdom, because it can thoroughly understand the meanings of all sutras;
fourth is the treasury of dhāraṇī, because it can retain everything that is heard;
fifth is the treasury of eloquence, because it can inspire a heart of joy in sentient beings.
Sixth is the treasury of the true Dharma, for the purpose of guarding and protecting the Buddha-dharma;
seventh is the treasury of the bodhicitta, for the purpose of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed;
eighth is the treasury of practice, for the purpose of attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"If there are good sons or good daughters who read and recite this sutra, upholding its words and meanings without forgetting them, such persons shall attain eight kinds of perfection:
first, perfection of giving, because they are free from stinginess;
second, perfection of precepts, because they achieve the fulfillment of their vows."
Third is the perfection of extensive learning, because one attains unattached wisdom;
fourth is the perfection of śamatha, because all samādhis manifest before one;
fifth is the perfection of vipaśyanā, because one is fully endowed with the three types of higher knowledge.
Sixth is the perfection of merit, because he purifies the Buddha-fields by being endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
seventh is the perfection of sublime wisdom, because he fulfills the various inclinations of all sentient beings;
eighth is the perfection of great compassion, because he brings sentient beings to maturity without weariness.
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to this thought:
'How may I cause all sentient beings to enter this Dharma-gate?
and having formed this thought, explain it for others, they shall, by virtue of these roots of goodness, obtain eight kinds of vast merit."

What are these eight? First is the merit of a wheel-turning sage king; second, the merit of a world-protecting heavenly king; third, the merit of Śakra; fourth, the merit of the heavenly king of Yāma; fifth, the merit of the heavenly king of Tuṣita; sixth, the merit of the heavenly king of Nirmāṇarati; seventh, the merit of the heavenly king of Paranirmita-vaśavartin; and eighth, the merit of Mahābrahmā up to that of the Tathāgata.
"If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this sutra, believe it with confidence and do not oppose it, these people shall attain eight kinds of pure minds.
What are the eight? "
First, one attains the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because it bestows happiness upon sentient beings;
second, one attains the mind of great compassion (*karuṇā*), because it uproots the suffering of sentient beings;
third, one attains the mind of great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), because it extinguishes the grief and affliction of sentient beings.
Fourth, they attain the mind of great equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), because they extinguish the greed and anger of sentient beings;
fifth, they attain the mind of the four dhyānas, because they achieve mastery over the mind within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
sixth, they attain the mind of the four concentrations (*samādhi*), because they achieve mastery over the mind within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Seventh, they shall attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) because they travel to and fro among the Buddha-fields;
eighth, they shall be able to sever all outflows (*āsrava*) because they have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"In whatever land, city, town, or village this scripture may be found, know that such a place shall be free from the eight kinds of fear."
What are the eight? First, freedom from fear of hostile nations;

second, freedom from fear of thieves and robbers; third, freedom from fear of wild beasts; fourth, freedom from fear of famine; fifth, freedom from fear of litigation and disputes; sixth, freedom from fear of battle; seventh, freedom from fear of yakṣas; eighth, freedom from all fears.
"You should know this!

Even if the Tathāgata were to use his unimpeded eloquence in the perfections of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, to constantly preach the merits of this sutra day and night for an entire kalpa, he could not exhaust them."
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain it, you should know that the merit obtained by such persons is likewise inexhaustible.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, as well as the Elder Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, saying:

"For incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, I have cultivated the Buddha-way and have now attained the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have expounded this sutra; such sutras as these I entrust to you. You should receive and uphold them, and widely proclaim and disseminate them."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"With my Buddha-eye I observe, seeing all sentient beings completely.
Even if all these sentient beings were each like Śāriputra,"
If someone were, for hundreds of millions of eons, to offer various kinds of incense,
flowers, robes, bedding, and other requisites to such a multitude as this,
the merit they would thereby obtain would not equal that of a single day and night [of practicing the Dharma].
If one were to make offerings to a single Pratyekabuddha—
treating each exactly as one would a Pratyekabuddha— and if someone, throughout hundreds of millions of eons,
were to offer various kinds of incense, flowers, robes, bedding, and other requisites;
The merit obtained from making offerings to such a multitude as this is not equal to that gained by reciting "Namo Buddha" once with a pure mind.
Even if all those in the world were like the World-Honored Buddhas, [the merit would still not equal that of a single recitation].
If someone, throughout billions of eons, were to offer various incenses,
flowers, robes, bedding, and other requisites to all the Tathāgatas,
the merit they would thereby obtain would not equal that of a single person who—
One who is able to read and recite this sutra throughout the day and night—
should there be countless people who, for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas,
offer various kinds of incense, flowers, clothing, bedding, and other such things;
The merit obtained from making offerings as previously described to countless assemblies of śrāvakas,
to all pratyekabuddhas, and to those various Tathāgatas, is not equal to that of a single person—
Whoever upholds this sutra, even as much as a single four-line verse,
and explains it in detail for others—
for them this sutra is the most supreme among all the Tathāgatas.
All [teachings] emerge from this sutra.
Wherever this sutra dwells, there is a Tathāgata present.
To widely disseminate it everywhere, one need only expound a single phrase.
Throughout infinite kalpas, one’s merit and wisdom will naturally be adorned, becoming as full as the great ocean.
Those who hear this sutra should constantly practice it; their merit shall be immeasurable.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, Maheśvara, and all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, were all greatly delighted; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
